grupos.texto: WHAT: NewMetricsMiddleware captures a single shared *MetricsMiddleware (`imw`) and mutates `imw.next = next` inside the middleware factory, which is re-invoked on every request because Decorator rebuilds the chain per call. WHY: concurrent requests write/read `imw.next` without synchronization, causing a data race (flagged by -race) and the possibility that a request dispatches into another request's inner chain. HOW: build a fresh instance per chain, e.g. `return plugins.ClientMiddlewareFunc(func(next plugins.Client) plugins.Client { return &MetricsMiddleware{pluginMetrics: imw.pluginMetrics, pluginRegistry: imw.pluginRegistry, next: next} })`.

The HELP text for grafana_plugin_request_size_bytes says "histogram of plugin request sizes returned", but the metric only measures the request sent to the plugin: QueryData sums len(v.JSON) over the outgoing queries (lines 145-148) and CallResource passes len(req.Body) (line 161). Nothing "returned" by the plugin is observed. This HELP string is surfaced to users in Prometheus/Grafana metric descriptions, so it documents the opposite of the recorded value; it should describe the plugin request (egress) size, not a response size.

TestInstrumentationMiddleware still carries the old name even though this PR renamed the middleware under test to MetricsMiddleware (newMetricsMiddleware/NewMetricsMiddleware) and the file to metrics_middleware_test.go. The identifier advertises the superseded "InstrumentationMiddleware" name; rename it (e.g. TestMetricsMiddleware) so the test name matches the code it exercises.

The request-size assertion is entirely gated behind `if tc.shouldInstrumentRequestSize`, so the `shouldInstrumentRequestSize: false` cases (CheckHealth at line 45, CollectMetrics at line 68) verify nothing about request-size instrumentation. The case names claim request size must NOT be instrumented for those endpoints, yet the body makes no assertion for them. If a regression made CheckHealth/CollectMetrics call instrumentPluginRequestSize, CollectAndCount(metricRequestSize) would become 1 and this test would still pass. Add a negative assertion for the false cases, e.g. `require.Equal(t, 0, testutil.CollectAndCount(promRegistry, metricRequestSize))`.

`foundLabels` is declared outside the `for _, m := range metricFamily.Metric` loop and never reset per metric, and the code returns an error as soon as a metric has a matching label key with a different value (rather than `continue`-ing). The correct-metric decision therefore relies on state carried over between metrics and on a premature error return instead of an exact per-metric label comparison. With more than one series in a family this produces false failures and wrong "expected N labels, got M" counts. Reset the counter per metric and `continue` to the next metric when the label set does not fully match, instead of returning an error.
outros: WHAT: in checkHistogram, `foundLabels` is declared before the `for _, m := range metricFamily.Metric` loop and is never reset between metrics. WHY: the counter accumulates across metrics, so the `foundLabels != len(expLabels)` check is evaluated against a stale/inflated count — a metric with only a partial label match can be accepted (false pass) and a valid metric after a partial match can error (false fail), letting the metric assertions miss real regressions. HOW: move `foundLabels := 0` inside the outer loop (reset per metric).

grupos.texto: The migration to the contextual logger dropped the traceID field. Before this PR, logRequest explicitly appended "traceID" (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)) to logParams. The change moved pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID into the context (ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext) and logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx), but instrumentContext does NOT add traceID. Result: "Plugin Request Completed" egress log lines silently lose their traceID, breaking correlation between plugin request logs and traces. Fix by having instrumentContext (or the logParams here) also carry the trace ID, e.g. append "traceID", tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) in instrumentContext in contextual_logger_middleware.go, or re-add it to logParams here.
outros: LoggerMiddleware (logger_middleware.go:58) now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx) and relies on the context for all per-request attributes, but the middleware that replaced its enrichment (instrumentContext) re-adds only endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname. The traceID that logger_middleware.go previously appended itself (via tracing.TraceIDFromContext) is never put into the contextual logger, so the 'Plugin Request Completed'/grafana-data-egress line loses its traceID and log-trace correlation silently breaks. Add the trace id to the contextual attributes here (e.g. append 'traceID', tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) when non-empty) so the consumer's assumption holds.

The traceID key was dropped from logParams (along with the pkg/infra/tracing import) and is now expected to come from m.logger.FromContext(ctx). The only thing that populates that context is the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext, which adds endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname but never traceID. The metrics middleware in this same PR still has to read the trace ID explicitly (metrics_middleware.go:127), confirming it is not supplied by the logger itself. Restore an explicit "traceID", tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) entry in logParams, or have instrumentContext add the trace ID, otherwise 'Plugin Request Completed' logs lose trace correlation.

grupos.texto: The metric help text describes sizes "returned", but the observations measure incoming payloads: QueryData sums len(v.JSON) and CallResource uses len(req.Body), both before invoking the plugin. This description exposes request sizes as though they were response sizes to operators reading Prometheus metadata. Change the help text to describe incoming plugin request payload sizes.

The millisecond observations truncate the duration before converting it to float64: elapsed/time.Millisecond is integer division. For example, a 900µs request is recorded as 0ms and a 1.9ms request as 1ms, misclassifying observations against the fractional millisecond buckets declared above and understating the histogram sum. Use float64(elapsed)/float64(time.Millisecond) in both the exemplar and ordinary observation paths to preserve the actual duration.

The request-size cases pass an empty Body and no Queries, and subsequently check only that a histogram sample exists. Replacing either size calculation with a constant zero still passes this test. Use nonempty resource bodies and query JSON payloads and assert the histogram sample sum equals their expected byte count, so broken request-size instrumentation is detected.

Both duration metrics are checked only for labels and a nonzero sample count. Observing a constant zero, or feeding seconds into the milliseconds metric, still passes. Assert the observed durations using a controlled elapsed interval (or check the relationship between the two histogram sums with allowance for millisecond truncation) so the test detects broken duration values and units.

The shouldInstrumentRequestSize=false cases (CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) never assert that the request size metric is absent. If size instrumentation were wrongly added to those endpoints, the test would still pass. Add an else branch that requires testutil.CollectAndCount(promRegistry, metricRequestSize) to equal 0.

The traceID attribute that LoggerMiddleware used to add to "Plugin Request Completed" logs was removed and not re-added here. instrumentContext should append "traceID", tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) when it is non-empty, so these log lines keep their trace correlation.

WHAT: NewMetricsMiddleware reuses a single shared MetricsMiddleware instance and mutates imw.next on every CreateClientMiddleware call. WHY: Concurrent or multiple Decorator chains overwrite next on the same object causing data race and requests routed to the wrong next client, unlike Contextual/Logger middlewares that allocate per chain. HOW: Allocate a new MetricsMiddleware per chain (copy metrics handles, set next) instead of mutating the shared imw.

WHAT: logRequest dropped explicit pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID/traceID params and now relies solely on m.logger.FromContext(ctx) populated by upstream ContextualLoggerMiddleware. WHY: Creates hidden ordering dependency (requires Contextual before Logger in pluginsintegration.go:160-161); standalone/reordered use silently logs without plugin identity. HOW: Keep explicit fallback from req.PluginContext/tracing when ctx has no attributes, or document/enforce ordering.

WHAT: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh NewTestLogger instead of the receiver. WHY: LoggerMiddleware calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info so the write goes to a throwaway instance and assertions on the original TestLogger Calls/Message never observe it, diverging from real wrapper that preserves logger context. HOW: Return f (or a child sharing f) instead of NewTestLogger.
Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware but it constructs and asserts MetricsMiddleware (newMetricsMiddleware). Rename to TestMetricsMiddleware to match the renamed middleware.

Missing negative assertion: when shouldInstrumentRequestSize is false (CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) the test asserts nothing about grafana_plugin_request_size_bytes. If instrumentPluginRequestSize were incorrectly called for those endpoints, CollectAndCount would be 1 yet the test would still pass. Add else branch asserting CollectAndCount==0 / histogram absent.

Assertion too loose for duration-seconds: plugin_request_duration_seconds has labels source,plugin_id,endpoint,status,target but checkHistogram is called with only plugin_id,endpoint,target. A broken status or source label (e.g. wrong status mapping) would still pass. Require all 5 labels including status==statusOK and source==grafana-backend, and verify observed size values not just sample count.

Incorrect measurement: float64(elapsed/time.Millisecond) and float64(elapsed / time.Millisecond) do integer division before conversion, truncating all sub-millisecond durations to 0. Buckets start at 0.005ms so precision matters. Use float64(elapsed)/float64(time.Millisecond).

Best-effort metrics now fails the request: QueryData (and CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics via the same helpers) returns ErrPluginNotRegistered from pluginTarget/instrumentPluginRequestSize without calling next when the plugin is missing from the registry. Callers lose the previous contract that instrumentation never refuses the request. Fix: do not propagate registry miss as request error — default target to unknown/skip observation and always invoke next.
outros: WHAT: QueryData (and CallResource:161) abort the plugin call and return ErrPluginNotRegistered when instrumentPluginRequestSize/pluginTarget lookup fails. WHY: A best-effort observability lookup failure becomes a request failure, blocking the real plugin call that might have returned its own error. HOW: Log the target-lookup failure and continue to instrumentPluginRequest/next call instead of returning early.

grupos.texto: WHAT: QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics dereference req (req.PluginContext) without nil guard. WHY: Sibling LoggerMiddleware in same PR added explicit if req==nil guards, and direct middleware invocation with nil panics; inconsistent contract. HOW: Add same if req==nil passthrough guard before instrumentContext.
outros: QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics dereference req (req.Queries, req.Body, req.PluginContext) without the `if req == nil` guard that LoggerMiddleware uses. A nil request panics. Add nil guards forwarding to next like LoggerMiddleware does.

QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics read req.PluginContext without checking req == nil. A nil request panics before LoggerMiddleware's guard. Add `if req == nil { return m.next.<Method>(ctx, req, ...) }` guards.

goldens.comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

plugins-chore-renamed-instrumentation-mi.prTitle: Plugins: Chore: Renamed instrumentation middleware to metrics middleware

grupos.texto: Assertions that can never fail. `assert.Equal(t, obj, exampleObj)` compares the value the shared mock was configured to return (`m.On("Delete", ...).Return(exampleObj, false, nil)` at line 202) against that same fixture, so it restates the stub rather than exercising anything; `assert.NotEqual(t, obj, anotherObj)` compares against a different fixture value and is true for every possible return of `dw.Delete`, including `nil`. Either assertion would still pass if the storage call were removed and `nil, 0, nil` returned. The same pair (Equal-against-fixture + NotEqual-against-other-fixture) is repeated at lines 129-130, 183-184, 291-292 and 352-353 in the other tests. Assert something the code actually produces, e.g. that the name/argument passed through to the storage mock matches the input (`us.AssertCalled(t, "Delete", mock.Anything, tt.input, mock.Anything, mock.Anything)`) or assert on the returned error/async flag.

The legacy half of Mode 3 is never verified, so these tests cannot catch its removal. Mode 3 is documented as writing to BOTH LegacyStorage and Storage, and the implementation performs the legacy write in a detached goroutine (`go func(){ d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`, dualwriter_mode3.go lines 50-57, and likewise at 108-114, 134-141, 161-167). Each test registers legacy expectations (`setupLegacyFn`, e.g. lines 30-32 and 40-42) but never calls `m.AssertExpectations(t)`, `AssertCalled` or `AssertNumberOfCalls`, and never waits for or observes the goroutine — no channel, no polling. Additionally `legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `storageMock{m, s}` (lines 53-54, and the same pair in every other test function) share one `*mock.Mock`, so even a count assertion could not distinguish a legacy call from a storage call. Deleting every `d.Legacy.*` call from the implementation leaves all six tests passing, which is exactly the regression the names — and the Mode 3 contract — claim to cover.

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` installs the mode-level logger instead of the request-scoped `log` built on line 96 (which carries name, kind and method) — a copy/paste error, as every other method in this file passes the composed `log`. Storage.Delete and the legacy delete goroutine therefore log without the per-request fields this PR is adding (and without the metrics method/kind context).

The test-case name "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" still describes the old stub List (which returned nil, nil with a "List not implemented" log). List is now implemented at dualwriter_mode3.go:79 and delegates to Storage.List; the case merely checks that a Storage error is propagated. The name contradicts the code it now exercises — rename it, e.g. "error when listing objects in the unified store fails".

On a *storage* Create failure the storage-path timing is recorded with `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)` rather than `recordStorageDuration`; the same mistake is repeated for the Update storage-failure path (line 129) and even for the legacy delete-collection goroutine (line 166, which calls `recordStorageDuration`). The result is that the two duration series are swapped/misattributed for these paths, so any dashboard or alert consuming them will see legacy latency for failed unified-store writes and vice versa. The correct helpers already exist and are used correctly on the success paths (lines 48, 103, 156) — these call sites need fixing.
outros: On a Storage.Create failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) — the failing subsystem is Storage, not Legacy, and it passes the storage start time. This records storage failures under the legacy metric, corrupting the dual-writer error dashboards (and contradicts the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration). Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

On a Storage.Update failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), attributing a storage failure and its storage duration to the legacy metric. This is inconsistent with the success path on line 132 (recordStorageDuration) and with mode1's semantics. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

The async goroutine performing the LEGACY DeleteCollection measures it with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Every other legacy write in this file uses recordLegacyDuration (lines 56, 113, 140); recording it under the storage metric reports legacy latency/errors as storage latency/errors. Use d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

On the Storage.Create failure path the error duration is recorded with d.recordLegacyDuration, but the timed operation was d.Storage.Create (started at line 41). This attributes a unified-storage failure to the legacy datastore metric and leaves the storage-error metric unemitted, while the success path (line 48) correctly uses recordStorageDuration. Change line 45 to d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

In Update, the failing operation is d.Storage.Update (started at line 125) but the failure is recorded with d.recordLegacyDuration at line 129, whereas the success path at line 132 uses recordStorageDuration. The storage-error metric never fires and a legacy-error datapoint is fabricated. Line 129 should call d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

In DeleteCollection the goroutine invokes d.Legacy.DeleteCollection but records the result at line 166 with d.recordStorageDuration. The legacy operation is therefore counted as a storage operation (and the storage op at line 159 is double-counted), while legacy metrics stay silent. Line 166 should call d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...).

On the Storage.Create failure path the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` although the error came from Storage. The legacy write has not even been attempted here, so a storage failure is recorded as a legacy failure, mislabeling and hiding real storage errors in the legacy metric. Should be recordStorageDuration.

Same mixup in Update: the Storage.Update error path records `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` for a storage failure while the legacy goroutine is never launched. Update failures are attributed to the legacy back end instead of storage.

Inside the legacy goroutine of DeleteCollection the code records `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. A legacy DeleteCollection failure is written to the storage metric, misattributing the error. Should be recordLegacyDuration, matching the Create/Delete/Update legacy goroutines.

In the Storage.Create error path the duration of the *Storage* call is recorded with recordLegacyDuration; the function name says it measures the legacy store, so the legacy-duration metric receives unified-store timings (and the storage error path never increments the storage metric). Same mismatch at the Update error path (line 129). Use recordStorageDuration here so the metric name and the measured store agree.

Inside the Legacy.DeleteCollection goroutine the code calls recordStorageDuration with the timing of the legacy call. The name states it records the unified-store duration, but the value measured is the Legacy call's, so the storage series is polluted with legacy timings while the legacy series is never written. Should be recordLegacyDuration, matching the sibling Create/Delete/Update goroutines.

grupos.texto: The legacy write in Mode 3 became fire-and-forget, changing the contract callers relied on: previously Create (and, identically, Update/Delete/DeleteCollection) returned only after the LegacyStorage call had been made in-request; now it returns immediately and the write runs in a detached goroutine. Worse, the goroutine builds its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`), which the API server cancels as soon as the handler returns/flushes the response — so the legacy write and its 10s timeout will typically be cancelled outright and the legacy store silently stops being updated, which is precisely what the new mode-3 integration cases assume still happens. Any detached work must be given a context not tied to the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a server-lifetime context), and consumers that depended on the synchronous legacy write need to be updated.
outros: The async legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which is immediately after Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return — so the goroutine's Legacy.Create can be canceled before completing, silently dropping the legacy write that this mode exists to guarantee. The same applies to the goroutines at lines 108-114, 134-141 and 161-167. Detach the async context from request cancellation (e.g. derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) / context.Background()) before applying the timeout.

grupos.texto: The Delete success-path metric passes `name` where every other call site in this file (lines 48, 103, 113, 156, 159) passes options.Kind in the kind/name argument slot. The storage-success sample for Delete is thus labelled with the object name instead of the resource kind, breaking label consistency with the other operations and with the error sample emitted at line 103. Use options.Kind here (or insert name consistently everywhere, matching the metric's label semantics).
outros: recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) at line 106 passes the object name in the kind label slot.

recordStorageDuration is called with the object `name` as the `kind` label: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. Every other storage call site passes `options.Kind` (lines 73, 89, 103, 156, 159). This injects a per-object value into the kind label, corrupting the metric and giving it unbounded cardinality (one series per object name), which grows memory on every delete. Should be `options.Kind`.

grupos.texto: The test name says creation happens "only in the unified store", but this case configures a successful Legacy.Create as well, and Mode3.Create launches that legacy write after the unified write succeeds. Rename the case to describe creation in both stores (with the legacy write asynchronous), so test output does not communicate the opposite of the mode-3 write contract.

Independent goroutines remove ordering between successful writes to the same resource. For example, Storage commits update A and then update B, but the legacy goroutine for B can finish before A, leaving legacy with A while Storage contains B. Likewise a delete can run before an earlier create and leave a resurrected legacy object. Preserve per-resource commit order for mirroring (including across create/update/delete), rather than launching each write independently.

The legacy write is now asynchronous but still inherits the caller's request context. Once Create returns and the HTTP request completes, that context is canceled; WithTimeoutCause does not detach parent cancellation. Legacy.Create can therefore fail with context canceled despite a successful unified-store write. The same lifetime mismatch affects the new Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection goroutines. Detach cancellation while retaining request values before launching background work (and apply the bounded timeout to that context), or keep the writes synchronous.
outros: The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context, which is canceled when the HTTP request finishes. Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection return before this work completes, so their legacy database operations can be canceled immediately instead of receiving the intended ten-second window. Derive the bounded background context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to retain request values without inheriting request cancellation.

The background legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. Returning from the HTTP handler cancels that parent, so a legacy write that has not finished (or has not even started) receives cancellation despite the nominal ten-second timeout. Storage has already committed and the caller receives success, leaving legacy state missing or stale. Detach cancellation while preserving context values before launching background work, then apply the bounded timeout. The same issue affects Update, Delete and DeleteCollection.

grupos.texto: Legacy.Update previously received an updateWrapper containing the object returned by Storage.Update; it now receives the original objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute an update from the old object supplied by each backend (notably for patches), so evaluating it against a stale legacy object can produce a different result or reject an update that already succeeded in Storage. Preserve the canonical-result contract by passing an updateWrapper with updated: res and upstream: objInfo to the legacy consumer rather than replaying the original update against legacy state.
outros: Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo instead of the object successfully committed to unified storage. The playlist legacy implementation calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) against its own legacy object, so a patch is reapplied to potentially stale state and can persist a different result or fail rather than mirror the unified write. Pass an updateWrapper containing res, as the previous implementation did.

Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo rather than the updateWrapper containing the object successfully committed to Storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a patch/transform based on the supplied old object; replaying it against legacy's potentially different old state can persist a different result or fail, even though the authoritative update succeeded. Restore forwarding of the committed result via updateWrapper instead of recomputing the update against legacy state.

grupos.texto: The successful Storage.Delete measurement passes name instead of options.Kind, unlike the error path and other operation measurements. Use options.Kind consistently; successful and failed deletes otherwise land in different label series, with successful deletes split by individual object name.
outros: Successful Delete passes the resource name into the histogram's kind label. metrics.go retains a separate HistogramVec child for every distinct label set, so deleting uniquely named resources continuously grows process memory and exported metric cardinality. Pass options.Kind instead of name.

grupos.texto: The legacy DeleteCollection duration and error status are recorded in the unified-storage histogram. Every successful unified deletion therefore produces a second storage observation for a different backend, while legacy deletion failures are attributed to unified storage and no legacy observation is emitted. Call recordLegacyDuration here instead.
outros: The timed call is d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but its measurement is emitted using recordStorageDuration. Use recordLegacyDuration; otherwise storage receives two measurements for a successful collection deletion and legacy receives none, and legacy failures appear as storage failures.

grupos.texto: The successful Update case configures a legacy Update expectation but returns after checking only the unified-store result. It neither waits for the asynchronous legacy update nor verifies its expectation, so removing the legacy-update goroutine entirely still passes. Add explicit synchronization and verification of the legacy update (ideally with separate mocks), including the object propagated to legacy storage.
outros: The successful Create test never verifies the legacy write. Configuring m.On("Create", ...) does not require that expectation to be consumed, and these assertions only inspect the object returned by Storage.Create. Deleting the entire legacy-create goroutine would still pass this test. Use distinct storage and legacy mocks and synchronize on the legacy call, then assert that it completed with the intended object.

grupos.texto: The failing operation is d.Storage.Create, but its duration/error is recorded through recordLegacyDuration. Use recordStorageDuration here so storage create failures are not counted as legacy failures while disappearing from storage error metrics.
outros: This branch handles d.Storage.Update failing, yet records a Legacy duration/error. Use recordStorageDuration to attribute the elapsed time and failure to the backend actually called.

grupos.texto: The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers the failing Create expectation only through setupLegacyFn. It passes only because legacy and storage share one mock, so the storage Create gets that error by accident. Register the expectation in setupStorageFn and use separate mocks for legacy and storage, so the test really covers a storage failure.

The Mode3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write. The legacy call runs in a goroutine that the tests neither wait for nor assert on, and legacy and storage share the same mock. Removing the legacy Create, Update, Delete or DeleteCollection calls would not fail these tests. Use separate mocks, wait on a channel or use `Eventually`, and assert that the legacy call happened.

The async legacy write derives its context from the request ctx, so the legacy write is cancelled when the request completes. The goroutine can then be aborted before it finishes, and the legacy store silently falls out of sync. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) as the parent of the timeout context. The same applies to the Delete, Update and DeleteCollection goroutines.
outros: The background legacy write uses a context derived from the request ctx. That ctx is cancelled once the handler returns, so the legacy Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection can be aborted mid-flight and leave legacy storage out of sync. Derive the timeout context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) in each goroutine.

The legacy writes were moved into fire-and-forget goroutines, but each derives its context from the request ctx. That context is cancelled when the handler returns, so the legacy Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection calls can be cancelled midway and silently dropped. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) as the parent of the timeout context.

grupos.texto: The legacy update now receives the raw objInfo instead of the updateWrapper that carried the object returned by Storage.Update. Legacy therefore recomputes the update from its own old object and can diverge from unified storage, which was the guarantee the removed wrapper provided. Wrap it again with &updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res} before calling Legacy.Update.
outros: The async legacy Update passes the original objInfo, so the legacy store recomputes the update against its own (possibly stale or different) old object instead of the object that unified storage wrote. The two stores can then diverge. Wrap the result in an updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}, as the previous implementation did.

The legacy Update now receives the original objInfo instead of a wrapper around the object already written to storage. Legacy therefore recomputes the update from its own stored state and can end up with different content from unified storage. Pass an updateWrapper holding the updated object returned by Storage.Update, as the previous code did.

grupos.texto: ctx is built with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the enriched `log`. The delete logs then lose the name, kind and method values. Use `log`.

recordStorageDuration is called with `name` as the kind label, unlike every other call, which uses options.Kind. This creates one metric label series per object name, which is unbounded cardinality and breaks the kind aggregation. Pass options.Kind.
outros: The Delete success metric is recorded with `name` as the kind label instead of options.Kind. The label is inconsistent with the other call sites, which creates a high-cardinality label.

On Delete success, recordStorageDuration receives `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. The value lands in the kind label, so the metric label does not match its name. Pass options.Kind.

grupos.texto: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its duration with recordStorageDuration, although it times the Legacy call. This attributes legacy latency and errors to the storage metric. Use recordLegacyDuration.
outros: The legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to storage. Use recordLegacyDuration.

The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration with the legacy start time and legacy error. This pollutes storage metrics and leaves the legacy metric unrecorded. Use recordLegacyDuration.

grupos.texto: A failed storage Create is recorded with recordLegacyDuration, so storage errors are attributed to the legacy metric. The same mistake is in the Update error path at line 129. Use recordStorageDuration.
outros: When the storage Update fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration, although this is a storage operation. Use recordStorageDuration.
When the storage Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration, although this is a storage operation. Use recordStorageDuration.
When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration, but the failure is in the unified store. The failure is therefore reported under the legacy metric. Use recordStorageDuration.
When Storage.Update fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration, but the failure is in the unified store. The failure is therefore reported under the legacy metric. Use recordStorageDuration.

grupos.texto: The Delete context uses d.Log rather than the per-call log. This is a logging-context inconsistency (not a data leak); use the per-call logger for consistency.

WHAT: Update reuses the original objInfo for the async legacy write instead of the object actually persisted to unified storage. WHY: Legacy.Update recomputes UpdatedObject from legacy old state, so legacy can converge to a different object/version than storage wrote; the removed updateWrapper (which pinned the stored result) guaranteed convergence. HOW: capture res from Storage.Update and write that fixed object to legacy via a wrapper, as the pre-PR code did.
TestMode3_Create claims dual-write but never synchronizes on or asserts the async Legacy.Create goroutine; removing the go func would still pass.
Goroutine captures mutable obj/options while caller returns object that can alias it; DeepCopy before handing to goroutine to avoid concurrent read/write race.

WHAT: Create storage-failure path calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. WHY: misattributes unified-store errors/latency to the legacy histogram and leaves storage failures unrecorded, breaking alerts/dashboards. HOW: change line 45 to d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).
outros: WHAT: Update storage-failure path calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. WHY: same metric misattribution as Create — unified-store update errors pollute legacy histogram. HOW: change line 129 to d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

Create storage-error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ..., startStorage)` for a Storage.Create failure timed with startStorage. Success path correctly calls recordStorageDuration. Error metric misattributes storage latency/failure to legacy histogram. Call recordStorageDuration on storage error.

grupos.texto: WHAT: DeleteCollection legacy async completion calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration. WHY: legacy delete-collection latency/errors recorded in storage histogram, legacy histogram stays empty. HOW: change line 166 to d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).
outros: DeleteCollection legacy background op calls `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` with startLegacy. Every other legacy background op (Create/Update/Delete) calls recordLegacyDuration. Legacy latency will be counted in storage histogram and legacy histogram will miss it. Call recordLegacyDuration.

grupos.texto: WHAT: Delete success path records storage duration with object name instead of kind (recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...)). WHY: Prometheus label kind becomes unbounded per-object cardinality — each distinct name creates a new series, causing memory/series blowup with many objects, inconsistent with error path using options.Kind. HOW: change third arg to options.Kind.
outros: Delete success records `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...)` passing resource `name` where the kind label belongs. Error path above (line 103) and every other storage record passes `options.Kind`. Metric will be tagged with high-cardinality name and disagree with queries by kind. Pass `options.Kind`.

grupos.texto: WHAT: Delete builds per-request log but installs parent d.Log into context (klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)). WHY: drops name/kind/method fields for downstream storage/legacy calls and diverges from Create/Update/List which propagate the enriched log. HOW: change line 97 to ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log).
outros: Delete builds enriched `log` with name/kind/method but then does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, discarding it and using the original `d.Log`. The computed log value is dead; context loses request fields. Use `log` in NewContext.

grupos.texto: WHAT: Async legacy writes derive timeout context from the request context (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)) where ctx is request-scoped. WHY: when the handler returns the parent request context is cancelled, immediately cancelling the child and aborting the best-effort legacy Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection, leaving legacy diverged — the 10s timeout is ineffective. HOW: derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or detached background context, e.g. ctx.WithoutCancel + WithTimeoutCause.
outros: Legacy Create was synchronous on the request ctx; now it is `go func()` with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx,...)` derived from the request ctx. After return the parent ctx can cancel, aborting the legacy write. Detach the async work (e.g. context.WithoutCancel / Background) before the 10s timeout, otherwise legacy consumers lose the completion guarantee they had before.
Background legacy write derives from request ctx so parent cancellation aborts it. Detach with WithoutCancel before timeout. Same at Delete/Update/DeleteCollection goroutines.

goldens.comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

grupos.texto: WHAT: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and, on error, returns `nil, err` without invoking the `cancel` func created at line 229 and without running any lifecycle cleanup. WHY: Init may have already started long-lived goroutines — searchSupport.init's event-consumption loop uses context.Background() (resource/search.go:202) and initWatcher starts a watcher bound to s.ctx (server.go:752-770) — so if search.init succeeds and initWatcher (or a later step) fails, the constructor discards the server while those goroutines keep running with no way to stop them, leaking the internal context and watcher goroutines. HOW: on the error path call `cancel()` (and any needed lifecycle.Stop) before returning, or defer the cancel until success.

The added `t.Skip` for `dbType == "postgres"` makes this the only test covering the storage-server target server's instrumentation HTTP setup stop running entirely for postgres: the early return at lines 36-38 happens before `InitializeModuleServer`/`ms.Run()` and before the `assert.Equal(t, 200, res.StatusCode)` at line 63, so the postgres path could regress (module server not starting, `/metrics` not serving 200, `InitializeModuleServer` erroring) and this test would still pass. Either fix the underlying postgres/Drone failure and keep the assertion running, or add an equivalent postgres-target test that actually brings up the server and checks `/metrics` returns 200, rather than silently removing the coverage.

`NewResourceServer` now performs initialization itself by calling `s.Init(ctx)`, changing the constructor's contract for every consumer. Previously the constructor returned a usable server and index building was lazy (getOrCreateIndex in search.go builds on first query and surfaces errors per-request). Now construction blocks on the full search-index build (search.init calls GetResourceStats and builds every namespace/resource index) and, on any failure, returns `nil, err` instead of a server — a single index build error now prevents the server from existing at all, rather than degrading to a per-request search error. Additionally, because `Init` is guarded by `sync.Once` (server.go:294), this internal call consumes the once and the context passed by any existing caller to `Init` is no longer the one used for `lifecycle.Init`, `search.init` and `initWatcher` — the constructor's ctx silently wins. Either keep initialization in the caller (revert this call) or make the callers explicitly aware of the new fail-fast, eager-initialization contract.

The newly added `s.search.TotalDocs()` call is unsafe: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:144-150) iterates `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`, while the bleve.go hunk in this same PR keeps `cacheMu` for the `b.cache[key] = idx` write only. Because search.go:207-213 already started the watch-event goroutine that can call `build` → `BuildIndex` → cache write, line 216 can iterate the map concurrently with that write, causing a `concurrent map iteration and map write` panic or data race. Either guard the `TotalDocs` read with `cacheMu`, or move this call to a point where no build can run concurrently.

WHAT: Removing the function-wide `b.cacheMu.Lock()/defer Unlock()` and keeping only the lock around `b.cache[key]=idx` removes the only thing that serialized GetIndex against an in-flight build. WHY: getOrCreateIndex (resource/search.go:287-307) does GetIndex -> if nil -> build; previously BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole body so a concurrent caller's GetIndex (RLock) blocked until the first build cached the index and then saw it (no second build). Now GetIndex can return nil while a build for the same key is still running, so two requests/watch events build the SAME key concurrently — producing two distinct index instances where the caller holding the non-cached one never observes later writes (stale search results), and, for file-backed indices (size > FileThreshold), two concurrent `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` opening the same on-disk directory. HOW: guard the build per key (e.g. re-check the cache under the write lock after acquiring it, or use a per-key single-flight/lock so only one build runs per NamespacedResource), rather than relying on a global write lock held for the entire body.
outros: The cache mutex was moved to cover only the cache assignment, removing the serialization that previously surrounded the whole BuildIndex. Two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can now both construct an index (including `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same on-disk path) and both write `b.cache[key]`; the second overwrites the first, so callers get distinct index instances for one key and writes made through the losing instance are invisible to readers of the cached one (and the file-backed build may collide on the same directory). Keep the build for a given key serialized (e.g. restore the lock around the build, or take a per-key lock) instead of locking only the map write.

grupos.texto: Locking only cache publication allows concurrent requests for the same uncached key to build separate indexes and overwrite each other's cache entries. Search and handleEvent both call getOrCreateIndex, whose GetIndex previously blocked behind the build-wide lock; now an event can update one newly built index before another build replaces it, losing that update from subsequent search results and leaving the discarded index open. Serialize builds per NamespacedResource and recheck the cache after acquiring that per-key guard.

The new startup log calls TotalDocs after launching the write-event listener, but bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu.RLock. A write event for an unindexed resource can concurrently publish an index through BuildIndex, causing a map iteration/write race and potentially a fatal runtime error during initialization. Protect TotalDocs cache iteration with the same read lock used by GetIndex.

The new postgres skip bypasses the entire instrumentation-server test for that backend. If the storage-server target stops starting its instrumentation HTTP server on postgres, this case now reports skipped rather than catching the regression, including locally where the comment says it works. Fix the CI-specific failure or isolate its actual environmental prerequisite instead of disabling verification for every postgres run.

BuildIndex now writes b.cache under Lock while TotalDocs (called from search.init after the watch goroutine starts) ranges over b.cache without any lock. This can cause a concurrent map read/write fatal error. Fix by taking cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.

The watcher is now started after search.init, so events written after the index snapshot but before initWatcher runs are never delivered to the index. The index stays permanently stale for those writes. Start the watcher (buffering events) before building the index, or replay events from the index's build resource version after the watcher starts.

Removing the function-wide cacheMu lock in BuildIndex lets concurrent builds of the same NamespacedResource run in parallel. For file-backed indexes, bleve.New(dir) on the same directory fails for the second caller, and for in-memory indexes the later build overwrites the cache entry and leaks the earlier index. Fix by serializing builds per key (a per-key mutex or singleflight), or by re-checking the cache under the lock before building.
outros: The cache mutex was removed from around the whole build and now guards only the final map write. Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can both run bleve.New on the same directory, and one fails or corrupts the file index. In the memory-only case, the later cache write overwrites the earlier index and leaks it. Serialize builds per key, or check the cache under the lock and close the loser.

grupos.texto: WHAT: BuildIndex no longer serializes whole builds, only the final cache store, so concurrent builds for the same key both run bleve.New/builder/Flush and last-writer-wins. WHY: Wastes parallel index work, double-counts IndexTenants metrics, leaks the loser's bleve index (never closed) and concurrent bleve.New on the same file dir can fail/corrupt; concurrent map write here also races unsynchronized TotalDocs iteration causing concurrent-map panic. HOW: Re-check cache under lock before/after build (singleflight per key) or restore per-key locking; add RLock to TotalDocs/GetIndex readers.

WHAT: NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously but returns nil,err without calling the cancel created for s.ctx. WHY: Failed startup leaks the server context (and any lifecycle/watch resources partially started by Init), leaving goroutines/channel watches alive. HOW: On Init error call s.cancel() (and lifecycle Stop cleanup) before returning.

goldens.comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

grupos.texto: WHAT: The grafana branch of the filtered list renders <GrafanaRuleListItem .../> without a `key` prop, dropping the `key={key}` that the replaced <GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} .../> had. WHY: `rules.map` renders a dynamic list keyed by getRuleKey/hashRule; without a key React logs duplicate-key warnings and reconciles rows by index, so as the async rule stream updates/reorders the wrong rule row can be reused/mutated (stale state, swapped actions). HOW: add `key={key}` (the value is already destructured on line 152) to the <GrafanaRuleListItem> element.

The skip path is not treated as 'not applicable'. useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable(undefined) returns loading:false, so in useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities `MaybeSupported = loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported` becomes AlwaysSupported, and `rulesPermissions = getRulesPermissions('grafana')` is used unconditionally. useGrafanaPromRuleAbility/useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities are called with skipToken (rule === skipToken ? undefined : rule), and AlertRuleMenu ORs the Grafana pair with the ruler pair. For AlertRuleAction.Duplicate, `toAbility(duplicateSupported, rulesPermissions.create)` yields [true, userHasAlertingRuleCreate] from a permission alone, so a caller that is not a Grafana rule (e.g. a cloud/datasource rule) can be granted Duplicate. The undefined/skipToken case should yield NotSupported abilities instead of permission-derived supported ones.

Test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never verifies any action menu option: the body only asserts the More button exists and has aria-label/text 'More'. It would still pass if the dropdown were rendered empty (Silence/Duplicate/Copy link/Export all missing), i.e. the behaviour the name promises is not covered. Either open the menu and assert the menu items, or rename the test to reflect that it only checks the trigger button's rendering/accessibility.

The `promRule` prop is declared as `Rule` (the combined-rule type from app/types/unified-alerting, the same type used for `useRulePluginLinkExtension`), but the body consumes it as a `GrafanaPromRuleDTO`: it feeds it to `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) ? promRule : skipToken` -> `useGrafanaPromRuleAbility(rule: GrafanaPromRuleDTO | SkipToken, …)` and to `isProvisionedPromRule(promRule: PromRuleDTO)`. The new producer GrafanaRuleListItem.tsx passes a raw GrafanaPromRuleDTO into this `Rule`-typed slot. Because `Rule` is not a prom-rule DTO, the type guard returns false for combined-rule callers (e.g. the RulesTable path) so the Grafana abilities resolve to NotSupported and the new menu entries are silently hidden, while the list-view caller only appears to work by passing a differently-typed object. Align the prop type with what the hooks/guards require (GrafanaPromRuleDTO) on the side the caller must satisfy, and update GrafanaRuleListItem accordingly.

The consolidation of useAllAlertRuleAbilities into useAllRulerRuleAbilities silently dropped federated-rule handling: the old implementation used `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, but the new body hardcodes `isFederated = false` (with the isFederatedRuleGroup import removed). Because `immutableRule = isProvisioned || isFederated || isPluginProvided` feeds `MaybeSupportedUnlessImmutable` for Update/Delete/Pause/Restore/DeletePermanently, federated Mimir rule groups are now reported as editable/removable. Every consumer relying on these abilities (RuleActionsButtons, AlertRuleMenu, RulesTable) will now offer mutating actions on federated rules, which are immutable and will fail when the request is made. Restore federated detection (pass the group/origin info needed to call isFederatedRuleGroup) or otherwise keep federated rules in the immutable branch.
outros: WHAT: useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities (line 228), whose body hard-codes `const isFederated = false;` (lines 243-245), whereas the replaced implementation computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. WHY: federated Mimir rule groups are no longer marked immutable, so Update/Delete/Pause abilities for federated rules flip from NotSupported to supported, exposing edit/delete on rules that must not be edited. This affects existing callers useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities (lines 180/188). HOW: pass the federated flag through (e.g. compute isFederatedRuleGroup from the CombinedRule group and forward it, or keep the federated check in the wrapper) instead of relying on the hard-coded false.

useAllAlertRuleAbilities no longer determines federation: the old body computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, but the function now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false`. Because immutableRule = isProvisioned || isFederated || isPluginProvided, federated Mimir rule groups are no longer treated as immutable, so the Pause/Update/Delete/Restore/DeletePermanently abilities report supported=true for rules that the backend will reject. This breaks the immutability invariant that the removed isFederatedRuleGroup check enforced.

grupos.texto: The JSDoc for GrafanaGroupLoader still says "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints." but this PR removed the ruler API query entirely — the component now only calls useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery (Prometheus). The documentation describes a data source the function no longer consumes; update it to state only the Prometheus endpoint is loaded (and the same stale "Ruler response" reference in the expectedRulesCount prop doc at lines 18–19 should be corrected).

The new Prometheus-based pause ability cannot display Pause or Resume for list-view rules because the menu still requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) before rendering MenuItemPauseRule. GrafanaRuleListItem now supplies only promRule, so these actions disappear even for editable rules. Adapt the pause menu item to accept the Grafana identifier and Prometheus pause state, or load the ruler rule on demand.

The new Prometheus-based delete ability is still gated by `canDelete && rulerRule` when rendering the Delete item. Both Grafana list-view paths now omit rulerRule, so users with delete permission lose the Delete action entirely. Render deletion using the available identifier and group identifier instead of requiring the ruler DTO, adapting the callback contract accordingly.

The test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never opens the menu or asserts any options: it only checks the button, aria-label, and text. It would still pass if AlertRuleMenu rendered an empty dropdown. Open More and assert the expected menu items here, or rename this case to explicitly limit its contract to the button's presentation (the separate menu-click case already tests options).

Make skipToken return neutral [false, false] abilities rather than forwarding undefined to useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities. AlertRuleMenu now passes skipToken for datasource rules and ORs these results with the ruler abilities, but the undefined-rule path sets Duplicate to supported and allows it whenever the user has Grafana rule-create permission. This enables Duplicate on datasource rules even when their ruler ability is unsupported or denied. The skipped Grafana branch must not grant any abilities.

Passing only promRule enables the Silence notifications menu item but leaves RuleActionsButtons.V2 unable to render its silence drawer, which is guarded by rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). Clicking Silence only updates showSilenceDrawer and displays nothing because rule is undefined. Update the drawer to accept a rule UID—the inspected SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only needs grafana_alert.uid—and allow the Prometheus alerting-rule path to render it.
outros: The new list item passes only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, but that component renders SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only under `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. With rule undefined, clicking the newly enabled 'Silence notifications' action only sets state and never opens a drawer. Adapt the silence rendering path to load/use the rule by its Prometheus identifier before switching this caller to promRule-only.

grupos.texto: Preserve the federated-group immutability check when delegating this CombinedRule hook. Previously useAllAlertRuleAbilities inspected rule.group with isFederatedRuleGroup and disabled modification/removal for federated rules. The replacement delegates to a hook that hardcodes isFederated=false and receives no group information. Existing useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities consumers therefore now receive supported update/delete abilities for federated rules when datasource permissions allow them, exposing operations that the previous contract explicitly prohibited. Pass the federation state through or retain that restriction in this wrapper.
outros: Delegating useAllAlertRuleAbilities to useAllRulerRuleAbilities discards the group's federation status and replaces the previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check with a constant false. Legacy RuleActionsButtons consequently enables editing rules in groups with source_tenants, although these groups were explicitly immutable before this change. Preserve the CombinedRule federation check in the wrapper or pass federation status into the delegated ability calculation.

Hard-coding isFederated=false now also affects useAllAlertRuleAbilities, which delegates to this helper after the refactor. Previously that hook checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), so federated Mimir groups were immutable. The refactor discards that information and can expose edit/delete actions for federated rules whenever the ordinary datasource permissions allow them. Preserve the federation check for CombinedRule callers or carry group federation information into the shared helper.

grupos.texto: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities treats an undefined rule (the skipToken case) as always supported, so Duplicate becomes [true, grafanaCreatePermission]. AlertRuleMenu ORs this with the ruler ability, so the Duplicate menu item can show for data-source (cloud) rules whenever the user has the Grafana rule-create permission, even if the ruler check denies it. Fix: when rule is undefined, return NotSupported for every ability, for example MaybeSupported = (loading || !rule) ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported.

The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the variable it describes is `isAlertingRule`. That variable is true only for alerting rules and false for Grafana recording rules. Fix the comment, or rename the variable, so it says the check is for alerting rules. As written, readers will expect Pause, Export and Silence to be enabled for recording rules.

The comment says there is no loading state, but the next line is `loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported`. `loading` comes from the folder fetch. Update the comment to say that support depends on the folder loading state.

The test 'should render More button with action menu options' only checks that the More button exists. It finds the button by name 'More', so the aria-label and text assertions are tautological. It would pass even if the menu had no actions or the abilities were broken. Click the button and assert the expected menu items, or rename the test to match what it checks.

useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated = false. The previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check is gone, so federated Mimir rules are no longer treated as immutable and can show edit and delete abilities. Keep the federation check in this wrapper, or pass the federation state into the shared hook.

The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the check used is alertingRule(rule), which is false for recording rules. Pause, Restore, ModifyExport and DeletePermanently are therefore wrongly disabled for Grafana recording rules, where the old isGrafanaManagedAlertRule check allowed them. Use prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule) for these abilities, and keep alertingRule only for Silence.

WHAT: Grafana branch of FilterViewResults renders GrafanaRuleListItem without key={key} while datasource and unknown branches pass key. WHY: Breaks React list reconciliation — wrong item reuse, stale actions/state and console key warnings for every Grafana hit. HOW: Add key={key} to the GrafanaRuleListItem element.

WHAT: useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes isFederated=false with TODO, dropping the prior isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check. WHY: Mimir federated rule groups were immutable (no Update/Delete/Pause); now MaybeSupportedUnlessImmutable stays true so federated rules appear editable/removable. HOW: Restore federated detection for the datasource path or thread group info through groupIdentifier.

WHAT: getEditableIdentifier now enables a prom-only path (Grafana uid identifier with rulerRule undefined) but the silence drawer still renders only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. WHY: In the list view Silence menu item can be shown via grafana abilities, clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer but the drawer never mounts, so Silence silently does nothing. HOW: Gate the drawer on promRule as well or provide a prom-based silence drawer.

WHAT: isProvisioned derived from promRule.provenance (new optional field) instead of ruler grafana_alert.provenance. WHY: If the Prometheus groups response omits provenance, provisioned rules render as non-provisioned and abilities (isProvisionedPromRule) fail open to editable/removable. HOW: Ensure Prometheus API populates provenance or fall back to ruler/folder metadata for the provisioned check.

Test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never opens the menu nor asserts menu items — it only checks More button presence/aria/text. Click More and assert expected menuitems (or rename to 'should render More button') so it fails if menu actions break.

WHAT: canDuplicate ORs ruler ability with grafana ability where grafana path is skipToken=>undefined for cloud rules, and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) returns Duplicate=[true,true] whenever the user has global Grafana create permission. WHY: Any user with Grafana rule-create gets Duplicate menu item on cloud/Mimir rules even when ruler abilities deny it — incorrect authorization gating. HOW: Return NotSupported for all abilities when rule is skipToken/undefined, or gate grafana branch on prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) before ORing.
outros: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities returns AlwaysSupported for Duplicate when rule is undefined (skipToken): loading is false from the !rule early-return, so MaybeSupported=true and duplicateSupported=true. ORed in AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons this leaks Grafana create permission into non-Grafana rules. Gate MaybeSupported/duplicateSupported on rule existence (e.g. NotSupported when !rule).

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities must return NotSupported for all actions when rule is undefined (skipToken). Currently MaybeSupported falls back to AlwaysSupported when !loading, so Duplicate=[true, global-create] is true for a cloud rule passed as skipToken, and AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons OR-logic then incorrectly enables Duplicate (and Explore). Guard with if (!rule) return all-NotSupported abilities or make MaybeSupported require rule.

goldens.comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

grupos.texto: The Javadoc says getShortcut() returns 'usually like 3-letters shortcut', but every implementation introduced in this PR returns a 2-character shortcut ('ac','cc','pg','pc','rt','ro','te','ci','dg') and the encoder relies on exactly 2 chars (encoded context length 6 = 2+2+2). The doc states a length the code does not produce; it should say 2-character shortcut.

WHAT: the constructor validates `grantType` a second time instead of `rawTokenId` (`Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`). WHY: a null `rawTokenId` is silently accepted, so `encodeTokenId` produces a token id ending in `:null` and any later consumer of the raw id gets an invalid value instead of an early failure. HOW: change the argument to `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.
outros: Line 73 calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") — it validates grantType a second time (line 72 already does) with a message naming a different field. rawTokenId is never validated, so a null rawTokenId is accepted at construction and the advertised check/message is wrong. It should be Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed").

The null-check message names the wrong parameter: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` validates `grantType` but reports `rawTokenId`, and it duplicates the check on line 72 while `rawTokenId` is never validated at all. The message that reaches the reader contradicts the code it guards; it should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

Copy-paste validation: line 73 calls `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` instead of validating `rawTokenId`. Because rawTokenId is never null-checked, a null rawTokenId is silently accepted, and a null grantType is reported with a misleading message. It should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

Copy-paste null check: line 73 calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") again instead of validating rawTokenId. The constructor's declared invariant that rawTokenId must be non-null is never enforced, so a null rawTokenId is silently accepted (and would later produce 'null' concatenation in encodeTokenId). It should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`.

grupos.texto: The isAccessTokenId(expectedGrantShortcut) matcher never verifies the grant shortcut, so all four callers (expectCodeToToken, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectAuthReqIdToToken) keep passing even if the encoded grant shortcut is wrong. Two defects combine: (a) items[0].substring(3, 5) reads indices 3-4, but the grant shortcut is encoded at indices 4-5 (decoder uses substring(4, 6)), so the slice is the token-type/grant overlap like "tc" and never equals a 2-letter shortcut; (b) the comparison is inverted — `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false on a *match*. Because of (a) the branch is never hit for valid tokens, so the body always falls through to isUUID().matches(items[1]) and passes for any token with a 6-char context and UUID suffix, regardless of the grant actually encoded. Fix to `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.
outros: WHAT: `isAccessTokenId` reads the grant shortcut from the wrong offset and inverts the comparison — `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. WHY: for the encoded id `ssttgg:raw` the grant shortcut occupies 0-based indices 4-5, so `substring(3,5)` inspects the token-type/grant boundary and can never equal the expected shortcut; combined with the inverted `return false`, the equality branch is unreachable and the matcher validates only the UUID part. As a result the new assertions in `expectCodeToToken`/`expectRefresh`/`expectDeviceCodeToToken`/`expectAuthReqIdToToken` do not actually assert the grant type and would pass even if the grant shortcut were wrong. HOW: use `items[0].substring(4, 6)` and negate the condition (`if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`).

The matcher logic is inverted: line 483 returns false when the extracted grant shortcut EQUALS expectedGrantShortcut, so a token that actually carries the expected grant fails the matcher, while a token with any other grant shortcut falls through and passes. The condition should be negated: `if (!items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. Also note the encode site writes the grant shortcut at chars 4-6 (substring(4,6)); substring(3,5) reads one character early into the token-type field, so the offset is off by one relative to TokenManager.encodeTokenId.

The comment 'Grant type shortcut starts at character 4th char' disagrees with the encoding that this PR defines (sessionType chars 1-2, tokenType 3-4, grantType 5-6, e.g. 'trltcc'), and the code reads substring(3,5) — the 4th-5th chars, i.e. the token-type second char plus the grant first char, never the grant shortcut. The comment (and the index) should point at the 5th char / substring(4,6).

The comparison is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` rejects the token when the grant shortcut MATCHES the expected value and accepts it when it does not. It should negate the test, e.g. `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. As written, every expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectAuthReqIdToToken assertion that relies on this matcher fails for a correctly encoded access token.

Off-by-one slice: the grant-type shortcut is read with substring(3, 5), but encodeTokenId writes a 6-char context as sessionType=[0,2), tokenType=[2,4), grantType=[4,6) (see DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId / getTokenContextFromTokenId which reads substring(4,6)). For 'trltcc:1234', substring(3,5) yields 'tc' — the last token-type char plus the first grant char — instead of 'cc'. The comment on line 482 ('starts at 4th char') is also wrong; the shortcut starts at index 4 (5th char). Use substring(4, 6).

Inverted comparison in isAccessTokenId: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` fails the matcher when the token's grant shortcut DOES match the expected one, so it only returns true when the grant type differs. The negated check `if (!items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` is what was intended. As written, the new TOKEN_ID assertions (expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectAuthReqIdToToken) and any other caller never actually validate the encoded grant type, silently weakening the coverage this PR adds.

The grant shortcut is encoded at index 4-5 of the token-id context (sessionType 0-1, tokenType 2-3, grantShortcut 4-5), as produced by DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId and read by its own decoder substring(4,6). This matcher reads items[0].substring(3, 5), which is the token-type second char plus the grant's first char, so it never equals the expected 2-char grant shortcut and the grant check never actually validates the token id. Use substring(4, 6) to match the encoder's layout.

isAccessTokenId's condition is inverted and off by one. It reads items[0].substring(3, 5), but the grant shortcut occupies the 4th-5th characters (indices 4..6), and it returns false when the value EQUALS the expected shortcut instead of when it differs. Result: the matcher never verifies the grant portion and accepts any UUID-suffixed id, so all rely-on-it assertions (expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectAuthReqIdToToken) pass vacuously. It should be `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.

The grant-shortcut comparison is inverted. `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false precisely when the characters DO equal the expected shortcut (and true otherwise), so the matcher can never assert that the token was issued by the expected grant, defeating the whole purpose of the new `isAccessTokenId(...)` check added for the encoded token-ID contract. It should return true when the substring matches (or compare `!equals(...)` for the failure branch).

Wrong substring offset for the grant shortcut. The encoded token ID is sessionType(2) + tokenType(2) + grantShortcut(2) + ':', so the grant shortcut occupies indices 4-5 (`substring(4, 6)`). Using `substring(3, 5)` reads the last char of the token type plus the first char of the grant, so even after fixing the inverted comparison the matcher would test the wrong characters and not validate the grant type.

grupos.texto: The new grant metadata falls back to 'na' for client-credentials and UMA tokens because their issuance paths never set Constants.GRANT_TYPE on their fresh ClientSessionContext. ClientCredentialsGrantType calls responseBuilder.generateAccessToken directly, and PermissionGrantType delegates to AuthorizationTokenService, so neither executes the new assignment in createTokenResponse; tokens from these known grants therefore carry unknown grant context. Set the grant attribute in both issuance paths before generating the access token.

Catching RuntimeException allows this negative test to pass for an unrelated fixture failure. The fixture constructs the factory without postInit, leaving sessionFactory null; resolving the unregistered `ac` shortcut calls sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream and throws NullPointerException before the decoder's intended unknown-grant IllegalArgumentException. Catch/assert IllegalArgumentException specifically and provide a factory fixture whose lookup returns no matching grant, so removing the decoder's validation would fail the test.

Enforce shortcut uniqueness during lazy registration rather than overwriting grantsByShortcuts. If a newly deployed grant B uses existing grant A's shortcut, this path replaces shortcut→A with shortcut→B while retaining both forward entries. Previously issued A tokens then decode as B. Concurrent registrations of two new grants with the same shortcut likewise both succeed, with the last inverse-map write winning. Use collision-aware atomic registration and reject the conflicting grant before publishing its forward mapping.

The event matcher does not follow the new token-ID contract. The encoder places the grant shortcut at indices [4, 6), but this consumer reads [3, 5) and returns false when it equals the expected shortcut rather than when it differs. Consequently, for example, expectCodeToToken accepts `onrtrt:<valid UUID>` even though that is a refresh-token grant instead of an authorization-code grant. Check the prefix length and reject when `!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)` so the updated event assertions actually validate the grant.
outros: The access-token ID matcher extracts substring(3, 5) instead of substring(4, 6) and returns false when the extracted value equals the expected grant. This allows tokens with incorrect grant shortcuts to pass the authorization-code, refresh, device and CIBA event assertions, while malformed short prefixes can throw instead of producing a mismatch. Require a six-character prefix and reject when !items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut).

The expectedGrantShortcut parameter and accompanying comment promise validation of the expected grant, but this implementation extracts substring(3, 5) and returns false on equality. The encoder places the grant at zero-based positions 4–5, so typical IDs with any grant pass this check, contradicting the matcher’s expected-grant contract and allowing incorrect grant context to pass the new event assertions. Compare substring(4, 6) with the expected shortcut and reject inequality (after validating prefix length).

The grant assertion uses substring(3, 5) and rejects equality. The encoder places the grant at indices 4–5, so this matcher generally accepts any grant prefix with a UUID suffix. For example, an authorization-code event containing `onrtna:<uuid>` still passes the expected `ac` check. Validate the prefix length and return false when substring(4, 6) does not equal expectedGrantShortcut.

The grant segment is at indices [4,6), not [3,5). For example, `onrtac:<uuid>` yields `ta` here rather than `ac`, preventing the matcher from actually checking the encoded grant. Extract `substring(4,6)` (after checking the prefix length) to match the encoder layout.

The equality condition is inverted: it returns false when the extracted grant equals the expected grant and accepts mismatches. Independently of correcting the slice indices, negate this equality check so that wrong-grant token IDs fail and correct-grant IDs pass.

The encoder places the grant shortcut at indices 4–6, but this matcher reads substring(3, 5) and returns false on equality. Consequently a token with the wrong grant normally passes the assertion as long as its suffix is a UUID. Require substring(4, 6) to equal expectedGrantShortcut (and validate prefix length before slicing).

The encoder produces a prefix consisting of two session characters, two token characters, and two grant characters (for example `onrtac`), but this matcher reads substring(3, 5) and rejects equality instead of requiring it. Thus expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/etc. accept token IDs with the wrong grant, hiding failures in the grant-context propagation this PR introduces. Validate a six-character prefix and require substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut).

grupos.texto: The new getShortcut contract describes a shortcut as usually three letters, but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider requires an exactly six-character context prefix and reads only two characters for the grant.
