Anything consuming this metric family by the `shard` tag (dashboards, alerts, tag-based aggregation) will silently receive no data for `wait_produce`, and per-shard breakdowns of produce latency will be incomplete. Change the tag to `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` so the tag contract matches the other flusher metrics.
outros: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with the key `"shards"`, while the other two metrics emitted in this same loop (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` at line 185 and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` at line 195) use the key `"shard"`. All three carry the same `shard_tag` value, so this is a pure key-name disagreement: any dashboard or alert that groups/filters by the `shard` tag will silently receive no data from `wait_produce`. Rename the tag key to `"shard"` so all flusher metrics share one tag.

grupos.texto: The new loop calls get_memory_info() once per flusher buffer even though SpansBuffer.get_memory_info delegates to iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client), which fetches INFO for the entire Redis cluster regardless of assigned_shards. With P flusher processes and memory backpressure enabled, each submitted batch now performs P identical cluster-wide memory queries on the consumer thread instead of one, increasing Redis traffic and blocking ingestion. Fetch cluster memory information once from a single buffer.

The new docstring says this creates one process per shard, but workers are capped by max_processes and shards are distributed among them. In particular, the CLI default of 1 means all assigned shards share one process. Describe capped workers with potentially multiple shards per worker so callers do not rely on per-shard process isolation.

An explicit max_processes=0 is treated as an omitted limit by `or`, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` starts one process per assigned shard instead of respecting or rejecting the supplied zero limit. The CLI accepts zero as an integer and the factory forwards it unchanged. Default only when max_processes is None, and explicitly validate that supplied process limits are positive so zero cannot silently enable potentially many workers.

The assertion counts shard entries rather than verifying shard assignment. A broken distribution such as {0: [0, 1], 1: [0, 1]} still passes all assertions in this test while shards 2 and 3 are never flushed. Assert that the flattened mapping contains exactly the expected assigned shards, with no duplicates (and verify each worker's shard buffer uses that mapping), rather than only asserting a total of four.

Workers created by multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process are SpawnProcess instances, not instances of the separate multiprocessing.Process class. Consequently this guard skips kill() for production workers. When a live worker exceeds max-unhealthy-seconds, the code starts a replacement and overwrites its handle while the original is still running. If the original resumes, both workers flush the same shards, and repeated hangs can exceed the configured process limit. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or explicitly distinguish threads) and stop the old worker before replacing it.
outros: The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard does not match the SpawnProcess instances created by self.mp_context.Process. When a worker hangs, the guard skips kill() and the replacement starts while the original worker remains alive, allowing overlapping flushing of the same shards if the original resumes and leaking hung workers. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or self.mp_context.Process, and kill and join the old worker before replacing it.

The workers are created with get_context("spawn").Process, which produces SpawnProcess instances; these are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class). Consequently this guard skips kill() for actual production workers. When a worker hangs, the replacement starts while the original remains alive and can resume flushing the same shards. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or the spawn-context Process class for the check, and fix the identical check in join() so shutdown also terminates surviving workers.

grupos.texto: Do not break out of worker cleanup when the join deadline expires. If the first worker consumes the timeout, the next iteration breaks before terminating that worker or any subsequent workers. They may still be blocked in Redis or producer calls despite the shared stopped flag, leaving old workers running after strategy shutdown/reassignment. Apply the deadline only to waiting, and perform termination cleanup for every worker regardless of remaining time (using a type check that recognizes spawn-context workers).
outros: join() breaks out of the worker loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping cleanup for every remaining worker. If next_step.join consumes the timeout or an earlier worker exhausts it, remaining flushers can continue running after shutdown or partition reassignment. Use the deadline only to limit waiting and still terminate and reap every remaining process.

grupos.texto: `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses a truthiness test, so an explicit 0 is treated as 'unset' and silently expands to one process per shard. Use `max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and reject values below 1.

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because the test patches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so nothing waits for the flusher threads before `step.join()` and the `messages` assertion. Replace it with a condition-based wait, such as polling until `messages` is non-empty with a deadline. Use the real sleep saved before patching if a delay is needed.

The docstring says the flusher 'Creates one process per shard', but the number of processes is capped by max_processes (--flusher-processes), and shards are shared across processes via i % num_processes. Reword it to say that shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

The wait_produce timer tags with "shards", while the sibling metrics in the same loop use "shard" for the same value (shard_tag). Use one tag key, "shard", so queries and dashboards that group by it cover all of these metrics.
outros: The wait_produce timer is tagged `shards`, while the other metrics in this function (produce timer, segment_size_bytes) use `shard`. Data for the same tag is therefore split across two names. Use `shard` consistently.

grupos.texto: The kill guard `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is likely False for spawn-context processes (`SpawnProcess` is not a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process`). A hung flusher is then never killed, and a new process is started for the same shards, so two flushers consume the same shards concurrently and may double-produce segments. Guard with `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`, or check `hasattr(process, 'kill')`, so the hung process is killed before it is replaced.
outros: The kill is now gated by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes are created via `mp_context.Process` (SpawnProcess), which does not subclass `multiprocessing.Process`, so the check is False and a hung process is never killed before a replacement is started. This leaves duplicate flushers running on the same shards. Check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`, or call `kill()` unconditionally as before.

The kill is now guarded by isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process), but spawn-context processes are SpawnProcess (a BaseProcess subclass), so the check is false and a hung process is never killed. Restart then creates a second process for the same shards while the old one keeps running. Check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`, or `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`, before calling kill().

grupos.texto: kill/terminate isinstance check against spawn context fails on Linux (SpawnProcess is not multiprocessing.Process) so kill is skipped, leaving hung/crashed flushers alive.
negative max_processes flows through `or` guard into min() -> empty map -> KeyError on i % num_processes; empty assigned_shards yields zero processes.
join() waits for processes sequentially against a single shared deadline and breaks without terminating remaining processes once it expires, leaking them.
submit() loop calls buffer.get_memory_info() per flusher but each call is cluster-wide from same client, repeating identical INFO N× per submit.

Metric tag key disagrees: produce timer uses tags={"shard": ...} but wait_produce timer uses tags={"shards": ...} for the same flush. Use the same key in both so queries/dashboards correlate the two stages.

Docstring 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing' is made untrue by the new max_processes-capped sharing (num_processes=min(max_processes,len(shards)), round-robin). With default --flusher-processes=1 one process handles all shards. Update doc to describe capped/shared-shard manager.

time.sleep(0.1) wait is neutralized by monkeypatch.setattr('time.sleep', lambda _: None) at top of test, so it returns immediately and provides no synchronization for flusher threads. Use unpatched sleep, poll condition with deadline, or rely on join instead of fixed sleep.

goldens.comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

span-buffer-multiprocess-enhancement-wit.prTitle: Span Buffer Multiprocess Enhancement with Health Monitoring

grupos.texto: The outbound task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` with a second argument. This PR updated the two base implementations (`IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync` and `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` in mixins/issues.py) to accept it, but any concrete integration that overrides `should_sync` with the pre-PR signature `(self, attribute)` was not updated. Such an override still works for the existing 1-arg caller `where_should_sync` (sync.py:48), but at this new 2-arg call site it raises `TypeError: should_sync() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given`, crashing the assignee-outbound task for that provider. Verify all `should_sync` overrides accept the new parameter (or pass it as a keyword so the mismatch is at least explicit), otherwise this call breaks them at runtime.

The dataclass field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value (which is exactly what `from_integration` does, and what `from_dict` falls back to when the key is absent) shares the same frozen import-time timestamp instead of the moment the assignment was actually queued. This makes the `queued` timestamp semantically wrong/meaningless (it reflects process start, not assignment time) and would silently misreport the queue time anywhere this value is later inspected. Fix by defaulting in a factory/`__post_init__` or making the caller pass the timestamp, e.g. set `queued` inside `from_integration` (`queued=timezone.now()`), or use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.
outros: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition (module import) time, so every AssignmentSource created by `from_integration` gets the same stale process-start timestamp instead of the moment the assignment was queued. The field is meant to record when the assignment entered the sync pipeline, so it silently reports the wrong time for the entire life of the process. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (importing `field` from dataclasses) so each instance gets a fresh timestamp; the added test at tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:29-38 only checks `is not None` and cannot catch this.

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the class body executes (module import), so every AssignmentSource instance shares the same timestamp — the time the module was imported, not the time the assignment was queued. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (or set `queued` explicitly at construction) so each source records its own enqueue time; as written the field cannot do the job it was added for and cannot be corrected afterwards because the dataclass is frozen.

grupos.texto: The test is named test_from_dict_empty_array but it passes an empty dict ({}), not an empty array; a caller reading the name will believe the empty-list/array input path is covered when it is not. Rename it to test_from_dict_empty_dict (or pass [] to actually cover the empty-array case) so the identifier agrees with the input it exercises.
outros: test_from_dict_empty_array names an empty array but constructs an empty dict (`data: dict[str, Any] = {}`), so it only re-exercises the empty/None path and never covers empty-array input; a regression specific to that input would pass unnoticed. Pass a real empty array or rename the test to match its body.

grupos.texto: `to_dict` emits `queued` as a raw `datetime` (dataclass field default in from_integration is a live timezone.now() value), but this dict is placed into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)` in src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:137-144 and serialized by the Celery task serializer on the way to the consumer in src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py, which reconstructs it via `AssignmentSource.from_dict`. A datetime is not JSON-native, so the value either fails to serialize at enqueue (breaking outbound propagation to other integrations) or comes back as a plain string, so `from_dict` builds an AssignmentSource whose `queued` silently violates the declared `datetime` type. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `datetime.isoformat()`) in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict` so the producer and consumer agree on the representation.
outros: `to_dict` uses `asdict`, which leaves `queued` as a raw `datetime` object in the dict. That dict is passed straight into a celery task kwarg in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (`assignment_source_dict=assignment_source.to_dict()`), i.e. it is the payload crossing the serialization boundary. Send a serializable form instead (e.g. `queued.isoformat()` / `queued.timestamp()`), and make `from_dict` parse it back to a `datetime`, so the value survives the queue round trip instead of raising at encode time or arriving as a string where the annotation promises a datetime.

grupos.texto: test_from_dict_empty_array passes {} rather than an empty array. It therefore only tests missing required dictionary keys and would still pass if rejection of an array input were broken. Pass [] to exercise the named case (or rename this test to empty_dict if that is the intended contract).

`timezone.now()` is evaluated once when this module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value carries the worker's import timestamp rather than the assignment's queue time. `from_integration()` always takes this default, and `to_dict()` propagates the stale timestamp into outbound task payloads; long-running workers therefore emit incorrect assignment metadata. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance receives its own creation timestamp.
outros: The queued default is evaluated once when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit timestamp shares the worker's import-time timestamp. Both inbound assignment and deassignment use from_integration without supplying queued, so their serialized context records the wrong queue time for all subsequent events. Use dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now) to generate the timestamp per instance.

`timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value reports the same worker-start timestamp, even for assignments queued hours later. This makes the serialized `queued` timestamp incorrect. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each source records its own creation time, and test creation at two different times.

grupos.texto: test_to_dict asserts `result.get("queued") is not None`, but `queued` always has a default value, so the assertion cannot fail. Pass an explicit `queued` datetime and assert that to_dict returns exactly that value, or compare the whole dict.
test_from_dict_empty_array passes an empty dict, not an array, so the name does not match the body. Rename it to test_from_dict_empty_dict.

The field `queued` reads as the time the assignment was queued, but `timezone.now()` as a plain default is evaluated once at import time. Every AssignmentSource therefore carries the same stale timestamp. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so the value matches the name.
outros: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition (import time), so every AssignmentSource gets the same stale timestamp. This makes the `queued` field meaningless and wrong for any consumer. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import time, so every AssignmentSource gets the same stale process-start timestamp instead of its creation time. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance records when it was actually created.

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import time, so every AssignmentSource shares the same stale timestamp instead of the time it was created. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

grupos.texto: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import time, so every instance gets the same timestamp. Use a default factory (e.g. `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` in a dataclass) so the timestamp is computed per instance.

WHAT: `to_dict()` via `asdict()` returns a raw `datetime` for `queued`, which is then passed as Celery task kwargs in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (`assignment_source.to_dict()`). WHY: datetime is not JSON-serializable for the task serializer and round-trips back as a string that `from_dict` never parses, leaving `queued` as str type or crashing serialization. HOW: serialize `queued` to ISO string in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict`.

WHAT: `AssignmentSource.from_dict()` returns None on invalid/extra/missing keys and the task treats None as no-source, so `should_sync('outbound_assignee', None)` returns True. WHY: a corrupt or tampered `assignment_source_dict` fails open and re-enables the outbound sync the PR intends to suppress, resuming the cycle. HOW: distinguish parse-failure from absent source (log + skip sync, or fail closed).

WHAT: `assignment_source` param was added to `sync_status_outbound` instead of `sync_assignee_outbound`, while the task calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)` whose abstract declares only `**kwargs`. WHY: concrete `sync_assignee_outbound` overrides without `**kwargs` will raise TypeError on the new kwarg, and the status method gains a dead param that is never checked. HOW: declare `assignment_source` explicitly on `sync_assignee_outbound` abstract (and update overrides) and remove it from `sync_status_outbound` unless status sync needs the same guard.

Test name claims empty_array but body passes empty dict {}: rename to test_from_dict_empty_dict or add a true empty-list case, otherwise the array behaviour it names is never exercised and the test passes even if array handling is broken.

Typo in test name test_from_dict_inalid_data hides it from name-filtered runs (e.g. -k invalid_data): fix spelling to test_from_dict_invalid_data so the invalid-payload guard is actually selected and verified.

WHAT: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates once at class-definition time so every AssignmentSource without explicit queued shares the same timestamp. WHY: queued time is wrong/stale for all later instances and defeats its purpose as a queue-time marker. HOW: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (with `field` import).
outros: Field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import so all AssignmentSources share the same timestamp. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance measures its actual creation/queue time.

goldens.comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

grupos.texto: The parameter is named `org` but the code treats it as the pipeline's active-organization context: it dereferences `org.organization` and every caller (error() and the GitHubInstallation sites) passes `self.active_organization`, not an Organization. The name misstates the argument's type/contract — a caller following the name and passing a real Organization would hit AttributeError on `.organization`. Rename the parameter (e.g. `active_organization`) and correct the corresponding name in `error()` at line 131 so the two signatures match what is actually passed.

The OAuth `state` value is compared to the secret per-flow `pipeline.signature` with a plain `!=` string comparison, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and leaks a prefix-match timing signal about the state nonce. Since this check is the CSRF/authenticity guard for the install flow, use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `hmac.compare_digest(request.GET.get("state", ""), pipeline.signature)` / `sentry.utils.security.constant_time_compare`) instead of `!=`.

This test no longer verifies the "installation not found" path it exists for. The second GET supplies state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the github pipeline signature (that is the 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3 asserted in test_github_setup and reused elsewhere). OAuthLoginView.dispatch (integration.py:412-413) therefore returns error() before GitHubInstallation runs, producing the same generic "Invalid installation request." message and the same failed template via the state-mismatch branch. The Integration.DoesNotExist handling at integration.py:493-498 is never reached, so the test would still pass if that handling were removed or broken. Use the real pipeline state so the request advances into GitHubInstallation, or assert on something that distinguishes the state-mismatch branch from the missing-installation branch.

GitHubInstallation now refuses the installation unless the pipeline already carries `github_authenticated_user`, but that state is produced only by the newly prepended OAuthLoginView (see the `get_pipeline_views` change at line 344). Any caller that drives this provider's second step without the new preceding OAuth view — e.g. a subclass/related provider that reuses `GitHubInstallation` (or keeps a GitHubInstallation-only `get_pipeline_views`) — will have `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` evaluate to None, never match `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, and always render the ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST failure page. The install path that previously succeeded is now unconditionally rejected for those consumers. Either update every consumer to include OAuthLoginView in its pipeline, or make the authenticity check fall back when the OAuth step was not part of the pipeline.

integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] is indexed without checking that "sender" exists, so an ACTIVE integration whose metadata has no sender raises KeyError (500) here. metadata["sender"] is only populated when state.get("sender") is set (integration.py:376-377), and the only writer of that state is the installation webhook (webhook.py:202-208); integrations created through the pipeline itself carry no sender (confirmed by installation.py:44 which explicitly guards `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`, and by the pipeline-created integration in test_integration.py:730-743). Previously this branch only bound state and called pipeline.next_step(), so this crash is newly introduced. Fix: guard the lookup, e.g. `if pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != (integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login"):` and decide the desired fallback when sender is absent.
outros: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError. build_integration (line 376-377) only sets metadata["sender"] when state.get("sender") is truthy, so an existing Integration without a sender entry makes this subscripting throw an unhandled KeyError (500) instead of routing to the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and treat a missing sender as a failed verification) so the mismatch/absence case returns error() rather than crashing.

grupos.texto: The token request is executed outside the try block. If GitHub's token endpoint is unavailable or the request fails with a connection/timeout error, safe_urlopen raises before the guarded response parsing is reached, and this new installation step returns an unhandled server error instead of the installation-failed response. Include the request itself in the error handling and handle the relevant transport exceptions.

The replacement assertion no longer verifies that a nonexistent installation is rejected: 'Invalid installation request.' is also returned for a state mismatch, missing access token, or missing authenticated login before GitHubInstallation is reached. This test can therefore pass with installation-not-found handling broken if the callback fails OAuth validation instead. Establish a successful OAuth exchange with the actual pipeline state and verify that the nonexistent installation lookup is reached and rejected, rather than accepting this shared authentication-error message alone.

Translate the short-message literals at their definition/call sites instead of calling `_(error_short)` on a variable. Django's message extraction cannot extract the default `"Invalid installation request."` or the plain-string arguments at the two call sites from this dynamic gettext invocation. The existing pending-deletion and already-installed messages previously appeared directly inside `_()`; this refactor removes their extraction sites, and the new default message cannot enter translation catalogs. Use a translated default and translated arguments, then place `error_short` directly into the payload so these user-facing errors remain localizable.

Do not use pipeline.signature as OAuth state. It is a deterministic MD5 of the pipeline identifiers, not an unpredictable nonce tied to this user's authorization attempt (the tests reuse it across users). An attacker can know the expected state and submit a callback containing a code authorized under the attacker's GitHub account, defeating the OAuth login-CSRF protection and the intended binding to the installing user. Generate a cryptographically random per-attempt state, store it in the session/pipeline, and validate and consume it on callback.
outros: The OAuth state is pipeline.signature, which Pipeline.__init__ computes solely from pipeline view class names and therefore shares across all users and installation attempts. An attacker can obtain an OAuth code for their own GitHub account and send a callback using this known state to a victim with an active installation pipeline, binding the attacker's GitHub identity to the victim's flow instead of rejecting the forged callback. Generate a random per-attempt nonce, store it in pipeline state, and validate that nonce on the OAuth callback.

grupos.texto: The missing Integration branch advances the pipeline without verifying that github_authenticated_user installed the supplied installation_id. When the installation webhook has not created a record, or the local record was deleted, finish_pipeline calls build_integration using app credentials and attaches the installation without checking the OAuth user's access, allowing a user with another account's installation ID to bypass the new ownership check. Fail closed until trusted installer information is available and apply the ownership check before every successful next_step.
outros: The record-absent path advances the pipeline before checking whether the authenticated GitHub user installed this app. Installation IDs arrive from the request, and a missing Integration record (for example before the installation webhook is processed) does not establish ownership. As a result, this path can attach an installation belonging to a different GitHub user despite the new authenticity check. Verify the authenticated user's authorization for the installation before advancing in this branch too, rather than relying on the webhook-created record existing.

grupos.texto: The new check treats `metadata['sender']` as required, but the integration producer still only adds it when `state.get('sender')` is present, and the existing installation code explicitly supports metadata without sender. An active integration without an OrganizationIntegration and without this optional field reaches this branch and now raises KeyError instead of completing the previously supported setup (or returning the invalid-installation response). Handle missing sender explicitly with a safe failure or a verified migration/backfill rather than indexing the optional field.
outros: The new ownership check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] even though GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration omits sender for normal pipeline-created integrations. Reconnecting an existing active integration without an OrganizationIntegration and without webhook-populated sender now raises KeyError and returns a server error rather than an installation failure. Handle missing sender explicitly and return the invalid-installation response when trusted installer metadata is unavailable.

grupos.texto: When no Integration row exists for the installation_id, the code calls next_step() without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the installer. An attacker can supply an installation_id they do not own before the installation webhook has created the row, and bypass the new verification. Do not skip the check in this branch. Either fail closed, or verify ownership another way, for example by confirming the user can access the installation through the GitHub API.

safe_urlopen sits outside the try block, and get_user_info can raise on network or API errors, so transport failures during the token exchange or user lookup propagate as unhandled 500s. Wrap both calls in try/except and return error(request, self.active_organization).

The OAuth `state` value is compared to `pipeline.signature` with a plain `!=`, which is not a constant-time comparison of a secret token. Use `django.utils.crypto.constant_time_compare(request.GET.get("state", ""), pipeline.signature)` instead.

The helper calls `_(error_short)` on a variable, and callers pass plain string literals. The translation extractor cannot see these strings, so the short error messages sent to the user are no longer translatable; the old code wrapped the literals directly in `_()`. Mark the literals with gettext_lazy at the call sites and the default, and pass them through without wrapping again.

test_github_user_mismatch asserts only the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message, which every error() path in OAuthLoginView and GitHubInstallation returns. A wrong hardcoded state, a token failure or a missing integration would pass it just as well as a real sender/login mismatch. Make the mismatch the only possible failure: derive the state from the actual pipeline signature, and assert that the same flow succeeds when the webhook sender is 'octocat'.

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` raises KeyError/TypeError when the existing Integration has no `sender` metadata, for example integrations created before the webhook stored it. The installation flow then crashes with a 500 instead of rendering the error page. Read it defensively, e.g. `(integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login")`, and return `error(...)` when it is missing or does not match.
outros: integration.metadata['sender']['login'] is indexed without a guard, but build_integration only sets 'sender' when it is present in state. Existing integrations without sender metadata will raise KeyError and return a 500. Use .get() chains and show the error page when the sender is missing.

The new check indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. `installation.py` line 44 already treats "sender" as optional in metadata. An Integration without a stored sender raises KeyError and the request returns a 500 instead of the install flow's error page. Read it with `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and return `error(...)` when it is missing or does not match.

grupos.texto: WHAT: The Integration.DoesNotExist branch returns pipeline.next_step() with no github_authenticated_user verification. WHY: The Integration row is created asynchronously by the installation webhook, so completing the pipeline before webhook delivery skips the installer-vs-OAuth-user mismatch check this PR is meant to enforce, letting a mismatched user finish setup. HOW: Require the Integration/sender record to exist (or defer/verify via live API) before advancing instead of auto-advancing.

error_short strings bypass translation extraction: _(error_short) uses a variable so makemessages cannot collect them. Wrap literals at definition/call sites, e.g. error_short=_("Invalid installation request.") and pass _("...") literals, then use data error value directly without re-wrapping.

First response (installation_id) is overwritten by second response (bad state) with no assertion, so the Integration.DoesNotExist / not-ACTIVE branch in GitHubInstallation is never verified. Keep/assert the first flow through a valid OAuth step to reach the installation check instead of only asserting the OAuth state-mismatch error.

WHAT: GitHubInstallation directly indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no guards for missing keys. WHY: Legacy integrations created before sender tracking (build_integration only sets sender conditionally; installation endpoint explicitly handles 'sender not in metadata') hit KeyError and 500 instead of the error page. HOW: Use .get() chain and return error() when sender/login is absent.
outros: Direct subscript integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] throws KeyError (unhandled 500) when metadata lacks sender/login (e.g., older integrations or unexpected webhook payload). Use chained .get() with fallback to error() instead of assuming keys exist.

grupos.texto: WHAT: safe_urlopen token exchange and get_user_info() (which calls resp.raise_for_status()) are called with no exception handling. WHY: Any network error, timeout, or non-2xx from GitHub bubbles up as an unhandled exception and 500s the install instead of rendering the invalid-request page. HOW: Wrap the exchange plus get_user_info in try/except and return error() on failure.
outros: safe_urlopen() and get_user_info() are called outside any try/except, so network errors, non-2xx responses, or API failures raise unhandled exceptions instead of returning error(). Wrap the token exchange + user-info fetch in try/except and return error() on failure, matching the handled missing-access_token path.

goldens.comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation

grupos.texto: The docstring says evaluate "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`", but this PR changed the method to return a dict keyed by group_key (`results = {}` ... `results[result.group_key] = result`). The documentation now contradicts the signature and body, so a caller trusting the docstring will treat the return value as a list. Update the docstring to describe the dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult] return (one entry per evaluated group key).

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler (an abc.ABC) with only `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler declares four abstract methods — counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data (detector.py:142-170) — none of which are implemented here. The class therefore remains abstract and cannot be instantiated; Detector.detector_handler's `group_type.detector_handler(self)` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler` for the metric_alert_fire group type. Previously this class was a concrete DetectorHandler with an implemented evaluate, so this PR newly makes it uninstantiable. Implement the required abstract methods (or revert to a concrete handler) to satisfy the base-class contract.
outros: WHAT: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with an empty body, so it does not implement the abstract methods counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data declared on StatefulDetectorHandler. WHY: the class is now abstract, and Detector.detector_handler (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86) instantiates it via group_type.detector_handler(self), so any detector whose type resolves to this grouptype will raise TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler — the previous version implemented evaluate and was instantiable. HOW: implement the required abstract methods (or keep a concrete evaluate override) so the handler can be constructed.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but with `pass`, so it implements none of the abstract methods it inherits (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data). The class is therefore still abstract and instantiating it (it is registered as `detector_handler` on MetricAlertFire and is constructed by Detector.detector_handler) raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. Before this change it subclassed DetectorHandler and implemented the single abstract `evaluate`, so it was instantiable; the PR makes the metric-alert handler path throw. Either implement the required abstract methods or keep the class free of unimplemented abstracts.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed to inherit from StatefulDetectorHandler with an empty `pass` body. StatefulDetectorHandler is an ABC that requires implementations of `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (all called from its concrete `evaluate`, and implemented by the test's MockDetectorStateHandler). Since none of these are provided, the class is now abstract and can no longer be instantiated — instantiating it (e.g. via Detector.detector_handler) raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class. It was instantiable before this change, so either implement these methods or keep it a non-abstract handler until the stateful abstraction is ready.

grupos.texto: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value: int` but never uses it (the occurrence is built only from `group_key`/`new_status`), and this same helper is also the implementation of `MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Because neither the expected occurrence nor the handler output depends on the value, tests like `test_state_results_multi_group` (which incorrectly builds the group_2 occurrence with `value=6` while the packet carries `10`) and `TestEvaluate.test_dedupe` (expected built with 6 vs packet 8) pass regardless of the value actually passed into `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. If evaluation passed a wrong value, these tests would still pass, so they do not verify the value/threshold path they appear to cover. grupos.texto: checkIfIsAvailable interprets date overrides in the wrong timezone: the producer (slots.ts:411-415) attaches `timeZone` (the override owner's tz) to each date override and packages/lib/slots.ts:211-225 consumes `override.timeZone` to place the override window; but here `dateOverrides` is typed/used without `timeZone` and the offset is derived from the function-level `organizerTimeZone` (`dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1`). When an override's owner timezone differs from `organizerTimeZone`, the day grid this validator uses to accept/reject a slot differs from the grid getSlots used to generate it, so generated override slots get incorrectly filtered (and the `* -1` sign is opposite to lib's `invitee - organizer`). Use the per-override `date.timeZone` (as lib does) so both files agree on which timezone defines an override.

WHAT: `end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — an exact duplicate of `start` — instead of using `slotEndTime`. WHY: the working-hours upper-bound test `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore compares the slot START against the working-day end, so a slot whose start is inside working hours but whose end (start + eventLength) overruns `workingHour.endTime` is never filtered and is reported as available, allowing bookings outside the host's working hours. HOW: compute `const end = slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute();`.
outros: `end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`, so it always equals `start`. The `end > workingHour.endTime` check is identical to the `start` check and never catches a slot that starts within working hours but ends past them. Use `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()` for `end`.

`end` is computed identically to `start` (both from slotStartTime), so the check `start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` can never reject a slot on the upper bound. A slot starting inside working hours but ending after workingHour.endTime is wrongly considered available; derive `end` from slotEndTime instead.

`end` is computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, making it identical to `start`. The working-hours guard `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore never detects a slot that ends after the working day, and slots overrunning an organizer's working hours are reported as available. Use slotEndTime (slotEndTime.hour()*60 + slotEndTime.minute()) for `end`.
Genuine logic bug: `end = slotStartTime.hour()*60 + slotStartTime.minute()` is incorrect.

grupos.texto: WHAT: when `dateOverrideExist` is true the function returns `true` before running the `busy.every(...)` check at the end. WHY: on any day that has a matching date override, a slot inside the override is reported available without checking the host's existing bookings (`busy` is spread via `...schedule`/`...userSchedule`), so a fixed/loose host who already has a booking during the override window is still shown as free — enabling double-booking. HOW: do not return early here; fall through so the override branch only decides whether the slot is inside the override window, and let the existing `busy` evaluation decide availability (e.g. `if (dateOverrideExist) { /* within override, still check busy */ } else { /* fall through to busy */ }`).
outros: The new `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` short-circuits the `busy` conflict check (and the workingHours check) for any slot that falls inside a date override window. Every caller of `checkIfIsAvailable` previously counted on it returning false for a slot that overlaps an existing booking; on days covered by a date override that guarantee is gone, so slots conflicting with the user's real bookings are now reported as available and can be double-booked. The override branch should let control fall through to the `busy.every(...)` check (returning true only for the availability-window part) instead of returning early.

grupos.texto: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two separate dayjs object references, so `===` is always false. The zero-length date-override branch is dead code and such an override is never recognised as covering the day; compare values (e.g. .isSame() or .valueOf() === .valueOf()) instead.
outros: This compares two separately constructed dayjs objects with `===` (reference equality), which is always false, so a zero-length override (start equal to end, whole day blocked) never returns true here. Compare timestamps, e.g. `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))`.

grupos.texto: The override bounds reject only non-overlapping slots rather than requiring the entire event to fit inside an override. A fixed host with a 10:00–11:00 override accepts a 10:30–11:30 event generated from another host's availability, despite being unavailable for its final half hour. Accept only when at least one override contains both slotStartTime and slotEndTime; this also avoids rejecting a slot merely because another interval on the same date does not overlap it.

A weekday with no matching working-hours entry falls through to the busy checks and is treated as available when there are no conflicts. In round-robin events, slots generated for a loose host can consequently include a fixed host whose schedule excludes that day. Reject slots unless a working-hours interval on the slot's weekday contains the event, when no date override applies.

Timezone conversion takes only hour and minute, discarding day rollover and turning intervals crossing attendee midnight into reversed ranges. A UTC organizer's 22:00–23:00 override viewed in UTC+01:30 becomes startTime 1410 and endTime 30, which buildSlots skips because start is greater than end, removing valid availability. Preserve the converted dates and split the interval across attendee-day boundaries before building slots.

The variable named end is calculated from slotStartTime, exactly like start, instead of slotEndTime. A slot starting at 16:45 with a 30-minute duration passes a working-hours window ending at 17:00 despite ending at 17:15. Calculate the end boundary from the slot end.

The equality check compares two separately created Dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, even when the override start and end represent the same instant. The intended zero-length/closed-day rejection is unreachable, and a slot beginning exactly at that instant can reach the dateOverrideExist success return. Compare timestamps or use isSame instead.

Do not return true before checking busy periods when a date override exists. Previously, checkIfIsAvailable rejected overlapping calendar events/bookings (apart from the explicit currentSeats exception), and the fixed-host and loose-host consumers still rely on that behavior when passing their schedules. With this early return, any slot accepted by the override branch is considered available even if the host has a conflicting booking. Let the override bypass only the normal working-hours check, then continue through busy.every.
outros: A matching date override returns true before checking busy periods. Both fixed-host and loose-host callers pass calendar and booking conflicts in busy, so a host with an override is offered even when an existing booking overlaps the slot. Continue to the busy checks after validating the override instead of returning true.

Do not return true before checking busy intervals when a date override matches. For example, with a 09:00–17:00 override and an existing 10:00–11:00 booking, a candidate at 10:00 sets dateOverrideExist and returns true here, bypassing busy.every entirely. The fixed-host filtering and loose-host assignment both call this predicate with date overrides, so an already-booked host can be advertised as available. Let a valid override bypass only the normal working-hours check, then continue through the busy checks.

A matching date override returns true before the busy.every check below. Consequently a host with an override is considered available even when an existing booking or calendar busy interval overlaps the slot. An override should replace normal working hours, not bypass busy-time checks; continue to the busy check after validating the override.

grupos.texto: The working-hours predicate rejects a slot if any interval on its weekday does not contain it. A split schedule of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00 therefore loses every slot, since each valid slot lies outside the other interval. Require at least one matching interval to contain the full event instead of finding an interval that excludes it.
outros: This search rejects a slot if it falls outside any working-hours window on that weekday. With split hours of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, a valid 10:00 slot is rejected because it is outside the afternoon window. Check for containment in at least one applicable window rather than finding any window that excludes the slot.

grupos.texto: The upper bound checks whether slotStartTime is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override end but finishes after it is treated as available. Compare slotEndTime with the override end using isAfter, so the slot must fit entirely inside the override.

The working-hours check computes `end` from slotStartTime, the same value as `start`, so `end > workingHour.endTime` can never be true unless `start` is also out of range. Slots that start inside working hours but run past the end are therefore not rejected. The slot start and slot end are also compared in UTC, while workingHour.startTime and endTime are minutes in the host's own timezone, so the check is wrong for any non-UTC host. Fix: use `slotEndTime.hour()*60 + slotEndTime.minute()` for `end`, and convert the slot into the host's timezone before comparing.
outros: The variable `end` is named as the slot end but is computed from `slotStartTime`, so it is identical to `start`. The `end > workingHour.endTime` check therefore never tests the slot's real end. Compute `end` from `slotEndTime` (hour*60+minute) so the name and the check agree.

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime`, so it equals `start`. The `end > workingHour.endTime` check therefore tests the slot's start, and slots that begin inside working hours but end after them are treated as available. Compute `end` from `slotEndTime`.

`end` is computed from slotStartTime, the same expression as `start`, so the `end > workingHour.endTime` check never looks at the slot's end. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past closing time passes this check. Compute `end` from slotEndTime (hour*60+minute).

The working-hours check rejects the slot if any one working-hour entry for that weekday doesn't contain it, so a host with split shifts loses every slot in each shift that isn't the entry being tested. It also compares UTC hour/minute against organizer-timezone minutes, and `end` is computed from the slot start rather than the slot end. Mark the slot available if at least one entry contains it (`some`), convert the slot to the organizer timezone first, and compute `end` from slotEndTime.

grupos.texto: The check `dayjs(a) === dayjs(b)` compares object references, so it is always false. The zero-length date override case (an unavailable-all-day override with start equal to end) is therefore never detected, and slots on a day the host marked unavailable are treated as available. Fix: use `dayjs(date.start).isSame(dayjs(date.end))`.
outros: This compares two dayjs objects with `===`, which is reference equality and is always false, so the branch never runs. The branch is meant to mark a day with a zero-length override (start equals end) as fully unavailable, and it never does. Compare with `.isSame(...)` or `.valueOf()`.
`===` on two dayjs objects compares references, so it is always false and the override-is-unavailable (start equals end) case is never detected. Use `.isSame(...)` instead.

grupos.texto: WHAT: Outside-working-hours test uses workingHours.find() returning true if ANY entry rejects the slot. WHY: With split schedules (two entries same weekday, e.g. morning+afternoon) a valid morning slot is outside the afternoon entry, find() matches and the slot is wrongly rejected as outside hours. HOW: Invert logic to accept if ANY entry contains the slot (e.g. !workingHours.some(entry contains slot) => outside).

WHAT: activeOverrides are filtered by UTC day (line 206-207) before the invitee/organizer offset is applied (lines 212-224), and shifted hours are not re-bucketed across midnight. WHY: An override that shifts to the previous/next calendar day in the invitee timezone is dropped from the wrong day or applied to the wrong day, so slots show open when the organizer is off (and vice versa). HOW: Filter/bucket overrides in the invitee-local date after applying the offset, or emit split entries spanning two invitee days.

WHAT: Line 114 compares two Dayjs objects with === (reference equality), which is always false. WHY: The all-day/unavailable override branch (start==end) can never trigger, so a full-day-off override falls through to partial-overlap checks and can be treated as available. HOW: Compare instants with .isSame()/.valueOf(), e.g. dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset,'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset,'minutes')).
outros: Compares dayjs objects with === which is always false (reference equality), so the start==end branch can never execute. Use .isSame() for value comparison.

grupos.texto: WHAT: Working-hours check computes both start and end from slotStartTime (line 141-142), ignoring eventLength/slotEndTime. WHY: Slots that start inside working hours but end after closing are wrongly accepted as available, allowing over-long bookings past closing. HOW: Compute end from slotEndTime, e.g. slotEndTime.hour()*60+slotEndTime.minute().
outros: end duplicates start: both use slotStartTime.hour()/minute(). Compute end from slotEndTime so slots overhanging workingHour.endTime are rejected.

Working-hours check computes both start and end from slotStartTime (lines 141-142 identical). end should derive from slotEndTime so eventLength is enforced; as written a slot starting inside hours but ending outside is reported available.

goldens.comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
