Rename the method to `include_website_name?` so the serializer base class honors it.
outros: WHAT: `include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?` required by ActiveModelSerializers. WHY: every other conditional-inclusion guard in this file uses the `?` form (`define_method "include_#{attr}?"` at lines 9/18/27, `include_email?` at line 117), and AMS 0.8.3 resolves the guard as `include_<attr>?`; because this method lacks the `?` it is never invoked, so the intended `website.present?` condition is silently ignored and `website_name` is always serialized. HOW: rename to `def include_website_name?`.

The guard method is named `include_website_name`, but ActiveModelSerializers (and this file's own convention, e.g. `include_email?` at line 117) resolves per-attribute guards via `include_<attribute>?`. Because the name lacks the trailing `?`, the framework never invokes it: the `website.present?` guard is dead code and `website_name` is serialized unconditionally, emitting `website_name: null` for users without a website. Rename to `include_website_name?`.

grupos.texto: Hostname comparisons are case-sensitive even though DNS hostnames are case-insensitive. With an instance hostname of example.com and a valid website of http://EXAMPLE.COM/user, neither the exact-host nor suffix comparison matches, so the profile displays only EXAMPLE.COM instead of the requested path. Normalize both hostnames to lowercase for comparison while preserving the desired display spelling.

Comparing all labels except the first incorrectly treats unrelated domains under multi-label public suffixes as the same domain. For example, with instance host `forum.co.uk` and website `https://unrelated.co.uk/user`, this returns `unrelated.co.uk/user` rather than the unrelated-site host-only label. Both hosts have three labels and their suffixes are `co.uk`, so this branch mistakes the public suffix for a shared site domain. Use registrable-domain-aware comparison (or a narrower explicit host relationship) before including the path.

Apply the same untrusted-attribute visibility policy to website_name as to website. website is listed in untrusted_attributes, which hides it for TL0 users viewed anonymously, but include_website_name checks only website.present?. Anonymous responses can therefore disclose the hidden website's hostname (and its path for matching domains) through this new field even when website itself is omitted.

The same-label-count branch treats two hosts as the same domain when everything after the first label matches. Unrelated hosts on shared suffixes, such as `a.github.io` and `b.github.io`, are treated as the same domain, so the full path is shown for an unrelated website. Compare against the registrable domain, for example with the PublicSuffix gem, or drop this heuristic branch.

WHAT: Else branch only tests `discourse_host.ends_with?('.'+website_host)` (discourse child of website) and misses the reverse (website subdomain of instance). WHY: With instance `example.com` and website `http://sub.example.com/page`, it returns `sub.example.com` instead of `sub.example.com/page`, contradicting the PR intent to show the full path for same-base-domain URLs. HOW: Also return host+path when `website_host` ends with `.`+discourse_host or shares the same registrable domain.

WHAT: include filter is named `include_website_name` without `?`, while AMS requires `include_<attr>?` (cf. include_email?, include_card_image_badge_id?). WHY: The predicate is never called so `website_name` is always serialized and bypasses the TL0-anonymous `restrict_user_fields?` hiding applied to `website` via `untrusted_attributes`, leaking a restricted user's website host+path to anonymous viewers. HOW: Rename to `include_website_name?` and add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` (or check `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` inside).
outros: Predicate is named include_website_name but AMS calls include_website_name? (with ?), as shown by include_card_image_badge_id? in the same file. Rename to include_website_name? so the website.present? guard is actually consulted.

goldens.comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

ux-show-complete-url-path-if-website-dom.prTitle: UX: show complete URL path if website domain is same as instance domain

grupos.texto: WHAT: runShardSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (line 52), but it then delegates each sub-request to runSplitQuery (line 163), which this PR also changed to call datasource.applyTemplateVariables again (querySplitting.ts:299), so each target is interpolated (and ad hoc filters applied) twice. WHY: double interpolation re-runs addAdHocFilters on an already-filtered expression; the stream-selector path masks the duplicate via labelExists() dedup in addFilterToStreamSelector (modifyQuery.ts:494), but parsed/structured-metadata labels use addFilterAsLabelFilter which does not dedup, producing duplicated label filters, and any interpolated value containing '$' can be re-interpolated. This is confirmed by the updated test expecting applyTemplateVariables toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5) for a single target (1 call here + 4 sub-requests through runSplitQuery) instead of 1. HOW: interpolate only once — either remove the interpolation added to runShardSplitQuery and let runSplitQuery do it, or have splitQueriesByStreamShard pass the already-interpolated targets without re-interpolating in runSplitQuery.

The `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters))` is correctly covered by the new test. If removed, the expr reaching runQuery would retain `$__auto` and step would remain `$step`.
Interpolation in `runShardSplitQuery` is covered by the new test, which uses a real datasource. If `applyTemplateVariables` were not applied, `$__auto`/`$step` would survive.

The order of operations was inverted relative to the previous contract: interpolation used to run before the `expr`/`hide` filters (interpolateVariablesInQueries(targets).filter(...)), and now the filters run on the *raw* targets before `applyTemplateVariables` is applied. Filtering on the un-interpolated `query.expr` means the previous fallback that dropped a target once variable substitution had emptied its expression no longer exists: a target like `{ expr: '$myVar' }` whose variable resolves to '' is truthy at filter time, survives, is then interpolated to `''`, and is passed into the shard splitting/execution loop as a blank query. To preserve the old contract the filters should run on the interpolated result (or the interpolated expr should be re-checked for emptiness).

Interpolating (line 299) before the splitting partition (line 300) breaks the `$__range` guard. `querySupportsSplitting`/`isQueryWithRangeVariable` deliberately keeps queries with `$__range` out of splitting because that variable is interpolated against the split time range and would be wrong (see the comment at lines 285-287). applyTemplateVariables/templateSrv.replace substitutes built-in variables like `$__range`/`$__interval`/`$__auto`, so by the time `partition(... !querySupportsSplitting(query))` runs the expression no longer contains `$__range`, the guard returns false, and such queries are now split — producing range-windowed results computed against each chunk instead of the whole query range. Keep the range-variable check on the un-interpolated expression: run the partition/querySupportsSplitting test on the raw targets (or capture the raw expr before mapping) and only interpolate the queries that actually go to execution.
outros: Interpolating the targets here (via applyTemplateVariables) happens before the partition that calls querySupportsSplitting(), so its `!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` guard now inspects the already-interpolated expression. $__range is resolved by the frontend templateSrv.replace used inside applyTemplateVariables, so the raw `$__range` token the guard looks for is gone by the time the guard runs, and queries using $__range are no longer excluded from splitting. Per the comment right above (lines 285-286), those queries must not be split because the $__range interpolation uses the split time range and yields incorrect results. Preserve the range-variable check against the original, un-interpolated expr (e.g. run querySupportsSplitting on request.targets, or evaluate isQueryWithRangeVariable before applying applyTemplateVariables).

grupos.texto: The newly interpolated targets are interpolated again by DataSourceWithBackend.query when runQuery executes each split request. TemplateSrv.replace scans the resulting string again, so a variable whose literal value contains another defined variable token (for example, a log-search value containing `$other`) is expanded a second time and produces a different query from the non-splitting path; shard splitting also passes through this additional interpolation. Preserve the early interpolation needed for partitioning while ensuring already-interpolated targets are not interpolated again on execution, and test through the real backend query preparation rather than mocking runQuery.

Targets are interpolated here with `applyTemplateVariables`, including ad hoc filters, and then sent to `datasource.runQuery`, which interpolates them again through the backend path (datasource.ts:324/377). The ad hoc filters may be injected twice, and already-substituted values are re-interpolated, which can produce wrong or invalid LogQL. Interpolate only once. Either clear `scopedVars` and `filters` on the sub-requests after the first pass, or skip interpolation in `runQuery` for already-interpolated requests. The same issue applies to shardQuerySplitting.ts:52.

The `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` assertion in the new interpolation tests is brittle because it hardcodes the number of split requests. It still fails if interpolation is dropped, but it may break on unrelated changes to the splitting logic. Consider asserting on the interpolated expr/step instead of, or in addition to, the exact call count.

WHAT: Queries are interpolated with applyTemplateVariables upfront but each sharded sub-request via datasource.runQuery re-applies applyTemplateVariables downstream (test expects 5 calls for 1 target proves it). WHY: Duplicates ad-hoc filters and repeats interpolation per shard group producing wrong/duplicated selectors. HOW: Interpolate once — either keep upfront call and bypass second application in runQuery path or revert to single interpolation point.
outros: WHAT: Queries are interpolated with applyTemplateVariables upfront but sub-requests via datasource.runQuery re-apply template variables/ad-hoc filters in DataSourceWithBackend.query. WHY: Causes duplicate ad-hoc filter injection (addAdHocFilters applied twice) and wrong output on split queries. HOW: Skip re-interpolation downstream (e.g. strip filters after first pass or route split requests to avoid second applyTemplateVariables).

goldens.comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

grupos.texto: The rejection message reads `"sqlExpressions is not implemented"`, but the guard it sits behind (`enableSqlExpressions`) tests whether the `FlagSqlExpressions` feature flag is enabled — it is a gating condition, not a missing implementation. The text tells the caller the feature does not exist rather than that it is turned off, so the message disagrees with the check that produced it; make the message describe the actual reason (the feature not being enabled).
We need to update the entire file, lines 1-26, to use sql.NewInMemoryDB().
The query interface has changed, we need to update lines 96 and 100.

WHAT: enableSqlExpressions always returns false regardless of the feature flag — the computed `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` value is never returned (both `if enabled { return false }` and the trailing `return false` yield false). WHY: the `sqlExpressions` toggle is read but has no effect, so SQL expressions are unconditionally dead-disabled and any intent to let the flag opt the feature back in is silently broken (dead code indicating a logic mistake). HOW: return the flag state, e.g. `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, with the polarization matching the intended enable/disable semantics.
outros: `enableSqlExpressions` always returns false: the value computed on line 195 (`enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`) is never used — both the `if enabled { return false }` branch and the final `return false` return false. Consequently the QueryTypeSQL branch (reader.go:128-132) always fails with "sqlExpressions is not implemented", so the feature flag can never enable SQL expressions. Return the computed value (and drop the erroneous `!` so the flag enables rather than disables the feature).

`enableSqlExpressions` always returns false: it computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` but then returns false in both the `if enabled` branch (line 197) and the fall-through (line 199), so the flag value is never propagated. The caller at reader.go:129-132 treats a false result as 'feature off' and returns an error, so QueryTypeSQL is permanently blocked regardless of FlagSqlExpressions. Return the flag's own value (drop the `!` and the constant returns), e.g. `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.

`enableSqlExpressions` is named as a function that enables SQL expressions, but it can never return true: `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)` computes the *negation* of the flag, and both the `if enabled { return false }` branch and the final `return false` return false. The name and the `enabled` variable thus state the opposite of what the code does, and the feature flag is effectively ignored (SQL expressions are always rejected). Either name the variable/function for what it checks (e.g. `sqlExpressionsDisabled`) or return the flag value so the name matches the behaviour.

enableSqlExpressions always returns false: it computes enabled, then has `if enabled { return false }` followed by `return false`, so neither branch can return true. The QueryTypeSQL case therefore always errors with "sqlExpressions is not implemented" irrespective of the FlagSqlExpressions feature flag, permanently disabling the feature. Return the feature-flag value (e.g. `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`).

enableSqlExpressions always returns false: `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, then both the `if enabled` branch and the fallthrough `return false`. The feature flag is ignored entirely, so the QueryTypeSQL case (reader.go:129-132) now unconditionally returns the "sqlExpressions is not implemented" error and SQL expression queries never execute, regardless of the flag. The function should return the actual enabled state (and/or the reader should not hard-error).

grupos.texto: The production `NewInMemoryDB` replaced the real `go-duck` implementation with stubs, but its consumers assume a working DB: `pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:23-26` feeds `RunCommands`'s return into `json.Unmarshal`, and `pkg/expr/sql_command.go:30-36/100` turns the resulting error into a `BadRequest("error reading SQL command")` / sets `rsp.Error`. Because `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` all unconditionally return `errors.New("not implemented")`/`""`, every SQL expression built or executed through these callers fails 100% of the time. The producer side must be implemented (or the consumers changed) so the DB contract the callers rely on actually holds.
outros: WHAT: TablesList now delegates to the stub `NewInMemoryDB()`, whose `RunCommands` (pkg/expr/sql/db.go:16-18) always returns errors.New("not implemented"), so TablesList can never return tables. WHY: its callers `sql.TablesList` in NewSQLCommand (sql_command.go:30) and the SQLCommand execution path (QueryFramesInto, sql_command.go:100) now always fail with an error, permanently breaking the parser contract (and the existing parser_test.go suite that expects real table lists). HOW: if SQL is intentionally disabled, remove the now-dead parser/command paths or keep a functional parser; otherwise restore a working DB implementation.

NewInMemoryDB() returns a stub whose TablesList/RunCommands/QueryFramesInto always return errors.New("not implemented"), replacing the working go-duck in-memory DB. This makes TablesList always fail (so NewSQLCommand always errors) and QueryFramesInto always fail in SQLCommand.Execute, so every SQL expression breaks at runtime. Wire up a real implementation (restore the go-duck-backed DB) instead of a stub that always errors.

The DB type that replaces duck.NewInMemoryDB() is a stub: TablesList, RunCommands and QueryFramesInto all unconditionally return errors.New("not implemented"). Its consumers were not updated to match this new contract — parser.go:26 calls RunCommands and now always errors, so NewSQLCommand (sql_command.go:30) rejects every SQL query as invalid, and sql_command.go:100 calls QueryFramesInto and always sets rsp.Error. Either these methods must be implemented or the callers must be guarded so a not-implemented DB does not silently break the SQL expression path.

grupos.texto: enableSqlExpressions returns false on both paths, including when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Consequently ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression and the enabled feature branch can never execute. Return the actual feature-enabled state rather than unconditionally returning false.

The replacement DB does not preserve the behavior required by its consumers: RunCommands and QueryFramesInto now always return "not implemented". sql.TablesList still calls RunCommands to discover dependencies, and SQL command construction calls that parser, so even valid SQL can no longer construct a command; commands reaching Execute also cannot produce frames. Implement the backing operations (or retain the existing duck implementation) before switching these consumers to this DB.
outros: The replacement database unconditionally returns "not implemented" from both RunCommands and QueryFramesInto. parser.TablesList now uses the former and SQLCommand.Execute uses the latter, so previously supported SQL parsing and execution always fail, even if the feature gate is corrected. Preserve the working database implementation or provide equivalent operations before switching these callers.

grupos.texto: SQLCommand.Execute now calls the stub sql.NewInMemoryDB().QueryFramesInto, which always returns "not implemented". Every SQL expression that reaches Execute fails, where before it ran through duckdb. The consumer was not updated to handle the stub, and no real implementation or gating guards this path.

TablesList now uses the stub DB, whose RunCommands always returns an error. Table extraction therefore always fails, and every caller that depends on it (for example, dependency resolution for SQL expressions) breaks.

`enableSqlExpressions` negates the feature flag and then returns false on both branches, so it always returns false and the `FlagSqlExpressions` value is ignored. The logic is confusing and would invert the flag if one branch were later changed. If the feature is meant to be hard-disabled, return false directly with a comment. Otherwise return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.
outros: enableSqlExpressions is named as an enabled-check, but `enabled` holds the negation of the flag and the function returns false on every path. It never reports true even when FlagSqlExpressions is on. Return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions) so the name matches what the function does.

enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path. The inverted `enabled` variable is checked, but the fall-through also returns false. SQL expressions are therefore rejected even when the feature flag is on. Return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` directly.

enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path. The flag value is inverted and then discarded, so SQL expressions are rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Fix: `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.

enableSqlExpressions returns false on both paths, so ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Callers that previously could use SQL expressions with the flag on now always get "sqlExpressions is not implemented". It should return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions).

grupos.texto: After replacing `duck.NewInMemoryDB()` with local `NewInMemoryDB()` and removing the duck import, the local `duckDB` still carries the old implementation name though it is no longer a duck DB. Rename to `db`/`sqlDB` (as done in sql_command.go) so identifier matches code.

Behaviour contract break: db := sql.NewInMemoryDB() + db.QueryFramesInto(...) replaces duck.NewInMemoryDB which executed SQL. New stub in pkg/expr/sql/db.go always returns errors.New("not implemented"), so Execute always fails and sets rsp.Error. Caller could previously count on frames being queried successfully. Consumer was switched syntactically but not updated for guaranteed-failure behaviour — restore functional implementation or add fallback/gating.

Variable `enabled` is assigned the negation `!IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` so it is true when the feature is disabled — the name states the opposite of what it holds — and the function then returns false on both branches so `enableSqlExpressions` never enables. Rename/fix to `enabled := h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)` and `return enabled`.
outros: enableSqlExpressions always returns false: negates IsEnabledGlobally then returns false on both paths, so caller `if !enabled` always rejects SQL. Fix to return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions).

goldens.comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

grupos.texto: The struct doc comment still reads "// Cache for user permissions, user team memberships and user basic roles", but this PR added the new `permDenialCache` field (line 58). The comment no longer enumerates what the struct actually holds and misleads a reader about the new denial-cache field; update it to mention the permission-denial cache so the prose matches the fields.

This test claims to prove the permDenialCache short-circuit (service.go:116-121) denies access, but it seeds the cached permission as map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} (a deny), contradicting its comment "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked". Because the cached set is already a deny, checkPermission returns allowed=false, the code falls through to the DB path, and the fake store also returns no permissions, so Allowed stays false. The assertion passes even if the entire permDenialCache early-return were deleted. Seed the cached permission as true (map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true}) so that only the denial-cache entry can force Allowed=false; otherwise the test does not verify the feature.

WHAT: The permDenialCache short-circuit (lines 116-121) runs before the newly-added requery-on-miss logic (lines 123-136), so a cached denial is returned as Allowed:false with no requery. WHY: The denial is written at line 154 only after an authoritative DB deny, but for the exact scenario this PR targets — a resource whose permission row is committed just after the deny was recorded (newly created dashboard/folder) — the stale denial is served for the whole shortCacheTTL (30s) even though the user now has access, defeating the requery fix added in the same function and producing a spurious permission-denied for newly created resources. HOW: When the denial-cache entry is hit, re-validate against fresh permissions (or skip the denial short-circuit for create/just-created resources), or invalidate the denial entry on resource creation/permission change instead of relying only on TTL.
outros: Check now consults permDenialCache first and returns Allowed:false without consulting the store. Previously a Check whose permission-cache lookup missed or evaluated to not-allowed always fell back to getIdentityPermissions (the store) before it could refuse, so a false result reflected current store state. Now every denial is memoized (service.go 153-155) and identical subsequent requests (same namespace/userUID/action/name/parent) are refused from cache for the whole shortCacheTTL, so a permission granted after the denial was cached is still refused. If the denial short-circuit is intended, make the contract explicit (document the TTL staleness) and ensure denial entries are invalidated on permission changes; otherwise remove the unconditional deny short-circuit or gate it so a fresh evaluation is still possible.

grupos.texto: Every distinct resource denied by the cached permission map triggers a reload of the entire user's action permission set, because the denial cache is resource-specific and a cached false result always falls through to getIdentityPermissions. Sequential checks of N inaccessible dashboards therefore execute N full permission queries and cache rewrites even with a current action-wide cache; getUserPermissions' singleflight only merges overlapping requests. Bound refreshes per user/action with a short refresh cooldown or generation marker so different resource misses can share a recent refresh.

Encode the denial-key components unambiguously rather than joining them with underscores. For the same namespace, user and action, (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") produce the same key. Check in service.go now treats any hit on this key as an unconditional denial before checking permissions, so a denial for one dashboard/folder pair can deny a different, authorized pair until expiry. Use a structured or length-prefixed encoding (or escaping) that preserves component boundaries, and add a test covering these two distinct tuples.
outros: The denial cache key does not distinguish underscores inside resource and parent UIDs from its field separators. For the same namespace, user and action, (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") generate the same key, so denying the first request makes Check return false for the second even if its permissions explicitly allow it. Encode the components unambiguously, for example as a JSON tuple or length-prefixed fields.

The denial cache key is not injective: for the same namespace, user and action, `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` produce the same key. After the first request stores a denial, Check's new early cache return denies the second request without checking its permissions, even if it is allowed. Encode the components unambiguously (for example a JSON tuple or length-prefixed components) and add a test verifying that these two requests do not share a denial entry.

Make the denial-cache key encode component boundaries unambiguously (for example, length-prefix or serialize the components). For the same namespace, user and action, name `a_b` with parent `c` and name `a` with parent `b_c` both produce the suffix `_a_b_c`. Underscores can occur in resource UIDs, so denying the first request caches a key that causes Check to immediately deny the second request without evaluating its permissions, even if that resource is allowed.

grupos.texto: The fixture described as allowing access sets `"dashboards:uid:dash1"` to `false`. This does not establish the competing allow that the explicit-denial-cache test is supposed to override, so a denial alone cannot prove that the denial-cache lookup worked. Set the permission to `true`, and verify that the same request is allowed without the denial entry before asserting that the entry makes it denied. This makes the test fail if denial-cache precedence is removed.
outros: The comment says this seeds an allow permission to prove that the denial cache takes precedence, but the seeded permission is false. This contradicts the documented test setup and does not establish the claimed allow-versus-deny scenario. Seed the dashboard permission with true so the fixture matches the comment and demonstrates the intended precedence.

grupos.texto: A denial cached for shortCacheTTL is returned before the permission cache is checked or refreshed. A user who is granted access within that window (for example, after creating the dashboard or folder) keeps getting denied until the entry expires, which is the case this PR is meant to fix. Invalidate the denial entry when permissions are refreshed or granted, or use a much shorter TTL for denial entries.

The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test would still pass if the permDenialCache check were removed. permCache is seeded with dash1:false, not true as the comment claims, so the normal path also denies. Seed permCache with {"dashboards:uid:dash1": true} and a store that grants the permission, so Allowed=false can only come from the denial entry.
outros: The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the code sets the permCache entry to `false`, which is a deny. The test therefore does not show that the permission cache is skipped. Set the value to `true`, or change the comment to match.

grupos.texto: userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_', and Grafana UIDs may contain underscores. (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") therefore produce the same key. A cached denial for one resource then wrongly denies the other for the TTL. Use a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or length-prefix the fields, and use a distinct prefix from userPermCacheKey.
outros: userPermDenialCacheKey joins attacker-influenced name and parent with '_', which is an ambiguous delimiter. Distinct (name, parent) pairs such as ("a_b","c") and ("a","b_c") collide, so a cached denial for one resource wrongly denies another. Use a distinct key prefix (e.g. ".perm_denial_") and an unambiguous encoding, such as length-prefixing or escaping the fields.

grupos.texto: WHAT: userPermDenialCacheKey builds keys by naive underscore concatenation without escaping (namespace+".perm_"+uid+"_"+action+"_"+name+"_"+parent). WHY: distinct tuples collide (e.g. name="a_b",parent="c" vs name="a",parent="b_c" produce identical suffix), so a denial for one resource falsely denies an unrelated resource.

WHAT: denial-cache hit returns deny immediately before consulting cached or fresh permissions, and the fresh-allow path never deletes the denial key. WHY: a permission granted after a denial (the newly-created dashboard case this PR targets) stays denied until TTL expiry because every retry short-circuits on the stale denial instead of requerying.

WHAT: List serves listPermission directly from getCachedIdentityPermissions on any cache hit with no outdated-cache requery, unlike Check which falls through to the DB when cached perms deny. WHY: newly granted dashboard/folder scopes missing from the cached map stay missing from List results for the full TTL, while pre-PR List always hit the DB via getIdentityPermissions.

WHAT: every denied Check inserts a per-resource denial entry keyed by (namespace,user,action,name,parent). WHY: cache cardinality explodes from O(users x actions) to O(users x actions x resources), causing unbounded memory growth and eviction pressure on the shared local cache as dashboard/folder counts grow.

Deny-precedence test seeds permCache with false instead of true, so both cached-allow path and DB fallback deny and the test passes even with permDenialCache check removed. Set the permCache entry to true ("dashboards:uid:dash1": true) so only the denial cache can explain Allowed:false.
outros: Comment declares permCache allows dash1 to prove denial short-circuits it, but code stores map value false (deny). Set it to true so only the denial path can produce deny; as written the test passes even if the denial check is removed.

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

grupos.texto: The bind-parameter workaround only handles SQLite's limit; the placeholder branch is used for every other engine with len(ids) placeholders and no bound. The previous implementation had no bind parameters, so this path is new. Postgres (extended protocol) and MySQL both cap bind parameters at 65535, so a configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize larger than that makes this DELETE fail at Exec with a parameter-limit error instead of cleaning anything. Clamp the number of ids per DELETE (e.g. chunk into <=1000/<=65535 id sub-batches) for all dialects, not just SQLite.
删除了this later

WHAT: Leftover debug logging calls `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)` (and the identical Error-level logs for 'by count' and 'Tags to clean', lines 554/557/576/579) run on every batch in production. WHY: These log the full ID slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767 elements) at Error severity on every cleanup iteration, flooding logs with false error noise and large payloads for a normal successful operation, and can trigger error-based alerting. HOW: Remove these log lines, or downgrade to Debug and drop the full `ids` slice (log only the count).
outros: Avoid using Error-level logging on the normal cleanup path. The new r.log.Error calls emit count, ids, cond, and err at lines 534/537, 554/557, and 576/579 during non-error execution, creating log noise; consider downgrading or removing these logs on the normal path.

These new cleanup progress lines are logged with `r.log.Error(...)` (lines 534/537, and likewise 554/557 for max-count and 576/579 for orphaned tags) even though they report normal, successful operation (the `err` passed here is nil, e.g. after a successful fetchIDs). Logging non-error informational messages at Error level makes every successful cleanup cycle surface as an error to operators and can trip error-based alerting; the message severity disagrees with what the code did. Use Debug/Info (and reconsider dumping the entire `ids` slice) so the log level matches the success being reported.

These new log calls use Error level on the normal success path and emit the entire ids slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries, e.g. 32767 ids) on every batch of every cleanup cycle. Besides flooding logs, they emit error-level lines with a nil err, producing false error signals. Use Debug level and drop the raw ids (log only the count).

grupos.texto: The cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, a 10x increase in how often the entire cleanup job runs. This job also drives the annotation/tag cleanup path changed in this PR, which now fetches ID batches into memory and emits Error-level logs per batch, so running it every minute substantially increases DB load and log volume with no functional benefit. Unless a 1-minute cadence is explicitly intended, this should stay at 10 minutes (it reads like a leftover from testing).
outros: WHAT: The cleanup job ticker interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. WHY: This runs all cleanup jobs (annotations, expired snapshots/versions/images, short URLs, query history) 10× more frequently, multiplying background DB load and lock contention — the opposite of the deadlock mitigation this PR targets — and appears to be a debug leftover unrelated to the described change. HOW: Restore the ticker to `time.Minute * 10`.

The cleanup job ticker interval was reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is unrelated to the annotation cleanup change and looks like a leftover debug value; it makes the temp-file cleanup job run 10x more often in every deployment. Revert to time.Minute*10 unless the shorter interval is intentional.

grupos.texto: The SQLite literal-ID path rebuilds the entire accumulated string for every ID, making SQL construction quadratic in batch size. Large batches explicitly supported by this PR, including the 32,767 setting in the integration test, generate substantial repeated copying and allocation before each delete, consuming cleanup time and memory. Build the list with strings.Builder and append each formatted ID once.

The ticker change runs the entire cleanup service every minute instead of every ten minutes, not just annotation cleanup. The clean method also processes temporary files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs and query history, increasing their database and filesystem workload tenfold; cycles lasting over a minute also leave a pending tick that starts another cycle immediately afterward. Preserve the ten-minute interval for the shared cleanup service, or schedule annotations independently if they require a shorter interval.

The comment states that SQLite has a parameter limit of 999, but SQLite >= 3.32.0 defaults to 32766 (as the added integration test also recognizes). This branch is choosing a conservative compatibility threshold, not expressing the limit of every SQLite database. Document 999 as the older-version/compatibility threshold so maintainers do not mistake this constant for the actual limit on modern SQLite.

The new SQLite-limit regression case does not exceed the parameter limit when deleting annotations. The 40,003 fixtures are distributed across alert, dashboard and API types, and CleanAnnotations selects/deletes each type separately, so each annotation DELETE receives only about 13,333 IDs despite the configured batch size of 32,767. On SQLite >=3.32.0, switching annotation deletion back to placeholders would therefore still pass this test (the tag cleanup can independently retain its workaround). Create more than 32,767 annotations of a single type, or enough total fixtures for at least one type's deletion to exceed 32,766 parameters, and assert that cleanup succeeds.

On Postgres and MySQL, deleteByIDs binds one placeholder per ID with no cap. A configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above the driver's bind-parameter limit (65535) makes every cleanup batch fail, and the cleanup job then never finishes. Split the IDs into chunks below the limit, or inline the integer IDs as the SQLite branch does.

These progress messages ('Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', and the matching by-count and tags messages) are logged with log.Error even though nothing failed, and they include a nil err field. This mislabels normal operation as errors. Use Debug (or Info) level, and log the error only when it is non-nil.
outros: Debug logging is emitted at Error level in every cleanup batch (also at lines 554-557 and 576-579) and includes the full ids slice and the SQL condition. This floods the error logs and triggers error alerts on routine cleanup runs. Remove these calls, or log at Debug level without the ID list.

Debug-style messages are logged at Error level on every batch, in all three cleanup paths (lines 534/537, 554/557, 576/579). They include the full ids slice and a misleading `err` that is always nil when logged. Remove them, or log at Debug level without the ids and the stale err.

grupos.texto: The cleanup ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which looks like a leftover debug change. Every cleanup job (temp files, annotations, and others) now runs 10 times as often, which adds database load and can make runs overlap. Restore `time.Minute * 10`.
outros: The cleanup ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which looks like a leftover debugging edit. It makes every cleanup job, not just annotation cleanup, run ten times more often. Restore `time.Minute * 10`.

grupos.texto: WHAT: Leftover debug logging calls r.log.Error on every cleanup batch (also duplicated at lines 554-557 and 576-579) dumping full ids slice, cond, and nil err at Error level. WHY: Fires Error-level log per batch and serializes up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs (32767 in new test), spamming error logs/monitoring on every normal cleanup run. HOW: Downgrade to Debug or remove; do not log full ids at Error.

WHAT: SQLite large-batch IN-list built with repeated fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop over ids. WHY: Quadratic string copying on large batches (e.g. 32767 IDs in added test) during cleanup, a background job path. HOW: Build with strings.Builder or strings.Join.

WHAT: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no justification. WHY: Runs all 8 cleanup jobs including the new multi-query (SELECT+DELETE per batch) annotation cleanup 10x more often, multiplying DB load. HOW: Revert to 10 minutes or justify the frequency change separately.

goldens.comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

grupos.texto: Dead computation: the two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls allocate encoders and encode rBigInteger/sBigInteger, but their results are discarded — the returned DER comes entirely from the expression at lines 117-121, which re-encodes the same BigIntegers. These two statements have no effect and should be removed (they are a leftover from an earlier formulation).

The test only checks self-consistency: it asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(g(asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign))) == asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign), i.e. that concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a right inverse of asn1derToConcatenatedRS. It never compares against the original DER `sign`, never verifies the ECDSA signature, and never asserts the emvider output is canonical DER. Because the decoder it reads back with (ASN1Decoder.readLength) accepts non-canonical long-form lengths (e.g. 0x81) and validates only tag numbers, a regression in ASN1Encoder.writeLength that always emitted long form would still round-trip and the test would still pass, even though the produced signature would no longer be valid DER and would be rejected by the Keycloak server / a JDK Signature.verify. Assert the encoded signature is valid DER (e.g. verify it with a JDK Signature, or compare asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign) against a known-good width-padded r||s and assert its length equals algorithm.getSignatureLength()).

readInteger() calls readLength(), which returns -1 for an indefinite-length element (first length byte 0x80). That -1 is passed straight to read(length) at line 72, which does `new byte[-1]` and throws an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException, even though readInteger declares only IOException. The signature bytes fed to asn1derToConcatenatedRS come from an externally supplied ECDSA signature, so a malformed signature escapes as an unhandled runtime exception instead of the declared IOException. readLength()'s -1 branch is handled for sequences but not here; guard the negative/indefinite value (throw IOException) before calling read(length).

order() was added as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now invokes order() on every ServiceLoader-discovered CryptoProvider via Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order). Any CryptoProvider implementation compiled against the previous interface (an external or separately built provider jar on the classpath) will throw AbstractMethodError at detection time, i.e. during AuthzClient.create()/server bootstrap, before any provider is usable. Giving order() a default implementation (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }) avoids the binary-incompatibility.

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default KeyStore provider (e.g. SUN) instead of a BouncyCastle provider, violating the method's contract ('@return BouncyCastle security provider'). This value is consumed by BouncyIntegration.loadProvider() (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/util/BouncyIntegration.java:34) to set the static BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER name, so whenever this authz-client provider is the one selected by CryptoIntegration, every Keycloak code path that does getInstance(..., BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER) silently looks algorithms up in a non-BC provider (e.g. 'SUN'), which can produce failures or different crypto implementation than expected. Returning a provider that is not BouncyCastle while claiming to be the BouncyCastle provider makes BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER point to the wrong provider.
outros: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), i.e. the JDK default keystore provider (SUN), yet the method name and the CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() contract say it returns the BouncyCastle provider. A caller that uses the returned Provider as the BouncyCastle provider (to look up BC algorithms or to register it) will silently get the wrong (often already-registered) provider. Either return the actual BC provider or rename/document the method so the name matches what it returns.

grupos.texto: detectProvider() no longer fails fast when multiple CryptoProviders are present and instead silently picks the first after sorting by order() descending. All Keycloak providers return the same order (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200), so a tie between two providers is broken by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader iteration order rather than the intended priority. The previous code threw an IllegalStateException forcing the classpath to be corrected; now a deployment with two provider jars (exactly the 'multiple providers on classpath' scenario this PR enables) can silently select the unintended provider — e.g. a non-FIPS/strict provider when FIPS is required — with no error. Use a stable tie-breaker (delegate to the provider name/type) or reject equal top orders instead of relying on ServiceLoader order.
outros: detectProvider's contract changed from failing fast to silently swallowing the ambiguous-provider case. Before this PR, more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw IllegalStateException, forcing the misconfiguration to be fixed. Now the code sorts by order() (line 57) and returns the first, logging the rest only at debug. Because DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order()==200, ties are resolved purely by ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, so a previously-rejected classpath (e.g. FIPS provider plus non-FIPS provider) can now silently select the wrong/lower-assurance provider instead of failing. Restore an error (or at least a warning plus deterministic tie-breaking) when more than one provider is discovered.

grupos.texto: FIPS1402Provider.order() returns 200, the exact same value as DefaultCryptoProvider.order() (also changed to 200 in this PR). CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now sorts providers with Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed() and silently takes the first, having removed the old 'throw on multiple providers' guard (common/.../CryptoIntegration.java). With equal order the tie is broken only by ServiceLoader/classpath discovery order, so if both crypto/fips1402 and crypto/default are visible to the classloader the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider can win and no exception signals it — a silent downgrade from FIPS. The FIPS provider must outrank the default one (give it a strictly higher order, e.g. lower DefaultCryptoProvider's value or raise the FIPS one) so preference is deterministic.
outros: FIPS1402Provider.order() returns 200, the same value as the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider. Since CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() now silently picks the highest-order provider instead of failing when several are present, a colliding order means FIPS gets no precedence and the selected provider is decided only by classpath/ServiceLoader ordering. In a FIPS deployment containing both crypto-default and crypto-fips1402, a non-FIPS provider can be selected silently, defeating FIPS. Give FIPS a strictly higher order (e.g. 400) so it always wins, or keep fail-fast on ambiguous equal-order providers.

grupos.texto: The newly registered client CryptoProvider does not satisfy the existing EC JWK parsing consumer: core's AbstractJWKParser calls createECParams(name) and getKeyFactory("ECDSA") to construct an EC public key, and both operations now throw UnsupportedOperationException when this provider is selected. Consequently, a standalone authz client using this provider cannot parse EC keys for ECDSA verification, even though signature conversion is implemented. Implement the JDK-backed curve-parameter and key-factory operations (mapping ECDSA to EC as needed), rather than leaving this existing consumer with an unsupported contract.

Reject ambiguous highest-priority providers rather than silently taking the first. Both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider return order 200 in this PR, so when both are present the stable sort leaves the decision to ServiceLoader discovery order. A deployment expecting FIPS can therefore initialize the ordinary Bouncy Castle provider without an error; previously this mixed classpath failed closed. Preserve the error for tied highest-priority providers (or require an explicit security-mode/provider choice), while still allowing the lower-priority authz-client fallback.

The assertion only establishes agreement between the two new conversion routines, not correctness of the converted signature. For example, swapping r and s in both routines makes this entire round trip pass, although the DER result no longer verifies the signed data. Verify `asn1Des` with the public key and original data (or compare against an independently specified encoding) so mutually compensating conversion defects fail the test.

Remove these two discarded encoder writes. Each allocates an encoder and encodes a BigInteger, but neither result participates in the returned signature; lines 119–120 repeat both writes on fresh encoders. This performs redundant encoding and allocations on every concatenated-signature conversion.

Reject INTEGER values that do not fit the requested component width instead of silently dropping their high bytes. Removing a single leading sign-padding zero is valid, but this branch also truncates actual magnitude bytes: a positive value 2^256 + 1 becomes 1 when qLength is 32. Thus DER-to-concatenated conversion can return a different signature from the one supplied. Validate nonnegative values and their bit length before padding or removing sign padding.

Bound each child TLV to the remaining sequence length before accepting it. Currently readNext() reads from the whole input and length may become negative, which silently ends the loop successfully. For example, `30 05 02 01 01 02 01 01` is accepted as a two-integer sequence although the second INTEGER crosses the declared sequence boundary. Decode through a stream limited to the sequence content, or reject a child whose encoded size exceeds the remaining length, so malformed DER cannot be converted as a valid signature.
outros: readSequence accepts a child whose encoded size exceeds the remaining declared sequence length. For example, `30 04 02 01 01 02 01 01` is accepted as a two-integer sequence even though its children occupy six bytes rather than the declared four, so asn1derToConcatenatedRS silently converts malformed DER instead of rejecting it. Restrict child decoding to the sequence's declared content boundary and throw IOException when a child exceeds the remaining length.

Reject a child whose encoded length exceeds the remaining sequence length. Currently bytes `30 01 02 01 01` declare a one-byte sequence body but readSequence returns the entire three-byte INTEGER and exits with length -2. Consequently malformed sequence boundaries are treated as successfully decoded results. Bound child reads to the sequence body and require the remainder to reach exactly zero.

Enforce the declared SEQUENCE boundary before reading each child and reject children whose full encoding exceeds the remaining length. For example, `30 04 02 01 01 02 01 02` declares only four content bytes, but this loop reads both three-byte INTEGER encodings, lets length become -2, and returns a two-element sequence. Consequently asn1derToConcatenatedRS accepts a malformed DER signature by consuming bytes outside its enclosing sequence. Parse through a bounded content stream and require exact consumption.

grupos.texto: Every case generates a default EC key rather than a key on the curve associated with the named algorithm. On the standard JDK this is P-256, so testES384 and testES512 just pad P-256 signature components to larger lengths. A converter that discards nonzero high bytes beyond 32 bytes would still pass all three cases. Initialize the key generator with the appropriate curve per case (P-256, P-384, and P-521) so the larger-component conversions are actually tested.
outros: Generate a key on the curve corresponding to each tested algorithm rather than using the provider's default EC curve for all three tests. On the standard JDK this generates a P-256 key even for testES384 and testES512, so those tests merely pad P-256 integers to larger output lengths and never exercise actual P-384/P-521 signature encoding (including P-521's long-form sequence length).

grupos.texto: The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` encode values and discard the results. The return expression re-encodes the same values, so these lines are dead computation left over from a copy-paste or refactor. Remove them.

The test uses one default EC key pair (P-256) for ES256, ES384 and ES512. The 384 and 512 cases therefore sign with 32-byte r/s values while the converters are told signLength 96 or 132. The tests pass without ever handling real P-384 or P-521 signatures. Generate the key pair per algorithm with the matching curve (secp256r1, secp384r1, secp521r1) via ECGenParameterSpec.

The only assertion compares two outputs of the code under test (rsConcat vs rsConcat2). It never checks the re-encoded DER against the original `sign` or verifies it with Signature.verify. A symmetric encode/decode bug would still pass. Also assert that asn1Des equals sign, or that the signature verifies with the public key.

WHAT: getBouncyCastleProvider returns KeyStore.getInstance(defaultType).getProvider() (e.g. SUN) as the BouncyCastle provider. WHY: BouncyIntegration.loadProvider caches this name for all Signature/Cipher/KeyFactory lookups, so standalone authz-client gets PROVIDER=SUN instead of BC/null and BC-specific algorithms/FIPS expectations break. HOW: return null like WildFlyElytronProvider does when no BC provider is available.

WHAT: detectProvider sorts by order() reversed and silently picks index 0, removing the previous multiple-providers error. WHY: Default/FIPS/Elytron all return order 200, so ambiguous classpath (e.g. default+FIPS) now nondeterministically picks one by ServiceLoader order instead of failing fast, risking wrong FIPS vs non-FIPS crypto. HOW: only auto-ignore lower-order providers; throw when the top two have equal order().

WHAT: readSequence loops while(length>0) subtracting child TLV lengths but never verifies sum equals declared length nor rejects trailing bytes. WHY: lets overlong sequences and trailing garbage after the two integers be accepted as valid, diverging from strict BC ASN1InputStream and enabling signature malleability in the ECDSA verify path. HOW: enforce length==0 after loop and no remaining bytes in the outer buffer.
Dead computation: two ASN1Encoder instances are created and written but immediately discarded; the method then re-creates identical encoders for the returned sequence. Remove lines 114-115.

Tautological round-trip assertion: rsConcat2 is derived from rsConcat via encode+decode that are inverses if self-consistent, so assertArrayEquals(rsConcat,rsConcat2) passes even if both directions are wrong. Verify against external oracle: Signature.initVerify + verify(asn1Des) and/or compare rsConcat to expected split, not just to itself.

Single default EC keypair reused for ES256/ES384/ES512: testES384/testES512 names claim larger curves but body signs with the same P-256 key and only pads to larger signLength, so full-width 384/521-bit handling is never exercised. Generate a per-algorithm keypair with the correct curve (e.g. secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) before signing.

WHAT: readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding 0x80 and callers pass it to new byte[length]. WHY: causes NegativeArraySizeException (unchecked) in readInteger/readNext instead of IOException, crashing signature-verification callers that expect checked failure on malformed DER. HOW: throw IOException for 0x80 since DER forbids indefinite lengths.
outros: readInteger passes readLength() result directly to read(length)->new byte[length]. readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length 0x80, so a crafted INTEGER with length 0x80 throws unchecked NegativeArraySizeException at allocation instead of IOException. Reject length<0 here (indefinite length not valid for DER INTEGER).

grupos.texto: WHAT: concatenatedRSToASN1DER splits signature without validating signature.length==signLength. WHY: short JOSE input throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and long input is silently truncated to signLength, breaking the ECDSACryptoProvider contract (IOException on malformed) used by verifier contexts. HOW: check length upfront and throw IOException.
outros: concatenatedRSToASN1DER never validates signature.length == signLength before System.arraycopy(signature,0,r,1,len) / (signature,len,s,1,len). A short JWS signature throws unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of the declared IOException, breaking verification on attacker-controlled input. Validate length and throw IOException.

goldens.comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

add-authzclientcryptoprovider-for-author.prTitle: Add AuthzClientCryptoProvider for authorization client cryptographic operations

grupos.texto: The javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false, but this method is the require-variant of canManageMembers, not canManageMembership. The text was copied from requireManageMembership above it. It should reference canManageMembers so the documented contract matches the method name and behavior.

searchForUser() dropped the stream.users()... filter(usersEvaluator::canView) that this PR removed. Visibility is now restricted only by the session UserModel.GROUPS attribute derived from getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), which is empty whenever the caller's view grant is a direct user-level FGAP policy rather than group membership. In that case the search query is unrestricted and the removed predicate no longer culls the rows, so the users search/count endpoints can return users the caller is not permitted to view. Restore a per-user canView filter on the stream (or otherwise ensure the query is filtered for non-group grants) when the caller lacks global view.

testManageGroupMembership does not verify the behaviour it names. It grants both an all-users MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP permission (line 295) and a group-level MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP permission on topGroup (line 298), then performs membership via UserResource.joinGroup, which authorizes through the user-scoped manage-group-membership path. The group-level MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP grant therefore never gates the successful join, and the final joinGroup(bob, topGroup) has no assertion confirming bob actually became a member. The test would still pass if group-level manage-membership evaluation were broken. Make the positive step exercise/verify the group-level permission (or assert the resulting membership list) so the claimed behaviour is actually falsified on regression.

GroupPermissionsV2 is now returned by the new MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() override, but its setPermissionsEnabled(GroupModel, boolean) throws UnsupportedOperationException. The fgap removal listener (AdminPermissions.registerListener, which this PR re-registers under the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature flag) still calls management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) from its group-removed handler. When the feature is enabled and a realm uses the admin-permissions (V2) client, deleting a group dispatches that event and this method raises an unhandled UnsupportedOperationException, breaking group removal. Previously groups() resolved to the V1 GroupPermissions, which does not throw. Either make setPermissionsEnabled a no-op in V2 (V2 has no per-group permission resources to disable) or stop the listener from invoking it when the V2 admin-permissions client is in use.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission builds the set from `groupResource.getId()` (the generated resource UUID) instead of the group id, and feeds that UUID back into `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)`. In V2 the group id is stored as the resource NAME (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId(), which becomes the resource name), while `hasPermission` resolves via `resourceStore.findByName(...)`. WHAT: the set contains resource UUIDs, not realm group ids. WHY: every consumer treats these strings as group ids — UsersResource passes them to `session.users().getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)` and stores them as the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute for user filtering, so the group-based user visibility restriction is computed from non-existent group ids and yields wrong results (users filtered out or not filtered as intended); additionally the per-group permission lookup always misses and silently falls back to evaluating the all-groups resource. HOW: use the resource name (the group id), matching the sibling V2 implementation ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission (line 140) which adds `resource.getName()`; pass that same name/id to hasPermission - e.g. `String groupId = groupResource.getName(); if (hasPermission(groupId, ...)) granted.add(groupId);`
outros: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds groupResource.getId() (the authorization-store Resource id) but the interface contract and the base GroupPermissions implementation return group ids, and UsersResource uses the result as group ids (getUsersCount(...) and session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, ...)). In V2 the group resource's name already equals the group id (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId()), so this method should collect groupResource.getName(). As written it returns unrelated resource ids and group-filtered user search/count will not match members of visible groups.

grupos.texto: The no-arg canManage() returns true when the caller holds only an all-groups VIEW permission (`hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`), whereas the per-group canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) requires MANAGE. WHAT: a caller with only the view scope on all groups is treated as having manage rights. WHY: canManage()/requireManage() gate group creation and other manage operations (e.g. GroupsResource.addGroup -> auth.groups().requireManage()), so a read-only viewer of all groups can create/manage groups — privilege escalation. HOW: drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() only returns true for MANAGE, aligning it with canManage(GroupModel): `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`
outros: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70) evaluates hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), identical to canView() at line 52, so a caller granted only the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is treated as a group manager. The per-group overload canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) correctly requires only MANAGE, and AdminPermissionsSchema defines MANAGE as the manage scope for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, so the two checks disagree. requireManage() therefore succeeds for read-only administrators, letting them create/update/delete groups, add subgroups and map group roles. Drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() checks MANAGE only.

grupos.texto: findByType(GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) does not enumerate the specific group resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource, because that method creates them without setting their type. Consequently, specific VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS grants are omitted from the group IDs used for user counts and database filtering. Assign the Groups type to specific group resources and ensure the all-Groups resource is not treated as a model group.

The new V2 group permission IDs are passed into a JPA filter that still requires a legacy group.resource.<groupId> authorization resource. JpaUserProvider.groupsWithPermissionsSubquery checks for that prefixed name, whereas AdminPermissionsSchema creates V2 group resources named only with the group ID, so authorized group members are excluded from user searches even with valid group IDs. Update the database filtering path to support V2 resource naming rather than requiring a legacy V1 resource.

The new documentation for requireManageMembers points to canManageMembership rather than canManageMembers. These are distinct permissions: V2 checks manage-members for managing members, but manage/manage-membership for membership changes. Link to canManageMembers(GroupModel) so callers do not infer that membership permission authorizes this guard.

The new @return documentation promises a Stream of IDs, but the method declares Set<String> and both implementations return sets. Describe a set of IDs instead, so the documented return contract matches what callers actually receive.

The global canManage check should require MANAGE only, as canManage(GroupModel) does. Including VIEW makes an all-groups read-only grant satisfy requireManage() and authorize group creation (the creation path exercised in testManageAllGroups). This returns manage authorization for a scope intended only to permit viewing.
outros: canManage() grants management access for an all-groups VIEW permission. Inherited requireManage() uses this result in GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup, allowing a view-only administrator to create groups or reparent an existing group to the top level. Evaluate only AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE here.

grupos.texto: Use the group resource's name (the group-model ID), not its authorization Resource.getId(), both when calling hasPermission and when adding to granted. AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup now names resources with GroupModel.getId(), and hasPermission looks them up with findByName. Passing the authorization-resource ID fails that lookup and falls back to all-groups permissions rather than evaluating the group's permission. Moreover, UsersResource consumes this returned set as UserModel.GROUPS, so authorization-resource IDs cannot select the actual group members. Consequently a specific VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS grant does not make its members appear in user searches (including the newly added tests).
outros: The callback passes and returns the authorization resource ID instead of the model group ID stored in the resource name. hasPermission interprets its argument as a resource name, and UsersResource passes the returned IDs to membership queries, so permission evaluation targets the fallback resource and membership filtering uses unrelated IDs. Use the specific group resource's name for both the permission lookup and the returned group ID.

Preserve the model-group-ID contract here: use groupResource.getName() for both hasPermission and granted.add, rather than getId(). AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup names the authorization resource with GroupModel.getId(), whereas Resource.getId() is the authorization resource's own ID. hasPermission resolves its argument with resourceStore.findByName, so the current argument misses the specific group permission and falls back to all-groups. Even if that fallback grants access, UsersResource passes the returned IDs into group membership filtering/counting, which expects model group IDs, so authorized members disappear from searches and counts.

Use the resource name (the model group ID), not groupResource.getId(), both for hasPermission and for the returned set. resolveGroup names the authorization resource with group.getId(), and hasPermission resolves that name with findByName. The authorization resource's own ID is a different identifier: passing it here falls back to all-groups permissions instead of evaluating the specific group, and returning it as UserModel.GROUPS cannot match actual group memberships. Consequently specific VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS grants do not correctly populate user searches/counts.

grupos.texto: The Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a 'Stream of IDs', but the method returns Set<String>. Change the @return text to describe a Set of group IDs.

The Javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. It should refer to canManageMembers(GroupModel), which is a different check, so the doc misdescribes the method.

The per-user `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)` was removed from searchForUser. When the caller lacks global view and has no group-based view permission, GROUPS is not set and the search is unrestricted. Admins with only QUERY_USERS or per-user VIEW permissions can then receive user representations they are not allowed to see. Restore the `canView(user)` filter on the result stream, or return an empty stream when the caller cannot view and has no granted groups.

canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE, so an admin with only a view permission on groups is treated as able to manage groups. That lets a view-only admin pass group-level manage checks such as creating top-level groups. Check only AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE here.
outros: canManage() grants access when the caller only has the VIEW scope on all groups. A view-only admin therefore passes requireManage() checks, for example group creation. Check only AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE here, as canManage(GroupModel) does.

canManage() accepts the VIEW scope, so a caller who can only view groups is treated as able to manage them, including creating groups. Only the MANAGE scope should be accepted: hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE).

grupos.texto: The loop passes groupResource.getId(), the resource's internal id, to hasPermission(). That method looks the resource up with findByName(server, groupId), and V2 group resources are named by the group id (see resolveGroup). The lookup misses, so the code falls back to the all-groups resource type. The returned set then holds resource ids rather than group ids. Use groupResource.getName() both for the check and for the value added to the set.
outros: The callback uses groupResource.getId(), which is the resource UUID, as if it were the group ID. V2 group resources are named by group ID, so findByName(server, uuid) misses and hasPermission falls back to the all-groups type resource. The returned set then holds resource UUIDs instead of group IDs, so group-scoped user searches filter wrongly. Use groupResource.getName() for both the permission check and the collected value.

grupos.texto: WHAT: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() grants global manage on VIEW scope (hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)). WHY: A caller with only view-all-groups permission passes the manage check, allowing group creation/management reserved for manage. HOW: Check only MANAGE, e.g. hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE).

WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() runs a full findByType scan with a per-resource evaluatePermission call for every user list/count. WHY: User searches and counts call this on each request, so cost grows O(N) with group count (N policy evaluations per request). HOW: Cache the result per request or evaluate via a single bulk permission query instead of per-resource evaluation.

Javadoc for requireManageMembers references canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers (copy-paste). Fix link to {@link #canManageMembers(GroupModel)} so the contract describes the method it guards.
@return says 'Stream of IDs' but method returns Set<String> getGroupIdsWithViewPermission. Fix doc to 'Set of IDs' to match the signature.

WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses authz resource IDs (groupResource.getId()) as group IDs and looks them up via findByName. WHY: Resource names equal group IDs (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId()), so findByName(resourceId) misses and the returned set contains unusable IDs, breaking user search/count filtering by group. HOW: Use groupResource.getName() like V1 does (resource.getName().substring prefix / name) for both the hasPermission lookup and the granted set.
outros: findByType callback passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission() and granted set, but AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup defines resource name (not UUID) as groupId and hasPermission looks up via findByName(server, groupId). Use groupResource.getName() for both check and granted set, otherwise lookups miss to all-groups fallback and callers receive authz UUIDs instead of group IDs.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses groupResource.getId() for lookup and result collection, but V2 group resources are named with the group ID (resolveGroup returns group.getId()) and hasPermission does findByName. Use groupResource.getName() in both places to evaluate the correct per-group resource and to return actual group IDs.

goldens.comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

add-groups-resource-type-and-scopes-to-a.prTitle: Add Groups resource type and scopes to authorization schema

grupos.texto: WHAT: the new FeatureSpec/ROLLING_UPDATES enabling is placed after the pre-existing `if (updateStrategy == null) return kc;` early return, so for the null strategy the feature is never enabled. WHY: testCacheMaxCount(null) asserts eventuallyRollingUpgradeStatus and the PR docs state the operator requires the rolling-updates feature; the null-strategy parameter therefore exercises the operator WITHOUT the feature this PR gates on, so either the test passes for the wrong reason (feature gate ineffective) or it silently does not cover the gated path — the enablement should apply to every parameter that exercises update strategies. HOW: move the feature-enable block above the `updateStrategy == null` return (or set FeatureSpec whenever an update strategy behavior is asserted).

WHAT: RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is changed from 4 to 3 and the value 4 is reassigned to the new FEATURE_DISABLED constant. WHY: the exit code returned by the `update-compatibility check` command for a required recreate is an observable, explicitly-scriptable interface (the guide tells consumers to rely only on the exit code), so any automation keyed on the previously emitted value 4 will no longer detect the recreate case and could proceed with an unsafe rolling upgrade; exit code 4 silently changes meaning from 'recreate needed' to 'feature disabled'. HOW: if 3/4 are both free, keep RECREATE stable and use a distinct unused code for FEATURE_DISABLED; at minimum update the doc table so the reassignment is intentional and externally documented (the adoc context line shows 3 was already documented, so confirm old emitted behavior vs docs before shipping).
outros: RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was changed from 4 to 3 and the previously-meaningful value 4 was reassigned to the new FEATURE_DISABLED outcome. The recreate exit code is a CLI output contract that external tooling/scripts key off; reusing 4 for a different result silently changes its meaning (a caller testing for 4 now treats 'feature disabled' as 'recreate required'), and recreate now returns a different code than it did before. The new feature-disabled condition should be given a fresh, unused exit code while the recreate result keeps its existing value.

grupos.texto: The new disabled-feature test only verifies the error text, not the failure exit status. If the metadata command still prints this diagnostic but exits with 0 (or another incorrect code) instead of FEATURE_DISABLED (4), this test would still pass. Assert that cliResult.exitCode() equals CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED so the test actually protects the new disabled-feature failure contract.
