testFeatureNotEnabled only launches the `metadata` subcommand and never the `check` subcommand. Removing the feature guard from UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() would therefore not fail any test. It also doesn't assert the exit code (FEATURE_DISABLED=4). Add a case for `check` and assert the exit code on both.

WHAT: testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises the metadata subcommand disabled path and never the check subcommand. WHY: the feature gate in UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run can be removed or broken without failing any test since no assertion covers its disabled message/exit code. HOW: also launch/assert the check command without --features (e.g. parameterize over metadata and check subcommands or add a second Launch).
outros: testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises the metadata subcommand, leaving the identical ROLLING_UPDATES gate in UpdateCompatibilityCheck unverified. If the Check gate were removed, the suite still passes. Parameterize/add a second @Launch for {UpdateCompatibility.NAME, UpdateCompatibilityCheck.NAME} (with required --file or not) asserting the disabled message and FEATURE_DISABLED exit code.

goldens.comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

add-rolling-updates-feature-flag-and-com.prTitle: Add rolling-updates feature flag and compatibility framework

grupos.texto: WHAT: The new recovery-codes branch of isValid only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list and never removes the consumed entry. WHY: Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid (which calls removeRecoveryAuthnCode()+updateStoredCredential), the federated path never consumes a code and allCodesUsed() can never become true, so a used recovery code remains valid and can be replayed indefinitely. HOW: On a successful match, remove that entry from the stored codes (rewrite recoveryCodes.credentialData), mirroring the local provider's consume-on-success semantics.

WHAT: getCredentials builds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel via createFromValues but never sets its id from the stored myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() (createFromValues does not populate id). WHY: The returned federated model has a null id, so callers that identify/delete the credential by id — e.g. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used, or federated-credential deletion via getFederatedCredentialsStream — cannot target the actual credential. HOW: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after createFromValues.

Recovery-code verification compares the submitted credential against each stored code with `key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())`, a short-circuiting, non-constant-time String comparison. Combined with anyMatch (which stops at the first match), success/failure timing depends on the number of matching leading characters and on match index, leaking information about the secret recovery codes. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. MessageDigest.isEqual on the byte arrays, or the same constant-time helper used elsewhere for credential verification) for each candidate instead of String.equals.

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes `generatedCodes` (the raw, unhashed recovery codes from the form) with JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString and passes them as the UserCredentialModel value, which user-storage providers persist verbatim as the credential's credentialData (see BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential -> setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())). The DB path instead stores the hashed codes via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues. This leaves the recovery codes in cleartext in user storage, an invalid credential state that breaks the invariant that recovery codes are stored hashed. Serialize/hash the codes (e.g. derive the same value the credential provider stores, or hash each code) instead of writing the raw generated codes.
outros: WHAT: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (generatedCodes) into JSON and passes them as the UserCredentialModel challengeResponse to user storage. WHY: The local path stores only hashed codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes into secretData), but this user-storage path hands the plaintext one-time codes to the provider, so they are persisted in cleartext in external storage (the test provider stores input.getChallengeResponse() verbatim), exposing reusable credentials to anyone with read access to that store. HOW: Pass the already-hashed representation (the credentialModel built from createFromValues) rather than the raw code list, as the local provider does.

grupos.texto: Successful recovery-code creation in external storage leaves any existing locally stored recovery-code credential active. For a federated user who previously stored codes locally and now has an external provider supporting this type, regeneration no longer calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential's replacement cleanup; UserCredentialManager.isValid falls back to the local validator when external validation rejects an old code, so the supposedly replaced codes still authenticate. Remove the previous local recovery-code credential after successful external creation.

getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-code model without copying the ID assigned during updateCredential. createFromValues does not assign an ID, so the exposed federated credential has a null ID and CredentialDeleteHelper cannot resolve it by the stored credential ID for account deletion. Copy myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() to the reconstructed model before returning it.

The new recovery-code validator uses String.equals to compare a stored secret with attacker-supplied input. This comparison is not constant-time, and anyMatch additionally stops at the first matching code, making validation timing dependent on secret data. Even though this is a testsuite provider, it implements an actual authentication validator and exercises the newly added federation path. Compare fixed-length byte representations with a constant-time primitive and evaluate all candidate codes without short-circuiting.

The new recovery-code validator returns success without consuming the accepted code. The external storage retains the entire generated list, and getCredentials reconstructs a fresh model from that same list each time, so logging out and logging in again with the same recovery code succeeds indefinitely. This breaks the single-use recovery-code invariant (and concurrent validations can both accept the same code). Consume the accepted code in external storage atomically with validation, and add a second-login/replay test that requires the used code to be rejected.
outros: The new recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list without consuming the accepted code. Repeating a successful login with the same code succeeds indefinitely, while getCredentials reconstructs all original codes so the login form never advances or detects exhaustion. Validate the next unused code and persist its consumption before returning success.

The new federated recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list but never removes a successfully used code from myUser.recoveryCodes. Consequently the same recovery code remains valid on subsequent logins, and getCredentials reconstructs the full original set every time. Consume and persist the successfully validated code (and test a second login/replay), so federated recovery codes retain their one-time semantics.

The newly supported federated recovery-code validation returns true on a match without consuming the code. Registration now stores these codes in this provider instead of the local recovery credential provider, so the local provider's consume-on-validation behavior no longer protects them. Because getCredentials reconstructs the model from the unchanged stored list, subsequent logins can reuse the same recovery code indefinitely. Persist removal/advancement of the accepted code in the user-storage validation path and extend the test to reject reuse.

grupos.texto: The CredentialModel returned from getCredentials for recovery codes is built with createFromValues and never gets the stored credential's id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()). RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator later calls removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId()) once all codes are used, and this would pass a null id. Fix: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after creating the model.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a credential from user storage, but exhausted codes are cleaned up with removeStoredCredentialById, which only targets the local DB. For a federated credential (possibly with a null id), the exhausted credential is never removed or the call misbehaves, so the user keeps a dead credential. Remove federated credentials through a path that covers user storage, for example by checking where the credential came from.
outros: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() can now return a credential from user storage (federated), but this code still calls removeStoredCredentialById() on it once all codes are used. That removal only targets local stored credentials, so a federated credential may not be removed. The user could then be left with an exhausted credential in user storage. Remove federated credentials through the federated path, or confirm the removal reaches user storage.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a federated credential. The authenticator still removes an exhausted one with removeStoredCredentialById(getId()), which only deletes from the local store, and the federated model's id may be null. Remove the credential through the path that matches where it was found, for example by checking whether it came from the federated stream and using the federated removal.

grupos.texto: WHAT: getCredentials rebuilds the federated recovery-codes model via createFromValues without propagating the stored credential ID. WHY: the returned CredentialModel has null ID so RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.removeStoredCredentialById(getId()) after allCodesUsed cannot remove the federated credential and leaves a stale exhausted credential. HOW: copy the stored ID onto the rebuilt model (model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId())) before adding it to the list.

WHAT: federated recovery-code validation only checks anyMatch(key equals input) and never consumes/burns the used code. WHY: a single recovery code can be replayed indefinitely for that user, defeating single-use recovery semantics that the local provider enforces by removing the used code. HOW: remove the matched code from the stored list (and persist/return updated credential) on successful validation, mirroring single-use consumption.

WHAT: constructor unwraps two Optionals without checks: credentialModelOpt.get() and getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get(). WHY: throws NoSuchElementException (500) when the user has no recovery credential or when all federated/local codes are exhausted, both now reachable since getCredential can return empty or an all-used model. HOW: guard both Optionals and fall back to a safe codeNumber or throw a handled authentication/flow error instead of unguarded get().

goldens.comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

implement-recovery-key-support-for-user-.prTitle: Implement recovery key support for user storage providers

grupos.texto: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` subclasses `BasePaginator` but its `get_item_key` (and the `self.desc` used at line 903) rely on attributes `self.key` and `self._is_asc` that are set up by the concrete `DateTimePaginator`, not by `BasePaginator`. This method was copied verbatim from the datetime paginator, which suggests the class was meant to extend a cursor/datetime paginator. As written, instantiating it and calling `get_item_key` raises AttributeError (missing `self.key`/`self._is_asc`) before any results are produced. Subclass the appropriate concrete paginator (or initialize `key`/`desc`/`_is_asc`) so the attributes exist.

WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator reimplements get_item_key/value_from_cursor exactly like the numeric Paginator (math.floor/ceil on a raw attribute) instead of DateTimePaginator, yet the only caller (organization_auditlogs.py:76-83) uses it with order_by='-datetime'. WHY: item.datetime is a DateTimeField (models/auditlogentry.py:69), so math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError inside build_cursor on the first non-empty page, returning a 500 for the exact endpoint this class was added for; value_from_cursor also returns the raw cursor value rather than converting to a datetime, so the build_queryset comparison against the datetime column would be wrong even if the floor/ceil call were fixed. HOW: subclass DateTimePaginator (or copy its get_item_key/value_from_cursor datetime conversion) in OptimizedCursorPaginator so the key extraction matches the -datetime ordering used by the endpoint.
outros: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies integer math directly to the raw field value: `int(math.floor(value) ... math.ceil(value))`. The endpoint that consumes this paginator (organization_auditlogs.py line 79) passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a datetime and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError. The pre-existing DateTimePaginator path this replaces is datetime-aware, so the new paginator's key contract was not matched by its consumer. Convert the value to a comparable numeric (e.g. .timestamp()) before floor/ceil, or reuse the datetime key handling.

The optimized path binds the datetime-ordered audit-log queryset (`order_by="-datetime"`, line 80) to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, but that paginator's `get_item_key` (paginator.py:838-840) applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to the order attribute. For this endpoint the attribute is `AuditLogEntry.datetime`, a datetime object, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError and the request 500s. The replaced `DateTimePaginator` existed precisely to convert datetime keys (e.g. `value.timestamp()`); OptimizedCursorPaginator only handles numeric keys. Either keep DateTimePaginator for datetime orderings or make OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime-aware.

grupos.texto: The negative-offset branch slices with a negative start plus a positive stop: `start_offset = cursor.offset` (e.g. -5), `stop = start_offset + limit + extra` (e.g. 95), then `queryset[-5:95]`. A negative slice start is relative to the END of the data, so for a dataset larger than `stop` the resolved start (`N-5`) exceeds `stop` and the slice returns an EMPTY list; for other offsets it returns rows from the tail rather than the requested page. The comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is wrong — for an unsliced queryset Django materializes the whole queryset and applies Python slice semantics (and raises IndexError for negative slicing on a sliced queryset). The advertised 'advanced' pagination therefore yields empty/wrong pages instead of the requested range. Clamp the start (e.g. use `max(0, ...)`, or map negative offsets to positive ones based on a known total) and slice a non-negative range.
outros: WHAT: The advanced branch slices the queryset with a negative start offset (queryset[cursor.offset:stop] when cursor.offset < 0). WHY: cursor.offset is parsed verbatim from the user-supplied cursor query parameter (Cursor.from_string, cursors.py:52-61, no sign check) and Django does not support negative indexing on QuerySet slices — it produces an invalid negative OFFSET / raises, so sending a cursor with a negative offset when optimized_pagination is enabled yields a 500; the comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is incorrect. HOW: reject negative offsets (raise BadPaginationError/ParseError) instead of slicing with them, or clamp start_offset to 0 before slicing.

The comment here claims "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" and that passing a negative `start_offset` is "safe", but Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative indices (`AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative start_offset cannot work. The prose documents ORM behaviour that does not exist and calls the path safe; either correct the comment or remove the unsupported negative-offset branch. (The class docstring at lines 826-828 advertises this same 'Negative offset support'.)

The advanced-pagination branch slices the queryset with a negative start offset (`start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0`). Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise "Negative indexing is not supported", so any request that reaches this branch throws an unhandled exception. The branch is reachable: the audit-log endpoint enables `enable_advanced_features` for superusers/global-access members, and `cursor.offset` is attacker-controlled via `Cursor.from_string` (`?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=0:-1:0` => offset -1). Clamp to a valid non-negative range or reject negative offsets instead of slicing with them; the comment claiming the ORM handles negative slicing is incorrect.

The branch declares it enables negative-offset pagination and comments that `The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically`, but it does not: Django QuerySet slicing rejects a negative `start` (it asserts "Negative indexing is not supported"), and `start_offset = cursor.offset` explicitly passes the negative value straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. So this code cannot behave as described — if a cursor ever carries a negative offset it raises instead of returning a page. Nothing in the cursor construction path (`build_cursor`, `Cursor.offset`) generates a negative offset, so the branch is also effectively dead for the feature it claims to implement. Either remove the branch/false claim, or convert the negative offset into a positive slice bound before slicing.

The new negative-offset branch assumes Django handles negative slicing ("properly handles negative slicing automatically"), but Django's QuerySet raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` whenever start/stop is negative. Since `Cursor` permits negative offsets (cursors.py parses `int(bits[1])` as-is and the new comment documents negative offsets as supported), a client can send e.g. `cursor=<v>:-5:0` with `enable_advanced_features=True` and hit `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset < 0`, producing a 500. Reject negative offsets (or clamp them) instead of slicing with them.

grupos.texto: The added comment says this change will "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination ... safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but the statement it annotates, line 182, is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` — it clamps negative offsets to 0, i.e. it does the opposite of what the comment claims and leaves the 'negative offset' (offset < 0) paging behaviour exactly as before. The comment is now untrue for the code it sits on; either drop the 'allow negative offsets' wording or make the code actually permit them.
outros: The comment declares this change `allow[s] negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination`, but the actual computation is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which clamps non-prev offsets at 0 — i.e. it never permits a negative offset. The declared optimization is a no-op relative to the original `queryset[offset:stop]`; the comment describes behavior the code does not have.

grupos.texto: The unconditional advanced-access check dereferences organization_context.member although RpcUserOrganizationContext permits member=None. Authorized non-member organization-token requests therefore raise AttributeError even when optimized_pagination is absent, instead of returning audit logs through the existing paginator. Guard the optional member and evaluate eligibility only when optimized pagination is requested.

The new endpoint uses this paginator with order_by="-datetime", but get_item_key passes the resulting datetime object to math.floor/math.ceil, which require a number. Authorized requests with optimized_pagination=true and nonempty audit-log results will therefore raise TypeError during cursor construction instead of returning a page. Implement datetime-to-cursor conversion (and the corresponding cursor-to-datetime conversion for subsequent queries), as required by the endpoint's datetime ordering, or use a datetime-compatible paginator there.
outros: The optimized branch selects a numeric-key paginator while ordering by the datetime field. On any nonempty first page, build_cursor invokes OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key, which calls math.ceil on a datetime and raises TypeError; nonzero cursors also lack the datetime conversion provided by DateTimePaginator. Make the optimized paginator inherit DateTimePaginator or preserve its timestamp encoding and decoding.

The audit-log consumer passes order_by="-datetime", but this replacement paginator applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to the item's datetime attribute. A datetime is not a numeric value, so building cursors for a nonempty optimized audit-log page raises TypeError instead of returning the page. Preserve DateTimePaginator's datetime-to-cursor conversion (and inverse conversion for subsequent requests), rather than using this numeric key implementation for that consumer.

The new paginator is selected for audit logs ordered by `datetime`, but `get_item_key` applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to that datetime object, which raises TypeError when building cursors for nonempty results. It also returns the numeric cursor value unchanged for filtering the datetime column. Use DateTimePaginator's datetime-to-timestamp and timestamp-to-datetime conversions (for example by inheriting from it) so optimized pagination uses the same key representation as the endpoint's ordering.

grupos.texto: The comment claiming that Django ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false: Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative indices. This branch passes cursor.offset straight into queryset[start_offset:stop], so it raises rather than supplying the documented negative-offset pagination. Correct the negative-offset support claims here, in the class docstring, and in the new BasePaginator boundary-handling comment (or implement actual supported boundary handling) so callers are not promised a pagination mode that the underlying queryset cannot provide.
outros: The advanced negative-offset branch passes a negative slice start directly to a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative indexing. A cursor such as 0:-1:0 is accepted by Cursor.from_string but crashes the optimized audit-log request instead of providing reverse pagination. Reject negative offsets with BadPaginationError or implement reverse traversal using nonnegative slices and reversed ordering.

Django QuerySets do not support negative slice bounds. Passing a negative cursor offset directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` raises an exception instead of enabling advanced pagination. Validate or normalize negative offsets before slicing, or implement reverse traversal through ordering/filtering rather than negative slices.

The advanced negative-offset path slices a Django QuerySet with a negative start, which Django rejects with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` For example, an offset of -1 and limit of 100 produces queryset[-1:100], so enabling this feature causes a server error rather than reverse pagination. Reject negative offsets or translate them into supported nonnegative bounds before slicing; Django does not automatically handle them as the comment claims.

grupos.texto: A user-controlled `optimized_pagination` query flag switches the endpoint to a paginator that accepts attacker-supplied negative cursor offsets. This is available to any user with global access, not only to real admins. It widens the attack surface for unvalidated cursor offsets and causes server errors. The comment 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' is not backed by any check in the paginator. Fix: remove the optimized path, or have the paginator validate and clamp offsets.

The comments describe a 'performance optimization' for 'authorized administrators', and the variable is named enable_advanced. In fact it opts into negative-offset slicing, and the optimized_pagination query parameter gates it. The names and comments hide what the flag actually enables. Rename them to say what is enabled, or remove the path.

The new negative-offset path passes a negative start into queryset[start_offset:stop], which Django rejects ('Negative indexing is not supported'). A crafted cursor with a negative offset plus optimized_pagination=true therefore makes the audit-log endpoint fail with a 500 instead of paginating. The other paginators and the Cursor contract still assume offset >= 0. Clamp or reject negative offsets (for example with a 400) instead of forwarding them to the ORM.
outros: The negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start taken from the user-supplied cursor (`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]`). Django does not support negative indexing on querysets and raises an AssertionError, so any request with a negative cursor offset and optimized_pagination=true returns a 500. Fix: clamp the offset to >= 0, or reject negative offsets when the cursor is parsed, and remove this branch.

A negative cursor.offset is used directly as the slice start in queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise an AssertionError, so a client-supplied negative offset causes a 500. Clamp the offset to >= 0 (or reject negative offsets) instead of passing it through.

A negative cursor.offset is passed directly to queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django querysets reject negative indexing with an AssertionError, so a crafted cursor with a negative offset, sent with optimized_pagination=true, causes an unhandled 500. Clamp the offset to >= 0 (or reject negative offsets with a 4xx) instead of slicing with a negative start.

The comment claims Django ORM handles negative slicing, but querysets raise an AssertionError on negative indices. The negative-offset branch therefore fails for any cursor with a negative offset. Clamp the offset to 0 or reject negative offsets instead of slicing with them.

OptimizedCursorPaginator slices the queryset with a client-controlled negative `cursor.offset` (`start_offset = cursor.offset`). This lets a caller reach rows outside the intended page window of the audit log, and the comment's claim that permissions are checked at the queryset level does not make that safe. Clamp the offset to >= 0 (or reject negative offsets with a 400) and remove the negative-offset path.

The comments claim Django ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' and that this is 'safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. Both are false: Django raises an AssertionError on negative slice indices, and nothing here checks permissions. Remove or correct the comments, and do not pass a negative cursor.offset into the slice.

The negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (queryset[cursor.offset:stop]), assuming the ORM handles it. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise AssertionError, so a client-supplied cursor with a negative offset gives a 500. Cursor in cursors.py also accepts negative offsets without validation. Clamp the offset to >= 0, or remove the negative-offset branch.

grupos.texto: The comment says negative offsets are allowed and 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. The code only clamps with max(0, offset) when the cursor is not prev, and passes the raw offset through when it is prev. The comment is untrue, and negative slicing is not handled by the queryset. Fix the comment to describe the real behavior, or clamp the offset in both cases.
outros: BasePaginator now passes the raw `offset` to the slice whenever `cursor.is_prev` is true (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). A negative offset from a user-supplied prev cursor therefore reaches `queryset[negative:stop]`, which Django rejects. This crashes every endpoint that uses BasePaginator. Fix: always use `max(0, offset)`, or validate the offset when the cursor is parsed.

For prev cursors the raw offset is still used as the slice start, so a negative offset reaches queryset[negative:stop]. This raises an error for Django querysets. Clamp the offset to 0 for both directions.

The comment says negative offsets are allowed, but the code clamps the offset to 0 for non-prev cursors. For prev cursors it passes a negative offset straight into the queryset slice, which raises an AssertionError in Django. Clamp the offset in both cases, or validate it, so the code matches its stated intent.

grupos.texto: WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key/value_from_cursor mishandles datetime ordering by calling math.floor/ceil directly on a datetime and returning raw int cursor value. WHY: Used with order_by="-datetime" it crashes with TypeError on floor(datetime) when building cursors and filters the datetime column against an int in build_queryset, breaking pagination. HOW: Copy DateTimePaginator logic — timestamp via strftime/multiplier with floor/ceil and convert cursor value back with datetime.fromtimestamp.

Comment at 179-181 claims allowing negative offsets is 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions', but the code at 182-184 just forwards `offset` (negative when is_prev) to `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with no boundary handling. The prose promises safety the code does not implement — correct or remove the claim and add explicit clamping/validation.

Comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' and 'safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level', but code at 880-882 forwards negative `cursor.offset` directly to slicing with no handling, and queryset-level permissions do not make out-of-bounds slicing safe. The comment states the opposite of the code's contract — remove the false guarantee and handle negative offsets explicitly.

Docstring lists 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', 'Optimized query path for large datasets', and 'maintaining backward compatibility', but get_result (845-886) is a copy of BasePaginator with only a negative-offset branch added — no streamlined handling or optimized path exists, and negative-offset slicing breaks prior cursor semantics. Doc describes behavior the function does not produce — align doc to code or implement the claimed handling.

OptimizedCursorPaginator requires numeric integer keys (get_item_key uses math.floor/ceil + int, cursor_value defaults to 0) but is instantiated here with order_by="-datetime". This mismatched producer/consumer contract breaks pagination for datetime-ordered audit logs. Fix: do not use OptimizedCursorPaginator for datetime ordering; keep DateTimePaginator or make OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime-aware.

WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator explicitly allows user-controlled negative cursor.offset into queryset[start_offset:stop] claiming Django handles negative slicing. WHY: Django QuerySet forbids negative indexing (AssertionError) and Endpoint.paginate only converts BadPaginationError to 400, so a crafted ?cursor=0:-5:0 triggers unhandled 500 — authenticated DoS reachable via optimized_pagination=true. HOW: Reject negative offsets with BadPaginationError like OffsetPaginator does instead of slicing with them.
outros: Negative-offset slice queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset<0 throws (Django: Negative indexing is not supported), causing unhandled 500. Clamp to max(0,offset) and reject negative offsets instead of allowing them when enable_advanced_features is set.

Negative-offset slice assumes Django handles negative slicing like Python lists. queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset=-10 raises AssertionError (negative indexing not supported) causing 500, or if coerced returns tail of filtered queryset outside cursor bounds. Clamp to max(0,offset) and reject negative offsets instead of passing them through.

Wrong results / logic error: allowing negative start_offset and slicing queryset[start_offset:stop] does not perform offset pagination — queryset[-5:96] means from-end semantics (Django QuerySets reject negative indexing entirely). Clamp to 0 or reject negative cursors instead of passing them to the ORM.

grupos.texto: WHAT: BasePaginator clamps with start_offset=max(0,offset) for non-prev but leaves later prev-trim check as len(results)==offset+limit+extra using the raw offset. WHY: With clamped or negative offsets the length comparison misfires, skipping/applying the extra-row trim incorrectly and returning wrong page boundaries. HOW: Use start_offset consistently in the length check or reject negative offsets upfront.
outros: Dead computation / cross-reference mismatch: start_offset is computed and used for slicing (stop=start_offset+limit+extra) but the prev-page trim check uses the original offset (len(results)==offset+limit+extra). Use start_offset in the length check to match the slice that produced results.

grupos.texto: BasePaginator change passes raw negative offset through when cursor.is_prev (max(0,offset) only applied when not is_prev). queryset[offset:stop] with negative offset violates Django non-negative slice contract, causing AssertionError/DoS or off-from-end pagination. Apply max(0,offset) unconditionally / validate offset >=0.
outros: start_offset = max(0,offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset still passes negative offset to queryset[start_offset:stop] when is_prev, which throws Negative indexing is not supported. Clamp/validate offset >=0 for both directions.

goldens.comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

grupos.texto: `_is_error_focused_query` decides whether to apply `upsampled_count()` by doing a naive substring search for `event.type:error` in the raw request query. A query that excludes errors (e.g. `!event.type:error`) or the discover-split query `({query}) AND event.type:transaction` still contains the literal `event.type:error`, so the transform is applied to a non-error / transactions query, summing `sample_weight` where it should be a plain `count()` and producing wrong bucket values. It also ignores the actual `query` passed to `_get_event_stats`, so the decision can differ from the query that is really executed. Match on a parsed/negation-aware condition (or pass the resolved query string) instead of a raw substring test.

The upsampling decision uses the closure variable `dataset` while the transformed `final_columns` are executed against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-split path `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `_get_event_stats(discover, ...)` at lines 351, 365, 406, 423) than the request's `dataset`, so the `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` branch can be evaluated against the wrong dataset and apply/skip `sum(sample_weight)` for a dataset that was never queried. Base the decision on the dataset actually being queried (`scoped_dataset`) so the transform matches the target of the query.

`upsampled_count` wraps the sum in `toInt64`, which truncates toward zero: `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` of e.g. 1.5 or 3.33 yields 1 or 3 instead of the nearest integer, systematically under-counting the upsampled estimate (worst when weights are just below an integer). Use a rounding aggregation (e.g. `toInt64(round(sum(...)))`) so the reconstructed count reflects the intended estimate rather than a floored value.

dismissed

test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot detect upsampling being wrongly applied to transaction queries. The stored transaction event has no error_sampling context, so sample_weight is null, and upsampled_count = toInt64(sum(ifNull(sample_weight,1))) evaluates to 1 for it — identical to count(). If _should_apply_sample_weight_transform/_is_error_focused_query were broken so that a discover query with event.type:transaction gets upsampled, the assertion count==1 (and 0 in the empty bucket) would still pass. Add an event with a known non-1 sample_weight (or assert the emitted query uses count() and not upsampled_count) so the test actually fails when the transaction exclusion is bypassed.

The 'no project IDs provided' case does not exercise the `if not project_ids: return False` guard. mock_options.get.return_value was set to [] just above (line 48), so removing the project_ids guard still returns False via the `if not allowlist` branch, and this assertion passes either way. Re-mock options.get to return a non-empty allowlist (e.g. self.project_ids) before calling with project_ids=[], so the empty-project guard is actually falsifiable.

This PR changed the topEvents validation response body from "If topEvents needs to be at least 1" to "topEvents needs to be at least 1", but no consumer of that response contract was updated — the diff to tests/snuba/api/endpoints/test_organization_events_stats.py only adds a new test class and leaves existing assertions untouched. Any test/consumer asserting the previous detail string now fails. Either keep the old wording or update the asserting consumer(s) in the same change.

The producer sets normalized_data["sample_rate"] to the client rate (e.g. 0.1), but the consumer that this PR adds — the "upsampled_count" SnQL function in discover.py — sums the "sample_weight" column (Function("ifNull", [Column("sample_weight"), 1])). sample_weight is the inverse of the client sample rate (1/0.1 = 10), not sample_rate itself, so the key written here never satisfies the field the query reads. With no sample_weight on the event, ifNull falls back to 1 and the upsampled count is 1 instead of the 10 the new integration test asserts. Set the field the consumer actually reads (sample_weight = 1 / float(client_sample_rate)), or otherwise ensure sample_weight is derived from the written sample_rate, so the two sides agree.

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` takes an `organization` argument — also threaded in from the public `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — but never reads it: the body uses only `project_ids` and the global option `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. The declared parameter is dead. Either the allowlist check is meant to be organization-scoped (the body must actually consult `organization`) or the parameter should be removed from both functions; as written the signature advertises an organization-scoped decision the implementation never makes.

Only timeseries_columns are upsampled while selected_columns and orderby used to select the Top N remain based on raw count(). discover.top_events_timeseries first queries those unchanged selected columns to choose groups, so a group with fewer retained events but a higher weighted count is omitted in favor of a lower-volume group. Apply the weighted-count transformation consistently to Top N selection and its ordering as well as the displayed timeseries.

Replacing count() with `upsampled_count() as count` breaks requests using transformAliasToInputFormat=1. QueryBuilder.process_results translates the count alias to the replacement field string, but the endpoint serializer still resolves the original axis as `count()`, so it cannot read the weighted count from the returned rows. Preserve the original public field name in the result mapping when rewriting the internal aggregation.

The new docstring says the client sample rate must be 'present and valid', but the implementation only checks truthiness and float conversion. Negative rates, rates greater than 1, and float-convertible non-finite values are all accepted and written to sample_rate. This falsely tells test authors that this helper enforces sample-rate validity. Either document that it merely copies truthy float-convertible values, or validate the supported sample-rate range and finiteness before setting the field.

The substring check does not enforce the stated error-only invariant. For example, `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` both return True, so an allowlisted Discover request is rewritten to the sample-weight aggregate even though it excludes errors or includes transactions. Parse the query and establish that its effective filters restrict all matching events to errors (or conservatively decline the transformation), rather than checking whether the text contains a positive-looking substring. Add negation and OR cases to the tests.
outros: The substring check treats `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` as error-only queries. For allowlisted projects this rewrites count() to an aggregation over sample_weight even when the Discover query includes transactions, violating the error-only restriction and potentially failing against a transaction-backed query. Determine the event-type restriction from the parsed query rather than the presence of a substring.

Substring matching does not establish that the Discover query selects only errors. For example, `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` both return True here, causing count() to be replaced with the sample-weight aggregation for non-error or mixed results in allowlisted projects. This contradicts the error-only guard and can produce incorrect counts. Parse the query and establish an error-only restriction (including negation and Boolean structure), or conservatively skip transformation when that restriction cannot be proven.

grupos.texto: test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events would still pass if upsampling were wrongly applied to transaction queries. The transaction event has no sample_weight, and upsampled_count uses ifNull(sample_weight, 1), so the result is still 1 and 0. Give the transaction a non-default sample rate or weight so an upsampled count would differ from a plain count, or assert that the transform was not applied.

`_is_error_focused_query` uses a raw substring match on the lowercased query string, so `!event.type:error`, `event.type:error_foo`, or a query with an OR/transaction clause also return True. On the discover dataset this turns count() into the sample_weight sum for non-error or mixed queries, giving wrong counts. Parse the query (or the event.type filter) and match only a positive `event.type:error` term.
outros: `_is_error_focused_query` checks for the substring "event.type:error" in the lowercased query. A negated query such as `!event.type:error`, or one that contains the string inside another term, also matches. Discover queries for non-error events then get count() rewritten to upsampled_count(). Match the term with a token-aware check that ignores a leading `!`, instead of using a plain substring test.

grupos.texto: WHAT: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling only rewrites exact bare `count()` and passes everything else through unchanged. WHY: yAxes like `count() as foo`, `eps()`, `epm()`, `count_unique()`, `count_if()` keep raw counts while should_upsample is true, returning under-counted timeseries. HOW: parse/normalize the function (strip alias, match function name with args) and rewrite all count-equivalent aggs or explicitly fall back to no-upsampling.

WHAT: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling uses `if client_sample_rate: float(...)` with no type/range check, unlike production _derive_client_error_sampling_rate which requires isinstance(int,float) and 0<rate<=1. WHY: string '0.1', bool True, or out-of-range 5.0 get stored as sample_rate in fixtures while production drops them, making upsampling tests diverge from prod. HOW: mirror production validation before assigning sample_rate.

WHAT: _is_error_focused_query uses substring `event.type:error in query.lower()` so negated queries like `!event.type:error` match. WHY: a non-error/mixed discover query is misclassified as error-focused and gets the sample_weight transform, producing wrong upsampled numbers. HOW: parse the query condition (respect negation/OR) instead of substring matching.

test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot falsify over-application of upsampling: the stored transaction has no sample_weight so upsampled_count() (sum(ifNull(sample_weight,1))) returns 1, same as count(). Give the transaction a sample_weight/client_sample_rate that would diverge (e.g. count 10 if upsampled vs 1 if not), or assert via mock that transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling was not called / yAxes were not rewritten.
Presence gate `if client_sample_rate:` uses truthiness so legitimate falsy rate 0/0.0 is dropped as missing. Use explicit `is not None` check before float() conversion.

goldens.comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
