grupos.texto: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts down the FixedQueuePool, but that pool is a singleton owned by the factory (created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and never recreated). Arroyo calls strategy.close() then join() on every assignment revocation/rebalance, and the factory's create_with_partitions is called again for the next assignment; the new strategy then reuses the already-shut-down queue_pool. Because q.shutdown(immediate=False) makes subsequent put() raise queue.ShutDown, submit()'s except branch (lines 317-325) swallows it and marks the offset complete, so after any rebalance every message is committed as processed without ever being handled — silent data loss. Fix: either let the factory own the pool lifecycle (don't shut it down from the strategy's close) and create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions, or reset/recreate factory.queue_pool when the strategy is closed.

The commit assertion contradicts the test's own docstring and cannot fail for the reason it claims. The docstring says "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the body asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` — i.e. it passes only when nothing is committed. In queue_consumer.py ordered worker's `finally` calls `complete_offset` even after result_processor raises (lines 148-149), so offset 100 should be committable and offset 101 should advance the commit; if the whole commit path were removed (commits blocked entirely) the test would still pass. Assert the positive behaviour instead: e.g. that the failing message's offset was still completed so commits progressed (expect `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`, matching the follow-on offset of the successfully processed message).

Each worker queue is created unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize) although the class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' and the strategy claims to guarantee backpressure. With no bound and no MessageRejected raised from submit(), a slow group continues to accumulate items in its queue while the consumer keeps polling, so memory grows without limit under a sustained backlog — the opposite of the intended protection. Fix: give the queues a maxsize and raise/return MessageRejected (or otherwise propagate backpressure to the caller) when a queue is full.
outros: The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but the queues this strategy drives are unbounded: `FixedQueuePool` creates each one as `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize (line 185), and `submit()` puts items unconditionally. Nothing ever blocks, so no backpressure exists. Either bound the queues (pass a `maxsize` and handle `queue.Full` / block in `submit`) or correct the docstring so it does not advertise a guarantee the code does not provide.

grupos.texto: The `WorkItem` docstring says it "includes the original message for offset tracking", but the `message` field is never used for offset tracking — `OffsetTracker` and the commit loop only ever read `partition`/`offset`, and `submit()` even re-derives the offset from `message.value` rather than from the stored `message`. Update the docstring to describe what the field is actually for (or remove the unused field) so it does not misdescribe the dataclass contract.
outros: `WorkItem.message` is declared with the comment 'includes the original message for offset tracking' and is populated in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, but nothing ever reads it — offset tracking uses the separate `partition`/`offset` fields. The declared purpose does not match any actual use, so the field (and the extra reference to each Kafka message it keeps alive) is dead; either use it for offset tracking or remove it.

grupos.texto: Test named/docstringed "Test that different groups are processed concurrently" never verifies concurrency. The body only asserts all 6 items ran and that three distinct group numbers were seen — a single worker draining one queue, or a fully serial FixedQueuePool, would satisfy both assertions. Either measure actual overlap (e.g. have result_processor block on a barrier/event until all three groups have entered, and fail on timeout) or drop the concurrency claim from the name/docstring.
outros: test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions claims to verify that different subscriptions are processed concurrently, but the only assertion is `mock_processor_call.call_count == 2`, which a strictly serial implementation also satisfies. Add a real concurrency signal (e.g. a barrier in the mocked processor that requires both calls to be in flight simultaneously before either returns), otherwise this test cannot detect loss of parallelism.

grupos.texto: The failed item's offset is completed unconditionally in the `finally` block, so `complete_offset` runs even when `result_processor` raised. This breaks the class's documented guarantee ('Only commits offsets after successful processing', line 254): the commit loop then advances past a message that was never successfully processed, silently dropping it (and, per the PR's own test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, a commit is produced where none is expected). Only call `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` on the success path (i.e. after `result_processor` returns normally), or explicitly decide and document the at-most-once semantics; do not complete on the exception path.
outros: The worker marks the offset complete in the `finally` block even when `result_processor(...)` raises, so a message whose handling failed is reported as committable and its offset is committed (it will never be retried). This contradicts the strategy's own guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and the new test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, which asserts the partition is not committed after a failure. Only call `complete_offset` on the success path (or track failed offsets separately) so failures are not silently skipped.

The worker marks the offset complete in `finally` even when `result_processor` raised an exception, so a failed item's offset is reported as committable and gets committed by the commit loop. This contradicts the strategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and the contract asserted in test_results_consumer.py (test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, which expects the failed partition NOT to be committed): the failed message is committed past and never retried. Track success separately and only call `complete_offset` when processing succeeded (or make the failure explicit so the offset is withheld/retried).

grupos.texto: Determine the commit boundary from received offsets rather than requiring every integer in this range to exist. Kafka offsets need not be consecutive: if 100, 102 and 103 are delivered and completed, this scan stops at the nonexistent 101 even though there is no unfinished record. Conversely, after committing 100 and removing it, the next scan starts at 102 and commits past the gap, contradicting the added gap tests. Iterate received offsets in sorted order and stop at the first outstanding record; add a test covering legitimate skipped Kafka offsets across multiple commit cycles.

The error-handling test can pass even when failed messages are committed. It waits for two processor calls, sleeps only 0.2 seconds, and asserts that no commit has happened, whereas _commit_loop waits 1 second. OrderedQueueWorker currently completes the failed offset in finally, so the unsafe commit can occur after this assertion. Synchronize with an actual commit-loop iteration before asserting that it cannot advance past the failed offset.

This does not verify graceful shutdown: factory.shutdown unconditionally clears queue_pool after calling pool.shutdown, so the assertion passes even if pending messages are abandoned or worker threads remain alive. Retain the pool reference and assert that all submitted work completed and its workers stopped; the current worker shutdown flag can stop workers without draining their queues.

The strategy ordering test submits five identical decoded results for sub1 and only asserts their count. Processing them in reverse order would still pass. Give each message a distinguishable sequence value and assert the exact processed sequence, so this tests ordering through SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy rather than only delivery.

The concurrency test only verifies eventual completion and that all group names appear. Routing every group to a single worker would satisfy every assertion, so it does not protect concurrent processing. Use distinct queue assignments and a barrier/event arrangement proving a second group starts while the first is blocked. The uptime concurrent-subscriptions test similarly only asserts two eventual calls and should verify overlapping execution as well.

Create a fresh queue pool for each processing strategy, or change the ownership contract so strategy.close()/join() does not shut down a factory-owned pool. This factory passes the same self.queue_pool to every strategy, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts that pool down and join() calls close(). On a partition reassignment, closing the old strategy therefore stops the workers and shuts the queues that the replacement strategy receives. Subsequent submissions cannot be processed (and the submit exception handler marks their offsets complete), potentially skipping results. Pool/offset-tracker state should be isolated to the strategy's assignment lifetime.
outros: Every recreated strategy receives the same factory-owned queue pool, although SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() permanently shuts down that pool and its workers. On an assignment change, the next strategy submits to shut-down queues; submit catches the resulting exception and marks those unprocessed offsets complete, allowing results to be skipped and committed. Create a fresh pool and offset tracker per strategy assignment, rather than reusing the closed pool.

Give each strategy a live pool rather than reusing the factory-owned pool after strategy closure. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts down this pool, but subsequent create_with_partitions calls reuse the same self.queue_pool. On a partition reassignment/rebalance the replacement strategy therefore has stopped workers (and shut-down queues); submissions fail and its exception handler marks those unprocessed messages complete, allowing them to be committed. Recreate the pool and offset tracker for each strategy generation.

Closing a strategy now shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, although ResultsStrategyFactory.create_with_partitions reuses that same pool for subsequent strategies. During a partition reassignment, closing/joining the old strategy therefore leaves the replacement strategy with stopped workers and shut-down queues. Its submissions fail, and the submit exception handler marks those messages complete, allowing offsets to advance without processing the results. Keep pool lifetime scoped to the factory (with appropriate draining between assignments), or create a fresh pool for each strategy rather than shutting down a resource that the factory will reuse.

Each new strategy reuses the factory's single queue_pool, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join() shuts that pool down. After a partition rebalance closes the old strategy, create_with_partitions returns a new strategy backed by stopped workers and shut-down queues; submissions then fail and are treated as completed by the submission exception handler. Create a fresh pool for each strategy lifecycle rather than reusing the closed pool.

grupos.texto: close() stops the commit thread and shuts down workers before draining accepted work, and join() only repeats close() instead of waiting for processing and making a final commit. Pool shutdown sets worker.shutdown before workers can drain their queues, so assignment revocation abandons queued results and completed in-flight work is not finally committed, causing replay and allowing unfinished old work to overlap a new owner. Make close() stop acceptance without blocking, then have join() drain accepted work within its timeout and commit completed offsets before releasing workers.
outros: Do not set worker.shutdown before draining the queues during graceful shutdown. If a worker is processing A while B is queued, shutdown sets the flag; after A finishes, the worker exits at `while not self.shutdown` without ever retrieving B. Calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False) does not override that loop condition. Drain accepted work before stopping workers, and keep committing available until that drain completes; currently close stops the commit thread before the workers as well, so even work finished during shutdown is not finally committed.

Setting worker.shutdown before shutting down the queues prevents graceful draining: run() checks this flag before every get(), so a worker exits after its current item even when queued items remain. shutdown(immediate=False) cannot override that loop condition. Allow workers to consume until the queue signals shutdown after draining, rather than setting the exit flag first.

grupos.texto: The pool creates unbounded queues, while strategy submit always accepts messages and poll never applies backpressure. When a queue's worker is slow or ingestion exceeds processing capacity, queued WorkItems retain both decoded results and original Kafka messages without any limit, causing growing memory consumption and eventual consumer OOM. Bound queued/in-flight work and raise Arroyo MessageRejected when capacity is reached, ensuring that rejection is not swallowed by the generic submit exception handler.
outros: The claimed 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' does not exist: FixedQueuePool constructs queue.Queue() without a capacity (line 185), and submit always puts into that unbounded queue. Document that submissions are unbounded, or implement bounded capacity/backpressure before advertising this guarantee. As written, callers may rely on a memory-safety/flow-control property this strategy does not provide.

grupos.texto: The guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' is false: OrderedQueueWorker catches processor exceptions and unconditionally calls complete_offset in finally (lines 144–149), after which the commit loop can commit that failed item's offset. The submit exception handler likewise marks failed submissions complete. Correct this documented contract to describe the actual failure policy, or implement the promised success-only completion; callers currently receive a misleading assurance about replay of failed work.
outros: Only mark an offset complete after successful processing. If result_processor raises (for example on a transient database failure), this handler logs the exception and the finally block removes the offset from outstanding anyway. The commit thread can then commit past that failed result, permanently skipping it on restart, contrary to the strategy's successful-processing-only commit guarantee. Propagate or retain/retry failed work rather than treating it as completed.

Processing exceptions are logged but the finally block still marks the offset complete. The commit loop can consequently commit past a result that was never successfully handled (for example after a transient database failure), permanently skipping it on restart. Only mark successful processing complete and propagate or retry failures. The error-handling test's short wait does not prove safety: the commit loop runs after one second.

grupos.texto: Queue selection uses the built-in `hash(group_key)`, which is randomized per process by PYTHONHASHSEED for str. Group-to-queue assignment therefore differs between consumer processes and after a restart. Ordering guarantees per subscription are lost across processes, and two processes can handle the same subscription concurrently. Use a stable hash such as `zlib.crc32(group_key.encode()) % num_queues` or md5.

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` exist only in Python 3.13+, and the worker blocks forever on `get()` when shutdown is not available. On older Python versions, `except queue.ShutDown` raises AttributeError when evaluated, and `q.shutdown` fails in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`, where the failure is swallowed. The worker threads then never exit. Use a sentinel item or a timeout on `get` for shutdown.

`commit_function` is called from the background commit thread, but arroyo's commit callback is expected to be called from the main consumer thread, and the Kafka consumer is not thread-safe. Committing from another thread risks races with polling and with rebalances.

The metric `offsets_committed` is incremented by len(committable), which is the number of partitions committed, not the number of offsets. Emit the actual offset count (for example, the sum of newly committed offsets per partition), or rename the metric to partitions_committed.

Offsets are only tracked for messages that were submitted, and there is no partition revoke handling. Contiguity is checked with `range(start, max_offset+1)`, so any offset gap (compacted topics, transactional markers, or offsets filtered out upstream) permanently blocks commits for that partition. The `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` state is never cleared on rebalance, so stale state survives partition reassignment. Treat gaps as committable once all lower tracked offsets are complete, and clear per-partition state when partitions are revoked.
outros: The commit scan assumes consecutive Kafka offsets and breaks at the first offset that is not in all_offsets. A permanent offset gap (compacted or transactional records) then blocks commits for that partition forever. Track the submitted offsets in sorted order and commit up to the highest offset below the lowest outstanding one, rather than requiring every integer in between to be present.

grupos.texto: Submission puts into unbounded `queue.Queue()` instances, so `submit` never blocks. The docstring claims backpressure, but a slow queue lets the consumer keep reading from Kafka and grow memory without limit. Use a bounded queue (`maxsize`) and raise arroyo's MessageRejected on `queue.Full`.
outros: The docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but the queues are created as unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit` never blocks. No backpressure exists. Remove the claim or bound the queues.

grupos.texto: The strategy docstring says it "Only commits offsets after successful processing", but the worker calls complete_offset in `finally`, so failed items are marked done and get committed. The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts that nothing is committed after a failure, which contradicts this code (its docstring says errors don't block commits). Align the behavior, docstring and test: either complete the offset only on success, or fix the docstring and test.
outros: The class docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing. The worker's `finally` block calls complete_offset even when the result processor raises, and `submit` also completes offsets for messages that failed to decode or enqueue. Failed messages therefore get committed. Reword the docstring to say offsets are committed after processing is attempted, regardless of outcome.

The docstring says errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages. The test asserts the opposite: `test_partition not in committed_offsets`. Make the docstring and the assertion agree, so the test states which behaviour is intended.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts that no offsets were committed. Its docstring says an error must not block commits, and the worker's finally block completes the failed offset, so a commit is expected. The assertion passes only because the test checks within about 0.3s, before the first 1s commit-loop tick. Wait on a commit event and assert that offset 102 (next to read) is committed after the failure.

The test asserts no offset is committed after a processor exception. But OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in a `finally` block, so failed items are still committed (101 -> 102) by the commit loop. The test's assertion contradicts the implementation and its own docstring; change it to expect the commit (test_partition committed at 102).

grupos.texto: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close(), terminate() and join() shut down the FixedQueuePool, but that pool is created once by ResultsStrategyFactory and shared by every strategy it creates. After a rebalance, Arroyo closes the old strategy and then calls create_with_partitions again, which reuses the dead pool. Messages then fail to enqueue, and the submit() exception handler marks them complete, so their offsets get committed without the messages being processed. The strategy should only stop its own commit thread. The pool should be shut down only by factory.shutdown(), or the pool should be created per strategy.
outros: The strategy's close(), terminate() and join() shut down the FixedQueuePool, but the pool is created once in the factory and shared by every strategy that create_with_partitions makes. After the first rebalance the pool's workers are dead and its queues are shut down. Later submits raise queue.ShutDown, which submit()'s except block swallows by marking the offset complete, so messages are silently dropped and their offsets get committed. Fix: leave pool shutdown to the factory's shutdown() and have strategy close() stop only its commit thread, or create the pool per strategy.

grupos.texto: WHAT: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/terminate shuts down the factory-owned shared FixedQueuePool. WHY: ResultsStrategyFactory creates one queue_pool and hands it to every strategy from create_with_partitions, so Arroyo rebalance (close old strategy, create new one reusing factory.queue_pool) reuses a dead pool with joined workers and shut-down queues, stalling all further processing. HOW: Make pool lifecycle owned only by the factory: strategy close should only stop its commit thread, not call queue_pool.shutdown().

WHAT: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True while OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on while not self.shutdown, so workers exit without draining queued WorkItems even though queues are shut down with immediate=False. WHY: Graceful shutdown silently drops queued items and leaves their offsets in outstanding forever, causing reprocessing/duplicates and failing the claimed graceful-shutdown guarantee. HOW: Remove the shutdown-flag short-circuit and let workers drain until queue.ShutDown, e.g. loop unconditionally and break only on ShutDown.

WHAT: ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown shuts down queue_pool but never stops SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy commit threads created in the strategy constructor. WHY: The daemon commit loop keeps running after factory shutdown and keeps calling the stale commit_function/mark_committed, leaking threads and committing after shutdown/revoke. HOW: Track created strategies and call their close/terminate (or at least set shutdown_event and join commit_thread) from factory shutdown.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling claims errors don't block commits but asserts len(committed)==0 / not in, and waits only for total==0+sleep(0.2) while commit loop is 1.0s. It passes if commits are correctly made (checked before loop fires) and if commits are never made. Wait for commit condition and assert contiguous commit includes both offsets despite the exception.

test_concurrent_processing_across_groups claims concurrent processing but only asserts 6 items processed and 3 groups seen. A serial/single-queue implementation would still pass. Verify overlap (blocking processor + timing/thread IDs) or remove concurrency claim.

test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions claims different subscriptions processed concurrently but only asserts call_count==2. Serial processing passes identically. Add concurrency proof (e.g., blocking first group, assert second completes) or rename to processing-correctness.

FixedQueuePool.submit calls offset_tracker.add_offset before work_queue.put with no cleanup if put raises (e.g. after queue shutdown). The leaked outstanding offset can never complete and blocks later contiguous commits for that partition.

metrics.incr passes len(committable) as second positional arg (instance), not amount, so commit count is always 1 and instance is polluted with an int. Pass amount explicitly, e.g. amount=len(committable).

get_stats/wait_until_empty measures only sum(q.qsize()); qsize drops at get() before processing completes, so it reports empty/0 while items are in-flight. Include in-flight work (e.g. OffsetTracker outstanding) or unfinished_tasks before declaring empty.

WHAT: FixedQueuePool uses unbounded queue.Queue() with non-blocking submit and poll() only emits a gauge, providing no backpressure. WHY: If workers are slower than submit (the slow-item case this PR targets), the Arroyo poll loop keeps enqueueing and total_items grows without bound, risking unbounded memory/OOM on the consumer. HOW: Create queues with maxsize and use blocking put with timeout, or gate submit/poll on get_stats depths.
outros: Docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but FixedQueuePool creates unbounded `queue.Queue()` (maxsize 0) and `submit` uses non-blocking `put`, so queues never fill/block the producer. Fix doc or use bounded queues with blocking put / poll-based backpressure.

grupos.texto: Docstring promises 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' but OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in `finally` even when result_processor raises (caught as generic Exception and logged), so failed items become committable and offsets advance past failures. Fix doc or don't mark failed offsets complete / route to DLQ/retry.
outros: OrderedQueueWorker.run marks offset complete in finally even when result_processor raised. Failed items become committable and are committed as if successful, violating the only-commit-after-success invariant.

goldens.comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

feat-uptime-add-ability-to-use-queues-to.prTitle: feat(uptime): Add ability to use queues to manage parallelism

grupos.texto: ZUNIONSTORE uses AGGREGATE SUM by default, so when the same span payload is present in both `set_key` and the merged `span_key`/`parent_key` (duplicate delivery is anticipated by this buffer's own comments), its score is added instead of being kept equal to `end_timestamp_precise`. Because eviction at line 63 (`zpopmin` by score) compares scores across all members of `set_key`, a summed score makes the duplicated span appear far newer than its real end timestamp and biases eviction away from legitimately-old spans, breaking the stated 'evict oldest end timestamps' contract. Use ZUNIONSTORE ... AGGREGATE MIN (or MAX) so a duplicate keeps a single end timestamp score rather than doubling it.

This hunk removes the only load-time span-count cap (`self.max_segment_spans`): previously a segment exceeding 1001 spans was logged, deleted from `payloads`/`cursors`, and skipped, but now every scanned span is unconditionally appended via `payloads[key].extend(...)`. The new bound relies entirely on insert-time eviction in the Lua script; if that eviction fails to bound a key (e.g. duplicated/scored members or the concurrent-writer case the code itself warns about at lines 457-461), this method will now materialize an unbounded number of spans into memory and emit them, whereas before it was safely skipped. Re-introduce a span-count guard (or verify the invite-time eviction strictly caps cardinality) to keep memory bounded.

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` indexes the field directly (unlike the adjacent `parent_span_id`, which uses `.get`). This consumer did not read `end_timestamp_precise` before this PR, so any ingest payload that omits the field (older/replayed producers, partial schema) previously processed fine but now raises KeyError and aborts the entire batch. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise")` with a fallback (e.g. a span timestamp or 0.0) or explicitly validate/skip payloads missing the field.

The loop bound was reduced from 10000 to 1000, but the comment on the line above still reads 'segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly'. The comment now contradicts the code it describes (the cap is 1000, i.e. depth ~1k); update it to match the new limit so readers are not misled about the redirect-walk depth.

The segment keys were migrated from Redis SETs to SORTED SETs (ZADD/ZSCAN/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN), but nothing handles the keys written by the currently deployed release. During a rolling deploy, an existing `span-buf:s:{...}:{id}` key is still a SET, so this `p.zadd(...)` (and the flusher's `p.zscan(...)`, and the Lua `zcard`/`zunionstore`) raises WRONGTYPE 'Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value'. That exception is unhandled: it aborts the whole pipeline/Lua invocation and crashes the consumer batch. Add a key-schema version to the key name (or a migration/fallback) so old SET-typed keys cannot be touched as sorted sets.

buffer.py declares the segment span limit as the configurable `max_segment_spans` (default 1001, line 150) and this hunk removed the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` size guard from the flush path, while the other changed file (add-buffer.lua line 62) now enforces a hardcoded cap of 1000 spans. The two changed files disagree on what the segment span limit is: the Lua cap (1000) is not the declared `max_segment_spans`, and the buffer no longer applies the declared limit at all. If `max_segment_spans` is configured below 1000 (or below the Lua cap), oversized segments that this code used to skip will now be flushed. Reconcile the constant: either keep/restore the buffer-side guard against `self.max_segment_spans`, or make the Lua cap derive from the same limit instead of hardcoding 1000.
outros: The segment size cap is hardcoded as 1000 here, but SpansBuffer still declares max_segment_spans = 1001 in src/sentry/spans/buffer.py, and this PR deleted the flush-time guard that used that constant. The declared limit and the actually-enforced limit now disagree (and the Python constant is no longer honored anywhere). Make the Lua cap and the Python constant agree — either pass max_segment_spans in as an ARGV instead of the literal 1000, or update the declared constant to 1000 — so the buffer's enforced bound matches the value it declares.

Ownership of the segment-size cap moved into this script, but the script hardcodes `1000` and receives no limit argument. The Python side previously enforced `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (configurable, default 1001) in `flush_segments` and that guard was deleted in this PR, so the cap is now a magic constant baked into Lua. Any deployment that configures `max_segment_spans` to a non-default value will have its contract silently violated (spans evicted at 1000 regardless). Pass the limit as an ARGV from `SpansBuffer` (or restore the Python-side check) so the configured cap is actually honored.

The `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans:` guard (and the segment_span_count_exceeded metric) was removed here, and the only remaining limit is the hardcoded `span_count > 1000` zpopmin in add-buffer.lua. `self.max_segment_spans` (constructor arg, buffer.py:150) is now unused, so the configured span-count limit is silently unenforced: setting it to a value below 1000 no longer bounds a flushed segment, and there is no Python-side protection if the Lua cap is ever changed. Either keep the check here or make the Lua cap use the configured value instead of the literal 1000.

grupos.texto: The missing test for the new trim path (zset ordering/trim by end_timestamp_precise, the >1000-span zpopmin path) is a coverage gap. Add a test that verifies the new trim behavior.

Removing the span-count check makes the existing `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter misleading: callers can still supply and inspect it, but it no longer sets the maximum segment span count. The replacement Lua trimming hard-codes 1000 instead. Preserve enforcement of the configured maximum (or explicitly remove/deprecate the parameter and update its contract) so callers requesting a smaller limit are not silently given segments exceeding that advertised maximum.

Handle `span_key == set_key` before merging/unlinking. Python now ZADDs the whole subsegment into the effective parent key before invoking this script. For a non-root span whose ID already resolves to that same set (for example a repeated span after its redirect was established), this branch unions the key with itself and then unlinks it, deleting the buffered segment. The sorted-set change additionally doubles its timestamp scores through the default SUM aggregation. Skip this merge/unlink when the keys are identical so the Python-produced buffer remains intact.

Version or migrate the Redis segment-key namespace when changing its type from set to sorted set. Existing `span-buf:s:{...}:...` keys created by the previous `SADD` implementation remain ordinary sets, so this `ZADD` (and the new Lua `ZCARD`/flush `ZSCAN`) raises Redis WRONGTYPE for buffered segments across deployment. During a rolling deployment, old workers also cannot consume keys written by new workers. Use a separate versioned namespace with a compatible drain strategy, or explicitly handle conversion before issuing sorted-set commands.
outros: The new ZADD writes sorted sets into the same span-buf:s namespace previously populated by SADD, without migrating existing set keys. During deployment, inserting into an existing buffered segment fails with WRONGTYPE, and the new ZSCAN reader likewise fails on pending old-format segments instead of flushing them. Introduce a coordinated migration/drain or a versioned namespace with compatible handling of pending old-format buffers.

Changing SADD to ZADD while retaining `span-buf:s:{...}:...` makes existing buffered Redis sets incompatible with this writer (and with the new ZSCAN/ZCARD readers). Deploying while spans are buffered will produce WRONGTYPE errors rather than insert or flush those segments; rolling deployment also lets old and new workers create incompatible types for one another. Use a versioned namespace consistently across the Python and Lua paths, or provide a coordinated drain/migration before switching the key type.

The storage type changes from set to sorted set without changing the Redis key namespace. Any unexpired buffer created by the previous version makes this ZADD fail with WRONGTYPE; the new ZSCAN and Lua ZCARD paths likewise cannot process existing sets. During a rolling deployment the two versions also write incompatible types to the same keys. Use a versioned namespace with an appropriate draining strategy, or provide a coordinated migration before switching commands.

grupos.texto: ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, so a payload present in both the destination and source has its timestamp doubled rather than preserved. This can happen when a previously merged span is replayed into its original subtree key. The duplicated span then sorts after genuinely newer spans and survives ZPOPMIN eviction incorrectly. Specify AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN, since identical payloads should have identical timestamps) on both union calls so merging remains idempotent and scores remain end timestamps.
outros: ZUNIONSTORE uses its default SUM aggregation, so replayed payloads present in both the temporary parent_key and the resolved set_key receive the sum of their end timestamps. Replaying a child whose parent already redirects to an ancestor therefore makes that old span score roughly twice its actual timestamp, protecting it from eviction over genuinely newer spans. Use AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN for identical timestamp scores) on both union operations to preserve timestamp scores when members overlap.

grupos.texto: The redirect-resolution loop limit was lowered from 10000 to 1000 with no explanation. For span trees deeper than 1000 the loop exits early, so set_span_id points to an intermediate node and the segment is split. Restore the previous limit, or make the new bound explicit and handled.

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is a hard key lookup, so any span message that lacks the field raises KeyError in process_batch and fails the whole batch. The old code did not require this field. Read it with a fallback, for example `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", time.time())`, or skip the malformed span.
outros: val["end_timestamp_precise"] is read with a hard key lookup. A span payload without this field raises KeyError in process_batch and fails the whole batch. Use val.get with a fallback (for example the batch timestamp), or skip the span.

grupos.texto: WHAT: Changed SET ops (scard/sunionstore) to ZSET ops (zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin) with no migration breaks in-flight segments. WHY: Old keys of type SET still live up to TTL; ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN/ZADD on the opposite type raises WRONGTYPE and fails inserts/flushes during rollout.

WHAT: Direct val["end_timestamp_precise"] indexing with no fallback crashes the batch on missing/null field. WHY: KeyError/TypeError aborts process_batch for the whole Kafka batch (poison-pill), dropping all spans in it; use .get with fallback/validation.

WHAT: zpopmin eviction by lowest end_timestamp has no protection for the segment/root span. WHY: Root with smallest or tied timestamp (tests use identical timestamps, ties break lexicographically) is evicted while hrs flag stays 1, flushing a root-marked segment missing its root.
WHAT: Redirect-chase limit silently cut from 10000 to 1000. WHY: Segment trees with depth 1001-10000 previously joined correctly and now stop early, leaving split segments/redirects unresolved.

All spans in the fixture use identical end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0, so the ZSET score-dependent behavior (ordering by end time, zunionstore score merge, and Lua zpopmin keeping newest 1000) is neutralised — tests pass even if scores are wrong or eviction keeps the wrong end. Use distinct timestamps and add a >1000-span trimming test asserting oldest evicted.

WHAT: zunionstore uses default AGGREGATE SUM for timestamp scores so duplicate members get summed timestamps. WHY: Re-ingested/merged payload present in both dest and source gets score ~2x timestamp, corrupting eviction order and future reads; use AGGREGATE MAX/MIN.
outros: ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, so duplicate payload in both inputs gets summed score instead of timestamp. Add AGGREGATE MAX to both ZUNIONSTORE calls to preserve ordering invariant for zpopmin trim.

goldens.comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

optimize-spans-buffer-insertion-with-evi.prTitle: Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert
